Technology Ethics: CAT Study Guide

22 sections, 180 questions with model answers, 379 flashcards, about 14 h 35 min of reading.

1. Read a section

Each section lists its source slides and a reading time. The notes replace the slides, so you should not need the PDFs.

2. Try the question first

Questions sit where the topic is taught. Click one to open the model answer. Write your own answer before you look.

3. Learn the marker words

The yellow-highlighted phrases are the wording to reproduce. Each major topic ends with a Marker words box and a recall drill.

4. Cards, then tick it off

Flashcards cover definitions and lists only. Tick the section as done; the planner on the right keeps your hours honest.

How the marker words work

Your lecturer is looking for particular word combinations in a definition, and particular vocabulary in an explanation. Everything else is filler to a marker. Each Marker words box has three parts:

  • Say it like this. A definition or one-line answer built from the slides' own wording. Reproduce the highlighted phrases exactly.
  • Vocabulary to weave in. Phrases to drop into your explanations and discussions. Each has a tag: Must means it is in the slides and has also appeared in a past question or a past-paper solution; Should means it is in the slides only.
  • Recall drill. Write the definition from memory on paper, then click the blanks to check which markers you hit. Aim to hit all of them before you move on.

Rule of thumb. In a definition, hit every highlighted phrase in the same order. In an explanation, spread the vocabulary phrases across your points, one or two per point, each followed by a short reason or an example.

Source of the keywords. The slides are the authority. The past-paper solution files are unofficial, so they are used only as a second signal for the Must tag and for the shape of an answer. Where they disagree with the slides, the section says so.

Part 1

Ethics and ethical theories

2 sections, about 1 h 45 min of reading.

What ethics is, Kantianism and utilitarianism

~1 h 05 min to readHigh priority16 questions

Source: Set 1, slides 1-20 (Introduction to Ethics, after Baase, A Gift of Fire, and Quinn, Ethics for the Information Age). Relativism, egoism, social contract and divine command theory are in the next section.

How to use this section. Ethics theory is the most keyword-heavy part of the course. For each theory you need three things: the definition in slide wording, the arguments for and against in slide wording, and one worked example. Each topic ends with a "say it like this" sentence and a cloze drill. Learn those sentences word for word.

What is ethics?

The slides open with the course title: Introduction to Ethics. The sources are two textbooks, Baase (A Gift of Fire) and Quinn (Ethics for the Information Age). You can cite them as the course texts.

The slide definition is short. Ethics is a branch of philosophy that studies principles relating to "right" and "wrong". Because it is a branch of philosophy, it works by argument and reasoning, not by experiment or measurement.

Ethics tries to answer four questions. Know all four, because they show what the subject covers:

  1. "What do people think is right?" This is a descriptive question: it asks what people actually believe.
  2. "What does 'do the right thing' mean?" This asks for the meaning of the phrase itself.
  3. "How should people act?" This is a prescriptive question: it asks what people ought to do.
  4. "What rules or laws should we have?" This links ethics to law and policy.

The goal of ethics

The slide gives the goal in one line: to help people to make moral decisions. Two further points qualify it.

  • Ethics assumes that people are rational and free to choose how they will act. If a person could not reason, or could not choose, it would make no sense to hold them to ethical standards. A falling rock is not unethical; a free, thinking engineer who ignores a safety defect can be.
  • Ethics can be used to describe how people do act, or how people should act. The first use is descriptive (what is). The second is normative or prescriptive (what ought to be). Exam questions usually care about the second.

Ethics, morals, values and law

Past papers (2017 Q1 and 2016 Q1) ask you to define and distinguish these terms. The slides give only the definition of ethics. The rest below is built from the lecturer's solution files and general knowledge, so treat it as beyond the slides.

Exact wording. 2017 Q1: Give clear definitions of the following terms as they relate to the course Technology, Ethics & Human Rights: Ethics (2 marks), Morals (2 marks), Values (2 marks), Law (2 marks), Utilitarianism (4 marks), Deontology (4 marks), Teleology (4 marks), Consequentialist theory (5 marks). 2016 Q1 (12 marks): Differentiate between the following: a. Values and Morals, b. Ethics and Morality, c. Profession and Occupation, d. Ethics of teleology and deontology.

TermMeaning
EthicsA branch of philosophy that studies principles relating to right and wrong. Also used for the rules a group or profession sets for itself (professional ethics, medical ethics).
Morals (morality)Principles of right and wrong behaviour that are generally accepted by society, shaped by religion, culture and personal belief. beyond the slides
ValuesThe beliefs and standards that an individual or a society considers important or desirable. They are general and wide. beyond the slides
LawRules of conduct made by a government and enforced by punishment. beyond the slides The full ethics versus law comparison is in section 6.

Ethics versus morality. Ethics is the study of, and reasoning about, right and wrong, and it is applied to a particular context such as a profession. Morality is the actual personal or social conduct and belief about right and wrong. In short: morality is the practice, ethics is the study of the practice.

Values versus morals. Values are broad: anything a person prizes, such as honesty, wealth, loyalty or comfort. Morals are narrower: they are the values that are turned into rules about right and wrong conduct. Every moral rests on a value, but not every value is a moral.

2017 Q1 · 2 marks eachGive clear definitions of the following terms as they relate to the course Technology, Ethics and Human Rights: (i) Ethics (ii) Morals (iii) Values (iv) Law.

Ethics is a branch of philosophy that studies principles relating to right and wrong. Its goal is to help people make moral decisions.

Morals are principles of right and wrong behaviour that are generally accepted by society, shaped by religion, culture and personal belief.

Values are the beliefs and standards that a person or society considers important or desirable, such as honesty and fairness.

Law is a system of rules made by the state, enforced by penalties, which all citizens must obey.

2016 Q1a, b · CAT 2021-22 Q1.1, 1.2Differentiate between the following: (a) Values and morals. (b) Ethics and morality.

(a) Values and morals.

  • Values are the beliefs and principles an individual or society considers important. They are general and cover a wide range of beliefs, for example honesty, wealth or loyalty.
  • Morals are principles of right and wrong behaviour based on personal belief, religion, society or culture. They are specific and focus on actions, for example "do not steal".

(b) Ethics and morality.

  • Ethics is a branch of philosophy: the study of, and the principles governing, right and wrong within a context such as a profession or society.
  • Morality is the actual differentiation between right and wrong behaviour held by a person or society, influenced by personal belief, culture and religion.
  • Ethics is the application of moral principles to specific situations. Morality is the broader sense of right and wrong that those principles come from.
2014/15 Q4a · 2011/12 Q1a · 2 marks each, 8 marksDefine the following terms: (i) Virtue (ii) Conscience (iii) Ethical dilemma (iv) Intrinsic good.

beyond the slides These four terms are not defined in the slides. Learn these wordings.

(i) Virtue is a good, settled quality of character that disposes a person to act rightly, for example honesty, courage, justice or integrity. The four classical (cardinal) virtues are prudence, justice, fortitude (courage) and temperance.

(ii) Conscience is a person's inner sense or faculty of judging whether an act is right or wrong. It warns before an act and produces guilt or peace afterwards.

(iii) Ethical dilemma is a situation in which a person must choose between two or more conflicting courses of action, each backed by a moral reason, so that choosing one means failing the other. Full treatment and the steps to resolve one are in section 6.

(iv) Intrinsic good is something good in itself, for its own sake, and not only as a means to something else. Examples: happiness, health, knowledge. Money is an instrumental good: it is good only for what it buys.

CAT 1 2015 Q1a-c · 5, 2 and 3 marks (scan order unclear)(a) Of what value is the study of the human person in Ethics? (b) Distinguish between human acts and acts of man. (c) Of what value is this distinction in Ethics?

beyond the slides The question is from the philosophy side of the course. Link it to slide 3: ethics assumes that people are rational and free to choose how they act.

(a) Value of studying the human person. Ethics judges the conduct of persons. Only a being that can reason and choose freely can be held responsible, so we must understand what a person is (rational, free, able to know right from wrong) before we can say what makes an act good or bad.

(b) Human acts and acts of man.

  • A human act is done knowingly and freely: the person understands what they do and chooses to do it (voluntary and deliberate). Examples: signing off a test report, choosing to report a defect.
  • An act of man happens in a person without knowledge or free choice. Examples: digestion, a reflex, a heartbeat, sleepwalking.

(c) Value of the distinction. Only human acts can be morally assessed: praised, blamed or punished. Acts of man are neither right nor wrong. The distinction also shows when responsibility is reduced, for example when a person acts under ignorance, force or fear, so the act is less than fully free.

Why study ethics? Negative and positive arguments

Slides 4 and 5 are a debate. First come the arguments that studying ethics is pointless (introduced by "But ..."). Then come the replies. Know both sides, because an exam question can ask you to justify the study of ethics.

Negative arguments (against studying ethics)

  • There are no universal norms of right and wrong. Nothing is right or wrong for everyone everywhere.
  • Ethical debates are disagreeable and pointless. The slide gives the reasons behind this:
    • We are all well-meaning and intelligent people, so why argue?
    • Each person may decide right and wrong for himself or herself: "What's right for you may not be right for me."
    • We can disagree on moral issues, and that is the end of it.

This view is what the later theories of subjective and cultural relativism formalise (see relativism).

Positive arguments (why we should study ethics)

  • Not everyone can do what they want. We must respect other people and their values. Living with others limits our freedom.
  • "Common wisdom" is not always adequate. What we picked up from family and friends may fail in new situations. We need to be prepared to face future ethical decisions, for example the new problems technology keeps creating.
  • Everybody shares the "core values" of life. This answers the claim that there are no universal norms. People disagree on many details but agree on basics such as not killing, not stealing and being honest.
  • Ethics provides bases to make the best rational decisions. It gives you reasons you can defend, not just feelings.

Key point. Each positive argument answers a negative one. "No universal norms" is answered by "everybody shares core values". "Each person decides for themselves" is answered by "not everyone can do what they want; we must respect others". "Debate is pointless" is answered by "ethics gives bases for rational decisions".

Practice · 4 marksSome people say that studying ethics is pointless because right and wrong are personal opinions. Give two arguments against this view.
  • Everybody shares core values. People across cultures agree on basics such as not killing and not stealing, so right and wrong are not purely personal.
  • Not everyone can do what they want. We must respect other people and their values, so personal opinion cannot be the only rule. In engineering, a personal opinion that a safety test is optional could kill people.

A further point: ethics provides bases to make the best rational decisions and prepares us for future ethical decisions where common wisdom is inadequate.

Ethical theories and Laudon's three questions, six answers

Ethical theory is not new. There are approximately 2,000 years of organized literature concerned with ethics, and many famous philosophers have contributed: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Kant, and others. With so many theories, Kenneth Laudon (1995) sorted them by asking three questions, each with two answers: "three questions, six answers". Any given theory can be placed by saying how it answers each question.

QuestionAnswer 1Answer 2
1. What is "goodness"?PhenomenologistPositivist
2. What does acting ethically mean?DeontologistTeleologist
3. What is the scope of morality?CollectivistIndividualist

Question one: what is "goodness"?

  • Answer 1, the phenomenologist. Goodness is a higher order, and it is given. One must understand the abstract concepts of right and wrong and act accordingly. Goodness exists independently of us and we discover it.
  • Answer 2, the positivist. Goodness is whatever we make of it. We have to derive ethical principles for ourselves according to our observations of the real world. Goodness is built from experience.

Question two: what does acting ethically mean?

  • Answer 1, the deontologist. Acting ethically means respecting one's duties and obligations. Each single act is itself good or bad, regardless of its consequences.
  • Answer 2, the teleologist. Acting ethically means acting in such a way that the outcome is good. An act can be judged only by its consequences. No act is a priori good (no act is good before and apart from its results).

This is the pair that exams ask about most. Deontology looks at the act and the duty. Teleology looks at the result. The word "deontology" comes from the Greek deon, duty. "Teleology" comes from telos, end or goal. beyond the slides

Question three: what is the scope of morality?

  • Answer 1, the collectivist. Ethical standards make sense only if they equally apply to everyone.
  • Answer 2, the individualist. Nobody should be committed to accepting ethical standards. Individuals should set their own rules through self-analysis and reflection.

Teleology, deontology and consequentialism in exam language

Past papers ask for definitions of teleology, deontology, utilitarianism and "consequentialist theory". The slides define the first two inside Laudon's question two, and say utilitarianism is "a consequentialist theory". Use these definitions.

  • Deontology (duty ethics). Acting ethically means respecting one's duties and obligations. Each single act is itself good or bad, regardless of its consequences. Example: Kantianism.
  • Teleology. Acting ethically means acting so that the outcome is good. An act is judged only by its consequences. No act is a priori good.
  • Consequentialist theory. A theory that decides right and wrong by the consequences of an act. Teleological theories are consequentialist. Example: utilitarianism. The solution files treat "teleological" and "consequentialist" as the same family.

Typical problems of consequentialist theories (QB E1): the consequences are hard to predict and measure; they must all be put on one scale; and they can justify sacrificing a minority, so they may not respect individual rights. These match the criticisms of utilitarianism below.

QB E2 · 6 marks · 2016 Q1d · CAT 2021-22 Q1.4Characterize and distinguish between consequentialist ethical theories and deontological ethical theories. Give one example of each.

Consequentialist (teleological) theories hold that acting ethically means acting in such a way that the outcome is good. An act is judged only by its consequences; no act is a priori good. Example: utilitarianism, which calls an act right if it increases aggregate happiness.

Deontological theories hold that acting ethically means respecting one's duties and obligations. Each single act is itself good or bad, regardless of its consequences. Example: Kantianism, where a rule is right if it can be universally applied and treats people as ends.

The distinction.

  • Focus: consequentialism looks at the outcome; deontology looks at the act and the duty.
  • Lying to save a life: the consequentialist may allow it because the outcome is good. The deontologist forbids it because "do not lie" is a duty.
  • Weakness: consequentialism can sacrifice a minority. Deontology allows no exceptions to rules.
2017 Q1 · 4, 4, 4, 5 marksDefine: Utilitarianism (4 marks). Deontology (4 marks). Teleology (4 marks). Consequentialist theory (5 marks).

Utilitarianism is a consequentialist theory that decides whether an act or rule is right depending on whether it results in an increase of aggregate happiness (utility). Act utilitarianism judges the benefits of a single act. Rule utilitarianism judges the benefits of all actions that follow a rule.

Deontology is the view that acting ethically means respecting one's duties and obligations. Each act is good or bad in itself, regardless of consequences. Kantianism is the main example.

Teleology is the view that acting ethically means acting so that the outcome is good. An act is judged only by its consequences; no act is a priori good.

A consequentialist theory judges the rightness of an act by the consequences or outcome it produces, not by the act itself or the motive behind it. Utilitarianism is the standard example. Its main problems: all consequences must be aggregated on a single scale, and it may sacrifice individual rights for the majority.

QB E1 · 6 marksWhat is the defining characteristic of consequentialist theories in ethics? Identify at least two problems with consequentialist theories.

Defining characteristic. They judge an act only by its consequences. The act is right if the outcome is good, and no act is a priori good.

Problems.

  • Aggregating all consequences on a single scale: happiness, money, harm and life must be added up in one measure, and they are very hard to compare or predict.
  • Does not recognize or respect individual rights: a minority could be sacrificed for the greater happiness of the majority.
  • Consequences lie in the future and cannot be known with certainty, so the theory gives poor guidance when we must decide now. beyond the slides

The seven ethical systems on the slide.

Kantianism

Kantianism is attributed to Immanuel Kant (1724-1804). It is the standard example of a deontological theory.

  • It focuses on the rightness of moral rules ("good will"). What counts is acting from a good will, doing the right thing because it is right.
  • It disregards emotional feelings and consequences. How you feel, and what happens afterwards, do not decide whether the act was right.
  • It is founded on the view that all people are fundamentally rational beings, who can derive moral rules from the logic of the situation and act according to the rules.

Kant's criteria

To test a rule, ask two questions:

  1. Can the rule be universally applied to everyone? Imagine everybody followed it. If that is impossible or self-defeating, the rule is invalid. This is universalisation (the "universalizability" test).
  2. Does the rule treat people as ends, not means? People must be respected as persons with their own purposes. They must not be used only as tools to get what you want.

A rule must pass both tests to be a valid moral rule. These are two forms of what Kant called the categorical imperative. beyond the slides

Examples: valid and invalid rules

  • Valid rules: "Do not kill", "Do not lie", "Do not steal", "Follow the laws". Each can be applied to everyone without contradiction, and each respects people as ends.
  • An invalid rule: "Get this work done, whatever it takes." It fails because "whatever it takes" would allow lying, cutting safety corners or using colleagues as mere means to the deadline. It cannot be universalised and it treats people as means.

Worked example: promise-breaking

The slide asks: can a person in an extreme situation make a promise with the intention of breaking it later? Suppose someone is desperate for a loan and will only get it by promising to repay, though they know they will not. Follow the analysis step by step.

  1. Proposed rule: "I may make promises with the intention of later breaking them."
  2. Universalise the rule: "Everyone may make and break promises."
  3. Test it: If everyone did this, nobody would believe any promise. A promise only works if people believe it. So the rule would make promises unbelievable.
  4. Contradiction: This contradicts the person's own desire to have their promise believed. The lie works only because most people keep promises. A rule that destroys the thing it depends on cannot be a universal rule.
  5. Conclusion: The rule is flawed. The answer is "No."

Critiques of Kantianism

Arguments forArguments against
It is rational.It allows no exceptions to moral rules.
It produces universal moral guidelines.Sometimes no rule adequately characterizes an action.
It treats all persons as moral equals.There is no way to resolve a conflict between rules.

Examples revisited: the problems in action

  • Rule: "Do not kill." What if it is on a battlefield? A soldier, or a person defending their family, may have to kill. The rule allows no exception, so a strict Kantian is stuck. This is "no exceptions to moral rules".
  • Rule: "Do not lie." What if not lying will lead to bad consequences? Telling a murderer where his intended victim hides is a classic case. Kantianism ignores consequences, so it still says "do not lie". This also shows a conflict between rules: "do not lie" against "do not kill" or "protect life", with no way to rank them.

Watch out. Do not write that Kantianism "ignores people". It ignores consequences and feelings. It treats all persons as moral equals and as ends. Say "universal" and "ends, not means" every time.

QB E4 · 6 marks · 2018 Morality c"Kant's idea of universalization does not work in practice." Discuss.

Kant's idea. A rule is valid only if it can be universally applied to everyone and it treats people as ends, not means. We test a rule by asking what would happen if everyone followed it. Example: the rule "I may make promises intending to break them" is universalised as "everyone may make and break promises". That makes promises unbelievable, which contradicts the wish to be believed, so the rule fails.

Why it works. It is rational, produces universal moral guidelines and treats all persons as moral equals. It rejects "whatever it takes" reasoning and valid rules such as do not kill, lie or steal come out right.

Why it fails in practice.

  • It allows no exceptions to moral rules. "Do not kill" gives no answer on a battlefield.
  • Sometimes no rule adequately characterizes an action, so the test cannot be run. The same act can be described by several rules.
  • There is no way to resolve a conflict between rules. "Do not lie" and "protect life" collide when telling the truth endangers someone.
  • It disregards consequences: "do not lie" even when not lying will lead to bad consequences.

Conclusion. Universalisation is a strong test for clear cases such as promise-breaking, but real situations involve exceptions and competing duties. It works as a guide, not as a complete decision procedure, so the statement is partly true.

2018 Morality cHow relevant is Kant's universalizability principle today?

It remains relevant. It gives a quick, rational test: could everyone act on this rule? It is the reasoning behind the idea that rules must apply to everyone equally, as in laws, professional codes and fair competition. In engineering, the rule "skip the safety tests when a deadline is near" cannot be universalised, because if every engineer did it nobody could trust any product. It also requires that people be treated as ends, not means, which supports consumer safety and privacy.

Its limits are the lack of exceptions and no way to settle conflicts between rules, so today it is used together with other tests, such as the consequences of an act.

Kantianism, attributed to Immanuel Kant, is a deontological theory that focuses on the rightness of moral rules (good will) and disregards feelings and consequences. A rule is valid if it can be universally applied to everyone and treats people as ends, not means.

Kantianism: who and what does it focus on?
Attributed to Immanuel Kant (1724-1804). Focus on the rightness of moral rules ("good will"); disregard emotional feelings and consequences.
What is Kantianism founded on?
The view that all people are fundamentally rational beings, and can derive moral rules from the logic of the situation and act according to the rules.
Kant's two criteria.
Can the rule be universally applied to everyone? Does the rule treat people as ends, not means?
Arguments for Kantianism.

Valid rules and an invalid rule on the slide.
Valid: "Do not kill", "Do not lie", "Do not steal", "Follow the laws". Invalid: "Get this work done, whatever it takes."

Utilitarianism

Utilitarianism is a consequentialist theory. It decides whether an act or rule is "right" depending on whether it results in the increase of the aggregate "happiness" (or "utilities"). In plain words: add up the good and bad effects on everyone affected. The right choice is the one with the largest total good. The best-known founders are Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill. beyond the slides

Act and rule utilitarianism

  • Act utilitarianism: judging the benefits of a single act. Each act is weighed on its own.
  • Rule utilitarianism: judging the benefits of all actions that follow the rule. You ask what happens if everybody follows this rule, and choose the rule that gives the best total result.
Act utilitarianismRule utilitarianism
What is judgedA single actA rule, by all the actions that follow it
Question askedDoes this act raise total happiness?Would following this rule raise total happiness?
FlexibilityHigh; every case is newLower; rules give stability beyond the slides

Example 1: replacing a curvy highway

Problem. A state wants to replace a curvy stretch of highway with a straighter one. To build it, 150 houses would have to be removed, and some wildlife habitat would be destroyed.

Analysis. Add up the costs and the benefits.

  • Costs: $31 million. This covers compensation for the homeowners and for the wildlife habitat, plus the construction cost.
  • Benefits: $39 million in savings in driving costs.

Conclusion. Benefits exceed costs ($39 million against $31 million, a net gain of $8 million). It is a good action. Notice the method: turn everything, even homes and habitat, into a single money scale, and compare totals. That is what the later critique ("requires aggregating all consequences on a single scale") attacks.

Example 2: the Blaster worm and the Nachi worm

Background. In August 2003, the Blaster worm infected thousands of Windows computers. Soon after, someone wrote a "good" worm called Nachi. Nachi did four things:

  1. It took control of a vulnerable computer.
  2. It located and destroyed copies of Blaster.
  3. It downloaded a software patch to fix the security problem.
  4. It used the computer as a launching pad to try to "infect" other vulnerable PCs.

Proposed rule. "If I can write a helpful worm that removes a harmful worm from infected computers and shields them from future attacks, I should do so."

Evaluation. The slide tests the proposed rule: what happens if everyone who can write such a worm follows it?

  • Who would benefit: people who do not keep their systems updated. Their machines get cleaned and patched without effort.
  • Who would be harmed:
    • People who use networks, because the worm's spreading traffic slows and clogs them.
    • People whose computers are invaded by buggy anti-worms: an uninvited program may damage their systems.
    • System administrators, who must clean up and cope with the extra traffic and unplanned changes.

Conclusion. Harm outweighs benefits. The action is wrong. Even a helpful motive does not rescue the act, because utilitarianism judges by the total of consequences. If every programmer who thought their worm was good released it, networks would be flooded.

Critiques of utilitarianism

Arguments forArguments against
Focuses on practical "goodness".Requires aggregating all consequences on a single scale.
Comprehensive; can include exceptional situations.Does not recognize or respect individual rights. (A minority group could be sacrificed for the greater happiness of the majority.)

Explaining the criticisms.

  • Single scale. Happiness, lives, money, habitat and privacy are different kinds of things. To add them you must give each a number, and the numbers are arguable. How much is a house worth against a wildlife habitat? The highway example does this with dollars.
  • Individual rights. If the total is what counts, harming one person or a small group is acceptable whenever the majority gains more. The 150 families lose their homes, but the gain is larger overall. This is the main contrast with Kantianism, which treats every person as an end.
  • A third criticism often cited, which is not on the slides: the future consequences cannot be predicted reliably. beyond the slides
2016 Q5A · 4 marksIn your own words describe the central tenet of utilitarianism.

Utilitarianism is a consequentialist theory: an act or rule is right if it results in an increase of aggregate happiness (utility), and wrong if it does not. Right and wrong are decided only by the consequences, not by the act or the motive.

  • To decide, we add up the costs and benefits to everyone affected and choose the option with the greatest total benefit. In the highway example, benefits of $39 million exceeded costs of $31 million, so building is right.
  • Act utilitarianism judges a single act; rule utilitarianism judges all actions that follow a rule.
2016 Q5B · 6 marks · 2021-22 exam Q1dDescribe THREE frequently cited criticisms of utilitarian ethics. [Two drawbacks in the 2021-22 version.]
  1. It requires aggregating all consequences on a single scale. Different goods such as lives, money and habitat must be converted to one measure of utility, which is difficult and subjective. Different people value things differently.
  2. It does not recognize or respect individual rights. A minority group could be sacrificed for the greater happiness of the majority. In the highway example the 150 families lose their homes because the total benefit is larger.
  3. Consequences are hard to predict. We cannot know in advance every effect of an act, so the calculation rests on guesses. beyond the slides
2016 Q4A · 8 marks · CAT 2021-22 Q3b · [reconstructed from garbled scan]Construct two utilitarian-style arguments supporting, and two opposing, strong property rights over computer software.

A utilitarian-style argument weighs the total benefit and harm to everyone affected. The details of software ownership are in section 14.

Supporting strong property rights.

  • Incentive to innovate: if developers can profit from their creations, more good software will be written, and society gains. Total benefit rises.
  • Economic growth and jobs: protected software firms invest, hire and pay taxes, so overall welfare grows.

Opposing strong property rights.

  • Restricted access: high prices and strict control keep software away from the poor, schools and developing countries, so the total benefit of using it is lower.
  • Monopoly and reduced competition: owners can raise prices and block improvement by others, so consumers lose more than owners gain.
2018 Morality a, b(a) Define utilitarianism and absolutism and discuss the failings of each principle. (b) Utilitarianism is largely driven by the definition and measure of utility. Discuss the logic behind this evaluation criterion and explain how this might affect people.

(a) Utilitarianism. A consequentialist theory that decides whether an act or rule is right by whether it increases aggregate happiness (utility). Failings. It requires aggregating all consequences on a single scale, and it does not respect individual rights, so a minority may be sacrificed.

(a) Absolutism beyond the slides is the view that some acts are always right or always wrong, whatever the consequences, culture or circumstances, for example "do not lie" and "do not kill". Failings. It allows no exceptions to moral rules (a soldier in battle, lying to a murderer), and there is no way to resolve a conflict between rules. Kantianism is the standard absolutist example (see absolutism below).

Logic of utility (part b). Since the theory says the right act is the one that gives the most utility, everything depends on what utility means and how it is measured. The logic is that a common measure lets very different options be compared fairly and gives a clear answer. The effect on people is that whatever is easy to count (money, time saved) counts most, and values hard to count (a family's home, privacy, dignity) get undervalued. A group whose loss is small in total can be ignored, as the highway example shows.

Virtue ethics and absolutism beyond the slides

The slides teach two theory families, duty (Kant) and consequences (utilitarianism). Past papers (2017 Q4A, 2021-22 Q2A and Q4C) also ask for a third, virtue ethics, and 2018 asks for absolutism. They are examined, so learn them in compact form.

Exact wording. 2017 Q4A (6 marks): What would you advise Holger Hjortsvang, Max Blankenzee and Robert Bruder to do after the response by the managers? Apply two out of the following three ethical theories (deontological ethics, consequentialist ethics, and virtue ethics) to decide how to act. 2021-22 exam Q2A (marks not printed): Describe the differentiate theories associated with morality. 2021-22 exam Q4C (marks not printed): Explain four virtues relevant for an engineer doing tests like those James wished to undertake. What actions are supported by these virtues? 2018 Q5, Morality (a) (Q5 is 20 marks; part marks not printed): Define utilitarianism and absolutism and discuss the failings of each principle.

Virtue ethics

  • Founder. Associated with the Greek philosopher Aristotle.
  • Focus. The character of the moral agent, not rules (deontology) and not outcomes (consequentialism). It develops virtuous character traits such as courage, honesty, compassion, justice and integrity.
  • Guiding question. Not "what rule applies?" or "what gives the best total?" but "what would a good, responsible person do?" or "which option leads me to act as a responsible person?"
  • Example. A person who consistently acts with honesty and integrity is virtuous, whatever the particular outcome.
  • Weakness. It gives little concrete guidance when virtues conflict (honesty against loyalty), and different cultures prize different virtues.
2021-22 exam Q2A · 2017 Q4ADescribe the different theories associated with morality (deontological, consequentialist and virtue ethics).

Deontological ethics (Kant) holds that acting ethically means respecting one's duties and obligations. Acts are right or wrong in themselves, regardless of consequences. Example: lying is wrong because it breaks the duty of truthfulness, whatever follows.

Consequentialist ethics (utilitarianism) judges an act only by its consequences: the right act produces the most aggregate happiness (utility). Example: building the highway because benefits of $39 million exceed costs of $31 million.

Virtue ethics (Aristotle) focuses on the character of the moral agent and the cultivation of virtues such as courage, honesty and compassion, rather than on rules or consequences. Example: an engineer who habitually acts with honesty and integrity.

Absolutism

Absolutism is the view that some acts are always right or always wrong, whatever the consequences, culture or circumstances. Rules such as "do not kill", "do not lie" and "do not steal" admit no exceptions. Kantianism is the standard example, and absolutism is the opposite of relativism (section 2) and of consequentialism. Its failings, in slide wording for Kantianism: it allows no exceptions to moral rules, and there is no way to resolve a conflict between rules.

Define virtue.
A good, settled quality of character that disposes a person to act rightly (beyond the slides).
Define conscience.
A person's inner sense or faculty of judging whether an act is right or wrong (beyond the slides).
Define intrinsic good.
Something good in itself, for its own sake, not only as a means to something else (beyond the slides).
Define virtue ethics.
A theory that focuses on the character of the moral agent and the cultivation of virtues such as courage, honesty and compassion, rather than on rules or consequences.
Define absolutism.
The view that some acts are always right or always wrong, whatever the consequences or culture.
The four cardinal virtues.
Prudence, justice, fortitude (courage), temperance.
Human act versus act of man.
A human act is done knowingly and freely and can be morally assessed. An act of man (reflex, digestion) happens without knowledge or free choice and cannot.

Applying the theories: the FANX case (James)

This 2021-22 exam question (Q4; marks not printed in the solution file) tests the three theories on one case. Retold in full:

The case. James is an engineer at AERO, a maker of aero-engines. He is responsible for testing the company's new engine, the FANX, and is partway through crucial reliability tests. His boss Bill tells him to finish the test report within a week because an important potential customer is visiting next week and wants to see the first test reports. James refuses: he cannot finish in a week and needs more tests to understand the engine's reliability. Bill orders him to abandon the planned tests and write the report now, with more tests later. Bill adds that if James refuses, Eric will write it. James objects that Eric does not know the tests and cannot write a sound report. James then asks Eric, who agrees with Bill and will write it if asked.

2021-22 exam Q4 A-D(A) Suppose James the next day decides to follow Bill's order, finishing the report at once and abandoning the other tests. Can this choice be justified in utilitarian terms? Explain why or why not. (B) What should James do if he tries to apply Kant's categorical imperative to this situation? (C) Explain four virtues relevant for an engineer doing tests like those James wished to undertake. What actions are supported by these virtues? (D) Which moral framework (theory) is best suited to this moral problem? Justify your answer.

(A) Utilitarian view. Probably not. A utilitarian weighs the consequences for all stakeholders and chooses the option with the greatest aggregate happiness (utility). Following Bill gives short-term benefits: the deadline is met and a contract may be won. But skipping crucial tests risks an unreliable and unsafe engine: crashes, deaths, lawsuits, lost reputation and lost customers later. Those long-term harms to users, the company and the public are larger than the short-term gain, so harm outweighs benefits and the choice is not justified. (It would be justified only if the unfinished tests were shown to add no real risk, which James says is not the case.)

(B) Kant's categorical imperative. Act only on a rule you could will as a universal law. The rule "abandon crucial safety tests whenever a deadline or a boss demands it" cannot be universalised: if every engineer did so, no product could be trusted, which defeats the purpose of testing. It also treats the future users and the customer as means, not ends, because they are deceived about the engine's reliability. Kantianism puts duty and principle (honesty, integrity) above consequences, so James must do his duty to test thoroughly, report honestly and refuse to issue a report the tests do not support, even if this disobeys Bill.

(C) Four relevant virtues and the actions they support.

  • Integrity (honesty, adherence to moral principles): James refuses to compromise the reliability of the FANX and does not misreport results.
  • Diligence (careful, persistent effort): he completes all necessary tests meticulously to get accurate reliability data.
  • Prudence (sound judgment and caution): he weighs the risk of rushing and puts long-term safety before the deadline.
  • Professionalism (meeting the highest standards of the profession): he puts quality and thoroughness of testing before pleasing superiors.

(D) Best framework. Deontological (Kantian) ethics. The problem is a clash between an engineer's duty to ensure safe, reliable products and pressure from a superior and short-term gain. Deontology treats the duty as binding regardless of consequences, so James is supported in disobeying orders and accepting a missed deadline. Utilitarianism reaches the same verdict but relies on predicting future harm, which is uncertain, and virtue ethics describes the person James should be rather than telling him what to do in this dilemma. Whichever theory you choose, justify it.

Relativism, egoism, social contract and divine command

~40 min to readMedium priority9 questions

Source: Set 1, slides 21-37 (and slide 10 for the list of seven systems)

Slide 10 lists "a few ethical systems": Kantianism, utilitarianism, ethical egoism, subjective relativism, cultural relativism, social contract theory and divine command theory. Kantianism and utilitarianism are taught in section t01. This section covers the other five. Each system is taught the same way: the idea, the arguments for, the arguments against, then a marker block and cards.

The seven systems at a glance

Use this table to place each theory in one line. The five theories without a link are taught in full below the table. The two linked to t01 are included so you can compare all seven.

SystemCore ideaStrongest argument forStrongest argument against
Kantianism (t01)Right acts follow moral rules out of good will and duty, whatever the outcome.It is rational, produces universal moral guidelines and treats all persons as moral equals.Rules can conflict and it has no way to settle which duty wins.
Utilitarianism (t01)The right act increases the aggregate "happiness" (utilities).It focuses on practical "goodness" and is comprehensive: it can include exceptional situations.It can justify harming a minority and the consequences are hard to predict or measure.
Ethical egoismEach person should act out of long-term self-interest.Most people already act this way, and each person knows their own interest best.Some people gain power and abuse it, and many people do not act in their own long-term interest.
Subjective relativismEach person defines right and wrong: "if I think it is right, it is right".It gives everyone the right to define "goodness".It cannot tell "right" from "whatever I want", and we could never judge anyone else.
Cultural relativismRight and wrong depend on a society's actual moral guidelines, which vary by place and time.Different social contexts need different guidelines, and it is arrogant for one society to judge another.It gives no way out for cultures in conflict, and societies in fact share core values.
Social contractPeople accept rules, on condition others do too, to enjoy the benefits of social living, centred on natural rights.It is framed in the language of rights and stops self-interest turning into chaos.Rights can conflict, and it may be unjust to people who cannot follow the rules.
Divine commandGood acts are those aligned with the will of God, revealed in the holy books.God is all-good, all-knowing and all-powerful, so his authority is above any human system.There are many interpretations of God's word, and the holy books do not cover modern technology.

Subjective relativism

The idea (slide 21). There are no universal moral norms. Each person defines right and wrong independently. The slide's one-line summary is: "If I think it is right, then that makes it right." A thief who sincerely believes stealing from a rich man is fine is, on this view, right to steal. A second person who believes stealing is wrong is also right. Nobody is mistaken, because there is no standard outside each person's own opinion.

This theory is also called ethical subjectivism. A past paper (2021-22 exam, Q2C, marks not printed) asks: With the aid of examples define the following ethical concepts: 1. Ethical pluralism, 2. Ethical egoism, 3. Ethical relativism, 4. Ethical subjectivism. For this theory, define it with an example: moral judgments rest on individual feelings, attitudes or opinions and there are no objective moral truths.

Arguments for (slide 22).

  • It gives everyone a right to define "goodness".
  • It eliminates all further moral debate. If each person's view is right for them, there is nothing left to argue about.

Arguments against (slide 22).

  • There is no distinction between doing what is "right" and doing whatever you want.
  • We can never judge the acts of another person. Even a murderer's view of his own act would have to be accepted.
  • Ethics is not based on reason or principle. It becomes a matter of taste.

Key point. The strongest objection is the first: if "right" just means "what I want", then the word "right" adds nothing and ethics disappears.

Say it like this:

Subjective relativism: the idea.
There are no universal moral norms. Each person defines right/wrong independently. "If I think it is right, then that makes it right."
Two arguments for subjective relativism.

Three arguments against subjective relativism.

Cultural relativism

The idea (slide 23). What is "right" and "wrong" depends upon a society's actual moral guidelines. These guidelines vary from place to place and from time to time. A particular action may be right in one society at one time and wrong in another society or at another time. The difference from the previous theory is who decides: here it is the society, not the individual. Example: polygamy is accepted in some societies and condemned in others, and cultural relativism says each society's rule is right for that society.

Argument for (slide 24). Different social contexts demand different moral guidelines. It is arrogant for one society to judge another.

Arguments against (slide 24).

  • It does not explain how moral guidelines are determined. Who or what decides what a society's guideline is?
  • It provides no way out for cultures in conflict. If two societies disagree, each is right by its own standard, so there is nothing to settle the dispute.
  • Because many practices are acceptable does not mean any cultural practice is acceptable. Variety in morals does not prove that every practice is fine.
  • Societies do, in fact, share certain core values, for example a ban on murder, so the claim of total variety is exaggerated.

Watch out. Do not mix up the two relativisms. Subjective relativism: the individual decides. Cultural relativism: the society's actual guidelines decide. The 2021-22 solution file gave "ethical relativism" the definition that moral principles are relative to cultures, societies or individuals, with no universal standards.

Ethical egoism

The idea (slide 25). Each person acts out of self-interest. The slide names Ayn Rand, who wrote "Atlas Shrugged" and "The Fountainhead", as the best-known defender. The focus is your long-term best interest, not whatever you feel like today. Someone who lies and cheats for a quick gain damages his reputation and ends up worse off, so long-term self-interest does not mean grabbing everything now.

The slide then asks the awkward question: what keeps society from falling into anarchy, with everyone screwing everyone? The answer it gives is personal character traits. Under egoism these become important: reputation, trust, reliability, virtue and so on. Egoists keep their promises and deal fairly because other people will then deal with them in future.

Arguments for (slide 26).

  • Most people naturally act in their own self-interest.
  • Society as a whole benefits when each individual puts self-interest first. The slide's example is capitalism: the baker sells bread out of self-interest, not charity, and the town gets its bread.
  • Each individual knows what is in his or her best interest, so he or she should decide.

Arguments against (slide 27).

  • Many people do not act in their own long-term best interest (the slide says "Examples..." and leaves them to you: people who smoke, gamble, or take drugs for pleasure now). Other ethical systems might save us from ourselves.
  • Some people tend to gain power, and they use their power to get more power.
  • Some people are naturally "superior". The weaker people resent the successes of the strong, superior winners.

Key point. The anarchy question is the one examiners like. Answer: egoism is about long-term self-interest, so reputation, trust, reliability and virtue matter. These keep people dealing fairly even without rules.

2016 Q1B · 8 marksCompare and contrast ethical egoism and duty ethics as decision-making frameworks for engineers.

Ethical egoism. Individuals ought to act in their own self-interest, with the focus on their long-term best interest. An act is right if it benefits the person who does it. For an engineer, the decision test is "what is best for me and my career?" Its supporters say each individual knows what is in his best interest. Its weakness is that it can lead to selfishness and disregard for others. Some people gain power and abuse it, and a client or the public who depend on the engineer could be harmed.

Duty ethics (deontology). Actions are right or wrong in themselves, because they follow moral rules or duties, regardless of the consequences. It looks at intention (good will), not outcome. For an engineer the test is "what does my duty require?", for example to protect public safety even if it costs the firm. Its weakness is that it can be rigid, and duties can conflict (see Kantianism in t01).

Similarity. Both are action-guiding frameworks that tell the engineer what question to ask. (An egoism example, a manager choosing a supplier for a personal commission, is in the next question.)

Difference. Egoism judges an act by its outcome for oneself (it is teleological: consequences to the agent). Duty ethics judges the act by duty, regardless of consequences. Egoism puts self-interest first and measures an act by what it gains the agent; duty ethics puts duty and moral rules first and may demand sacrifice of self-interest. Egoism is outcome-for-me, duty ethics is rule-regardless-of-outcome. In engineering, duty ethics fits codes of ethics that bind the engineer to public safety; egoism fits badly, since a professional is trusted to put clients and the public above personal gain.

2021-22 exam, Q2C · define with an exampleWith the aid of examples define the following ethical concepts: ethical pluralism; ethical egoism; ethical relativism; ethical subjectivism. [reconstructed from OCR]

Ethical pluralism beyond the slides is the belief that there are multiple valid ethical principles that can guide moral decisions, and no single principle captures the full complexity of moral situations. Example: a doctor weighs beneficence (doing good) against respect for the patient's autonomy; both matter and they sometimes conflict.

Ethical egoism is the belief that individuals ought to act in their own self-interest and maximise their own well-being. Example: a manager who picks the supplier that gives him a personal commission, because it is good for him, would be justified under egoism.

Ethical relativism is the belief that moral principles are relative to a culture or society, with no universal standards. Example: polygamy is accepted in some societies and condemned in others, and each society's view is right for it.

Ethical subjectivism (subjective relativism) is the belief that moral judgments rest on individual feelings, attitudes or opinions and there are no objective moral truths. Example: "cheating on a test is fine because I think it is".

Social contract theory

The idea (slide 28). Individuals implicitly accept a "social contract", on the condition that others follow the rules as well. Nobody signs anything. You accept it by living in society and using its benefits.

  • Individuals act within a sphere of freedom, as long as the set of rules is respected.
  • The social contract rules are established simply to enable everyone the benefits of social living. They centre on respecting natural rights to life, liberty and property.
  • Everyone benefits when everyone bears the burden of following certain rules.

Kinds of rights (slide 29). According to John Locke (1632-1704) there are three natural rights: life, liberty and property. The slide gives two other classifications.

Kind of rightMeaningExample
Negative rights (liberties)The right to act without interference. Others only have to leave you alone.Free speech; the right to own property.
Positive rights (claim-rights)An obligation of some people to provide certain things for others.The right to health care or education, which someone must pay for.

Negative rights cost others nothing but restraint. Positive rights place a burden on others, so they can clash with someone else's negative rights. That is the source of the "conflicting rights" objection below and of the last discussion questions.

The example (slide 30): Bill's DVD stores. Bill owns a chain of DVD rental stores. He collects information about rentals from customers and sells customer profiles to direct marketing firms. Are Bill's actions wrong? The slide's method is to evaluate rights: Bill's rights versus the customers' rights versus the marketing firms' rights. The key question is who owns the information about the transaction.

beyond the slides A way to work the prompts: Bill can argue the information was created in his shop, on his records, so it is his property and he may sell it. Customers can argue it describes them and their private choices, so it belongs to them and they never agreed to its sale. The marketing firms' claim depends on whether the seller had the right to sell. The answer turns on who owns the data: if customers own it, Bill has broken the contract by taking their property; if the shop owns it, he has not.

Arguments for (slide 31).

  • It is framed in the language of rights.
  • Without common agreement, rational people may act out of self-interest.
  • It provides a clear analysis of certain government actions, for example "those who do not follow the rules will be punished".

Arguments against (slide 31).

  • The conflicting rights problem: one person's right can collide with another's, and the theory gives no way to rank them.
  • It may be unjust to people who are incapable of following the rules (not deliberately breaking them), such as young children or people with severe mental illness.
Set 1 slide 36-37 · discussionWhich of these should be considered legitimate positive rights by our society: a minimum standard of living; housing; health care; education (K-12 or higher); a paying job; two months of vacation each year? Give examples of conflicts between the positive rights of one person and the negative rights of another.

Positive vs negative rights. A negative right is the right to act without interference. A positive right is a claim-right: an obligation of some people to provide something for others.

Which are legitimate. This is a judgment question, so give a position and a reason. A defensible answer: basic health care and basic education are the strongest, because they are needed to use any other right and life itself depends on health. A minimum standard of living and housing follow if the state can afford them, since they protect the right to life, one of Locke's three natural rights. A guaranteed paying job and two months of paid vacation are the weakest: someone must be forced to pay or to hire, which interferes heavily with the employer's liberty and property.

Conflicts with negative rights. The right to health care for all is paid by taxes, which limit the taxpayer's right to keep his property. The right to housing can conflict with a landlord's right to use his own property as he chooses. The right to a paying job would force employers to hire, against their liberty. The right to education requires teachers to be paid from other people's money. In each case the conflicting rights problem arises and the society must choose which right gives way.

Divine command theory

The idea (slide 32). Good actions are those aligned with the will of God, and bad actions are those contrary to the will of God. God's will has been revealed to us, so we can use the holy books as moral decision-making guides: the Torah for Judaism, the Bible for Christianity and the Koran for Islam.

Arguments for (slide 33).

  • God is all-good, all-knowing and all-powerful. "We'd better do what he says!"
  • God's authority is higher than any human-made ethical system.

Arguments against (slide 34).

  • There are many different interpretations of God's word. Who is right?
  • We live in a multicultural, secular society, so not everyone accepts the same book or any book.
  • The holy books do not apply to modern technological issues. The Bible does not mention the Internet.
  • It is based on obedience and duty, not on reason.

Past paper: which theory underlies each file-sharing argument?

This question asks you to match a statement to a theory and to say why. For each statement, name the theory in your first line, then quote its key idea and tie it to the words of the statement.

2016 Q5C · 10 marksIdentify the ethical theory that underlies each of the following 5 arguments for or against unauthorized online file-sharing of music (Kazaa, Gnutella, etc.), and say why. (I) I don't have any problem with downloading per se, but am afraid it will cut into the money going to the artists, and eventually will hurt the quality of the music available. So people shouldn't do it. (II) The problem with downloading is, what would happen if everybody did it? Then the artists wouldn't make any money, and I think that's wrong. So I don't think anybody should do it. (III) It's okay for people to download music if it's from a big label or a big group, because they have lots of money anyway. I try never to download from local artists and real independents though, because they're already struggling as it is. (IV) People shouldn't download music because it's a form of stealing, and stealing is just wrong. (V) I think everybody should download music. It's the only way to break the monopoly of the record companies. Then maybe it would be a more democratic market for music again. [reconstructed from garbled scan]

I. Utilitarianism. The speaker judges the act by its consequences: less money for artists and worse music in future. Downloading itself is not condemned; the harm it causes is. This is the consequentialist test of the greatest good for the greatest number (see t01).

II. Kantianism. "What would happen if everybody did it?" is the universalization test: could the rule "download without paying" be a universal law? If everyone did it, artists would earn nothing and the practice would destroy itself, so the maxim cannot be willed as a universal law (see t01). The wrongness comes from the rule failing, not from counting the harm. (The same wording could be read as rule utilitarianism, which asks what happens if everybody follows a rule; Kantianism is the safer first answer because the question is about universalising.)

III. Utilitarianism (act-by-act weighing of harm). The speaker weighs who is hurt: a rich label loses little, a struggling independent loses a lot, so the harm and benefit to each party decides the act. The weighing of the effect on different parties is consequence-based. [This statement is the least clear-cut; an examiner might also accept a fairness reading. Say why you chose utilitarianism.]

IV. Kantianism. "Stealing is just wrong" is a fixed rule applied regardless of consequences. Slide 12 lists "Do not steal" as a valid Kantian rule: it can be universally applied to everyone and respects owners as ends, not means (see t01). If the lecturer wants a rights reading, social contract theory also fits: stealing violates the natural right to property. State one theory first and mention the other in a line.

V. Utilitarianism (greater good). The speaker wants everyone to download because breaking the record companies' monopoly would produce a more democratic market, a better outcome for the many. The act is justified by its good consequences for most people. [If your lecturer reads this as a claim against an unfair arrangement of rights, social contract is the alternative; justify your pick.]

Watch out. The slides do not match these statements to theories, so statements III to V are interpretation. Marks go for naming a theory and quoting its slide wording. The safe pattern in the exam: name the theory, quote its slide wording, link one phrase from the statement. I and II are clear: consequences, then universalization.

Set 1 discussion questions (slides 35-37)

The slides end with five discussion questions. They have no single correct answer, so the answers below show the shape of a good one: a clear position, a reason, and an example. Slides 36 and 37 (positive rights and their conflicts with negative rights) are answered inside the social contract section above.

Set 1 slide 35What are some examples of contemporary technology issues for which our society's moral guidelines seem to be nonexistent or unclear?

Moral guidelines lag behind technology. beyond the slides Examples: deepfakes and AI-generated images of real people; facial recognition in public places; selling or mining personal data collected by apps; mobile-money loan apps that shame borrowers by messaging their contacts; AI tools used to write assignments; self-driving vehicles and who is responsible for a crash. In each case people have not yet agreed on what is acceptable, and the law has not caught up, so engineers need the ethical theories above to reason it through.

Set 1 slide 35(Ethical vs legal) Can you give examples where an action may be legal but unethical, or vice versa?

Legal but unethical. A company sells its customers' profiles to marketers in a country with no data law (this is Bill's DVD case). An employer legally keeps a worker on a poor wage because no minimum wage exists. A student tells a lie that causes no legal liability but breaks a friend's trust. An engineer who knows of a defect but is bound by no law to report it stays silent.

Ethical but illegal. A whistleblower leaks confidential documents to expose a safety hazard that endangers the public. A person breaks a traffic law to rush a dying patient to hospital. Civil disobedience against an unjust law.

Law sets the minimum standard enforced by punishment; ethics asks what is right, and so goes further. See t06 for the full law versus ethics answer.

Set 1 slide 35Do (or should) organizations have ethics? If so, who makes them? And who are affected: employees, customers, the society?

Yes. An organization is made of people and acts in society, so it should have ethics. They are made by the owners, board and top management, who set values and write a code of ethics; employees, professional bodies and sometimes regulators also shape them. Those affected are employees (fair treatment, safe conditions), customers (safe products, honest dealing, privacy) and society (pollution, jobs, public safety). Shareholders and suppliers are affected too. An organization with no ethics risks lawsuits, loss of trust and harm to the public (see t11 on codes of ethics).

Set 1 slide 36Which of the following should be considered legitimate positive rights by our society: minimum standard of living, housing, health care, education, a paying job, two months of vacation each year?

See the model answer under social contract theory above. Short form: health care and education are most defensible, minimum standard of living and housing follow where resources allow, and a guaranteed paying job and two months of paid vacation are weakest because they force others to pay or hire. State your position and give the reason.

Set 1 slide 37Give examples of conflicts between the positive rights of one person and the negative rights of another.

One person's positive right (a claim on others) needs resources that another person has a negative right to keep. Examples: the right to health care versus the taxpayer's right to his property; the right to housing versus the landlord's liberty to use or let his property as he chooses; the right to a job versus the employer's liberty to hire whom he wants; the right to education versus the property of those taxed to pay for it. This is the conflicting rights problem of social contract theory.

The seven ethical systems on slide 10.
Kantianism; utilitarianism; ethical egoism; subjective relativism; cultural relativism; social contract theory; divine command theory.
Part 2

Ethics in engineering

3 sections, about 1 h 30 min of reading.

Why ethics belongs in engineering

~25 min to readMedium priority3 questions

Source: Set 2, slides 1-24

What is meant by ethics, and the first clicker question

The lecture opens with a plain definition. Ethics is a system of moral principles. It is the set of principles of right and wrong. It is also the principles of conduct governing the behaviour of an individual or a group. Three phrases to remember: system of moral principles, principles of right and wrong, principles of conduct governing behaviour of an individual or a group. For the full treatment of ethics, morals, values and law, and the difference between them, go to section t01.

Clicker question 1. A person's behaviour is always ethical when one: A. does what is best for oneself; B. has good intentions, no matter how things turn out; C. does what is best for everyone; D. does what is legal.

  • A is ethical egoism. It ignores everyone else, so it cannot make behaviour always ethical.
  • B judges only the intention and ignores the outcome. This is the duty-based (deontological) view taken to an extreme.
  • C is the consequentialist, utilitarian idea of the greatest good for everyone affected. It is the closest to the lecture's way of thinking, because the lecture keeps stressing consequences for society.
  • D is wrong because law and morality are different things. An act can be legal and immoral. The lecture returns to this later (see section t06).

beyond the slides The slide does not print an answer. C is the usual intended answer, but no single one-line test makes behaviour "always" ethical. Treat the question as a warning: the other options are the traps (selfishness, intention only, legality only).

Where does ethics fit into an engineering course?

The lecturer asks the awkward question directly. Students have been studying design, analysis and performance measurement. So why is there a course on ethics? The answer comes in the next slides and it is the heart of this section: engineers build things that act on society, so their decisions carry moral weight.

Engineers build products. The slide lists cell phones, home appliances, heart valves, bridges and cars. In general, engineers advance society by building new technology.

Engineers develop processes. The examples are the process that converts salt water into fresh water and the process that recycles bottles. These processes change how we live and what we can accomplish.

Products and processes have consequences for society

The lecture gives four short "if" examples. Learn them, because they are the quickest evidence you can quote in an essay.

  • If a bridge has inadequate support, it will fail.
  • If a gas tank is positioned too close to the bumper, it might explode from a small accident.
  • If a medical instrument is not accurate, improper doses of medication can be given.
  • If a process for refining gas produces too many toxins, it harms the local community.

The pattern is the same each time. A technical choice leads to a consequence for people. The next slide states the principle: decisions made by engineers usually have serious consequences to people, often to multitudes of people. Therefore ethics and ethical reasoning guide decision-making.

Key point. The argument in one chain: engineers make products and processes; these have consequences for society, often for many people; so engineers' decisions need ethical reasoning to guide them.

Marker words: what ethics is and why consequences matter

Say it like this:

Ethics is a system of moral principles: the principles of right and wrong that govern the conduct of an individual or a group. Engineers' products and processes have serious consequences for society, so ethical reasoning guides decision-making.

Worked example: Fukushima and the ethics of nuclear power

The lecture uses one case to show ethical reasoning at work. On 11 March 2011 an earthquake of magnitude 8.9 struck near Sendai, Japan. It damaged the Fukushima I Nuclear Power Plant (Fukushima Dai-ichi). The damage led people worldwide to rethink the ethics of nuclear power. The slides then list the issues that come up in such discussions. Notice that the issues are not only about the reactor. They also cover the alternatives to nuclear power.

Issue 1: health and safety risks

The danger is to current and future generations from leakage of the radio-isotopes used in nuclear power. Plutonium-239 has a half-life of 24,110 years and is a particularly toxic radio-isotope. Normally, 10 half-lives must pass before a Pu-239 contaminated area is considered safe again. For plutonium that is roughly 250,000 years (10 x 24,110 = 241,100, rounded up). If plutonium leaked, say because of an earthquake, it would be a health risk for roughly 8000 generations. (The slide's figure implies about 30 years per generation.)

Two further considerations complicate this issue:

  • (a) Uncertainty. Medical science may discover a cure for cancer in the current or next centuries. That adds uncertainty to the long-term health risks of leakage.
  • (b) Possible benefit. Using nuclear power may increase our knowledge of the radio-isotopes used for medical purposes.

Issue 2: depletion of resources

This issue concerns the consequences of the alternatives to nuclear power. Fossil fuels (oil, natural gas and coal) are non-renewable. They also work against the goal of health because of their effect on pollution and climate change.

Issue 3: comparative economic costs of renewable sources

Renewable sources are hydro-electric power, wind power, solar power, geothermal heat, agricultural biomass and tides. They do not cause the environmental hazards that fossil fuels do. But they must be balanced against the energy needed to produce and maintain them, and against the environmental hazards that follow from that. The slide's example: at present, the energy needed to manufacture and install solar energy systems comes from fossil fuels.

The reasoning behind the issues: goals and means

The slide on reasoning explains what kind of thinking is going on. It involves certain goals: in this case health, safety and biodiversity. The reasoning then looks for the best, or at least a reasonably better, means of obtaining those goals. This type of reasoning is called practical reasoning. It uses different methods from mathematics and the sciences. Ethical reasoning is a type of practical reasoning that concerns certain societal or life-form goals, such as justice, equality, freedom, health and safety.

So the Fukushima discussion is a worked example of practical reasoning. Set it out as a table: fix the goals, list the possible means, test each means against the goals.

Means (energy source)Helps the goalsThreatens the goals
Nuclear powerDoes not burn fossil fuels; may add medical knowledge about radio-isotopesLeakage of Pu-239 is toxic for about 250,000 years (about 8000 generations); a cure for cancer is uncertain
Fossil fuels (oil, gas, coal)Existing supply of energyNon-renewable, so resources are depleted; pollution and climate change harm health
Renewables (hydro, wind, solar, geothermal, biomass, tides)No fossil-fuel type environmental hazardsEnergy and cost to build and maintain; solar systems are still made with fossil-fuel energy

Key point. No means is perfect. Practical reasoning does not prove one answer the way a mathematical proof does. It weighs the means against the goals and picks the best, or a reasonably better one. That weighing is what the lecturer calls ethical reasoning when the goals are societal ones such as health and safety.

The same example shows how the three issues connect. Issue 1 is about the risk of one means. Issues 2 and 3 are about the consequences of the alternatives. A good ethical argument looks at all of them, not at the reactor alone. For the wider environment material (pollution, fossil fuels, sustainable development) see section t22.

Marker words: practical reasoning and ethical reasoning

Say it like this:

Practical reasoning sets goals, such as health, safety and biodiversity, and then finds the best or a reasonably better means of obtaining them. Ethical reasoning is a type of practical reasoning concerned with societal goals such as justice, equality, freedom, health and safety.

Practical reasoning fixes   such as health, safety and biodiversity and then finds the best  . Ethical reasoning is a type of   concerned with   such as justice, equality, freedom, health and safety.

What is practical reasoning?
Reasoning that involves certain goals (here health, safety and biodiversity) and focuses on finding the best, or at least a reasonably better, means for obtaining them. It uses different methods from mathematics and the sciences.
What is ethical reasoning?
A type of practical reasoning that concerns certain societal or life-form goals, such as justice, equality, freedom, health and safety.
The three issues in the Fukushima discussion.
Issue 1: health and safety risks. Issue 2: depletion of resources. Issue 3: comparative economic costs of renewable sources.
The six renewable sources listed in the slides.
Hydro-electric power; wind power; solar power; geothermal heat; agricultural biomass; tides.
The three fossil fuels named in the slides.
Oil, natural gas and coal (non-renewable).

The essence of an engineering career, and social responsibility

The lecture now states why this matters to your career. Engineering is one of the most important professions in society. As engineers we do not just build things and develop processes. We build things and make processes in order to better society. To make society better we have to reflect constantly on the products and processes that we make.

Social responsibility is the first main connection between ethics and engineering. It comes from the impact that engineered products and processes have on society. Engineers have to think about designing, building and marketing products that benefit society. Social responsibility requires taking into consideration the needs of society.

Typical ethical issues that engineers encounter

Learn this list whole. The slide gives eleven items, the last being open-ended:

  • Safety
  • Acceptable risk
  • Compliance
  • Confidentiality
  • Environmental health
  • Data integrity
  • Conflict of interest
  • Honesty/dishonesty
  • Societal impact
  • Fairness
  • Accounting for uncertainty, etc.

Link them to cases: safety and acceptable risk are the subject of section t16; conflict of interest is in section t21.

Professional responsibility and the two dimensions of ethics in engineering

Ethics has a second connection with engineering. Being socially responsible puts duties and obligations on us individually. Ethics therefore also fits into engineering through professional responsibility.

Put the two connections together. The slide "Two dimensions of ethics in engineering" says ethics is part of engineering for two main reasons:

  1. Engineers need to be socially responsible when building products and processes for society.
  2. Social responsibility requires professional responsibility.

In short: the first dimension is about what engineering does to society; the second is about the personal duties that fall on the engineer because of it.

What ABET says

ABET is the US body that accredits engineering programmes. The slide quotes the outcome it requires: by graduation, students will have an understanding of professional and ethical responsibility. So ethics is not an add-on to an engineering degree. It is part of what an accredited degree must produce. beyond the slides ABET is the Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology. Your own university's accreditors set similar outcomes, which is why this course is examined.

What the course will discuss

The closing slide lists four coming topics: the code of ethics for engineers (section t11); practising ethics as an engineering student (section t05); how to identify and analyse ethical dilemmas through case analysis (t06 and t07); and specific examples of ethical situations you may encounter (t04 and t08). For what makes engineering a profession and what motivates engineers to practise well, see section t21.
