Exam questions on why ethics belongs in engineering

These two questions are the reason this section matters. The first is a 12-mark essay that has appeared in several papers. Note that one paper (QB) states it the other way round: "Ethics has a place in the practice of the engineering profession." Answer it the same way. The strategy is: take a position, give about six reasons, include the opposing view briefly, and rebut it. Motivation for engineers to behave ethically is covered in section t21.

2011 / 2013 / 2015 papers (also QB, reversed wording) · 12 marks"Ethics has no place in the practice of the engineering profession." Discuss this statement.

Position. I disagree with the statement. Ethics, the system of moral principles of right and wrong that governs the conduct of an individual or a group, is central to engineering practice.

1. Engineers' work has serious consequences for society. Engineers build products (bridges, cars, heart valves) and processes (water treatment, refining). A bridge with inadequate support fails; a process that produces too many toxins harms a community. These consequences often fall on multitudes of people, so decisions need ethical reasoning to guide them.

2. Social responsibility. Engineered products and processes have an impact on society. Engineers must design, build and market products that benefit society and take the needs of society into account.

3. Professional responsibility. Being socially responsible places duties and obligations on each engineer personally. Social responsibility requires professional responsibility.

4. Public safety comes first. The code of ethics requires engineers to hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public. Only ethics tells an engineer to put that above cost and deadlines.

5. Typical ethical issues arise in every branch. Safety, acceptable risk, confidentiality, conflict of interest, honesty, fairness and data integrity arise in civil, mechanical, electrical and software engineering alike. Technical skill alone does not resolve them.

6. Public trust and integrity. Without ethics the public cannot trust engineers, and the profession loses its standing. An engineer shows integrity by following the codes under the pressures of the role.

Opposing view and rebuttal. Someone may argue that engineering is purely technical, or that the law and employers' instructions are enough. But law sets only a minimum: something can be legal and immoral, and the law lags behind new technology. An employer's order does not remove the engineer's own professional responsibility. Cases such as Fukushima show that technical decisions always involve goals like health and safety, which is ethical reasoning.

Conclusion. Ethics has an essential place in engineering because engineers shape society and are personally responsible for doing so safely and honestly.

2017 Q3E · 5 marksExplain the need for ethics in the engineering profession.

1. Engineering decisions have serious consequences. Engineers' products and processes affect society, often multitudes of people, so decisions must be guided by ethical reasoning (a failed bridge, a toxic process).

2. Protect the public. Engineers must hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public. Ethics gives them the principle to act on when safety conflicts with cost or deadlines.

3. Social responsibility. Engineering exists to better society, which requires reflecting on the effect of what is built.

4. Professional responsibility. Being socially responsible creates duties and obligations for the individual engineer, including honesty, competence and avoiding conflict of interest.

5. Public trust. Ethical conduct builds trust and integrity in the profession, and ethics is a required outcome of accredited engineering education (ABET).

Set 2 slide 3-4 clicker · practiceA person's behaviour is always ethical when one: A. does what is best for oneself; B. has good intentions, no matter how things turn out; C. does what is best for everyone; D. does what is legal.

C is the best choice. It looks at the consequences for everyone affected, which fits the lecture's emphasis on the consequences of engineering for society. A is egoism, B ignores outcomes, and D confuses law with morality: an act can be legal and immoral.

The engineering code of ethics and its cases

~40 min to readHigh priority4 questions

Source: Set 2, slides 25-40 (Part 1: the Code of Ethics for Engineers), plus past-paper questions on competence, responsibility and cases

This section covers the first part of the engineering ethics lecture. It starts with role responsibilities, moves to the structure of the engineering code and its fundamental canons, works through the foreign-bolts and Larom cases, and ends with the point that ethics is practised, not memorised. The full canon lists, the functions of codes and their limitations are in section t11. The law versus morality grid (slides 41-43) is in section t06. Why ethics belongs in engineering at all is in section t03.

Role responsibilities (slides 26-27)

Ethics applies to your life in more than one way. The lecturer makes the distinction through role responsibilities. A role responsibility is a responsibility that attaches to us in virtue of a role that we have. Nobody has just one role. At any moment you may be an engineering student, a friend, a citizen and an employee, and each role carries its own duties.

Slide 27 gives five examples. Reproduce them as pairs of role and duty:

RoleRole responsibility
FriendLook out for the interests of your friend.
AthletePlay your sport in a professional manner.
EmployeePerform the duties of your job.
ParentLook after your children and their interests.
CitizenFollow the laws of the country in which you live.

The point of the table is that the engineer is one more role in the list. Being an engineer puts duties on you that a non-engineer does not have. The engineering code of ethics is the written statement of those duties. Compare this with the earlier argument in section t03: ethics comes into engineering through social responsibility, and social responsibility then becomes professional responsibility for each individual.

Key point. A role responsibility is a responsibility that attaches to a person because of a role they have. Different roles give different duties, and one person holds several roles at once. Roles can conflict, which is where dilemmas come from (see t06).

Define role responsibilities.
Responsibilities that attach to us in virtue of a role that we have. Each of us plays different roles in life.
The role responsibility of a friend, athlete, employee, parent and citizen.
Friend: look out for your friend's interests. Athlete: play your sport in a professional manner. Employee: perform the duties of your job. Parent: look after your children and their interests. Citizen: follow the laws of the country in which you live.

Ethics across the fields of engineering (slide 28)

There are many fields of engineering: civil, mechanical, electrical, software, industrial and others. The skills differ, but the ethical issues arise across all of them. A civil engineer who skimps on a bridge support, an electrical engineer who ignores a fault, and a software engineer who ships code known to be unsafe are all facing the same kind of choice: safety against cost, honesty against pressure.

Because of this, the code of ethics for engineers pertains to engineers of all kinds. One code serves every branch. That is why the canons are written in general words (public safety, competence, truthfulness) and not in terms of any one technology.

Why follow the code? (slide 29, clicker)

The slide asks: engineers should follow their professional code of ethics because...

  1. A. The public will trust engineers more if they know engineers have a code of ethics.
  2. B. It helps them avoid legal problems, such as getting sued.
  3. C. It provides a clear definition of what the public has a right to expect from responsible engineers.
  4. D. It raises the image of the profession and hence gets engineers more pay.

The slide does not print the answer. beyond the slides The best answer is C. A and D describe side effects (trust, image, pay) and B is self-protection. Those are selfish or incidental reasons. C is the real purpose: the code sets out, in clear terms, what the public may rightly expect of a responsible engineer. This matches the duty-based reasoning of the rest of the lecture, where engineers act because it is right, not because it pays. The functions of a code are listed in full in t11.

The three components of the code (slide 30)

The Engineering Code of Ethics has three components. Learn them as a trio, with the verb that the slide attaches to each:

ComponentWhat it does
The Fundamental CanonsArticulate the basic components of ethical engineering.
The Rules of PracticeClarify and specify in detail the fundamental canons of ethics in engineering.
Professional ObligationsElaborate the obligations that engineers have.

Think of it as three levels. The canons are the short, broad statements. The rules of practice take each canon and spell out what it means in specific situations. The professional obligations describe what engineers owe (to the public, employers, clients and the profession; see t09).

The NSPE fundamental canons (slide 31)

The slide gives the National Society of Professional Engineers canons. They all begin with the same stem: Engineers, in the fulfillment of their professional duties, shall:

  1. Hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public.
  2. Perform services only in areas of their competence.
  3. Issue public statements only in an objective and truthful manner.
  4. Act for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees.
  5. Avoid deceptive acts.
  6. Conduct themselves honorably, responsibly, ethically, and lawfully so as to enhance the honor, reputation, and usefulness of the profession.

Watch out. This is the six-canon NSPE list from the slide. Exam questions ask for seven canons from the Uganda (UIPE) or IEEE/ABET-style codes, and the wording differs slightly (for example, canon 1 in the UIPE version adds sustainable development). Use the exact seven-canon lists in section t11 when the question says "list seven".

Canon 1 is the top priority. beyond the slides The word paramount means this canon overrides the others when they conflict. Public safety comes before loyalty to an employer or client.

The principle of individual competence

This principle is canon 2: engineers shall perform services only in areas of their competence. It appears as a one-mark or three-mark question in several papers. Competence means having the education, training and experience needed to do the work safely. The slides tie it to student life too: to be competent you must actually know what you claim to know, which is why cheating undermines it (see t05).

CAT 1 2015 Q2a · 1 mark (also 2015 exam Q1a, 3 marks)State the principle of individual competence of an engineer.

The principle of individual competence states that an engineer shall perform services only in areas of their competence.

For a 3-mark version, add the reasoning beyond the slides: an engineer must have the education, training and experience for the task. If the work falls outside that, the engineer should decline it, or get help from a competent person, because incompetent work endangers the safety, health and welfare of the public. An engineer should also not sign or approve work he or she has not properly checked.

Try it yourself: the foreign bolts (slides 32-34)

The case. You are supervising a product whose specifications say that only U.S.-made parts may be used. Late in the project you discover that a sub-contractor has supplied a part with foreign-made bolts. They are not very noticeable and would function identically to U.S.-made bolts. Your customer urgently needs the finished product. What should you do?

The four options (clicker).

  1. A. Say nothing and deliver the product with the foreign bolts because the customer will not notice.
  2. B. Find some roughly equivalent violation of the contract or specs for which the customer is responsible, and tell them you will ignore their violation if they ignore yours.
  3. C. Tell the customer about the problem, and let them decide what you should do next.
  4. D. Find loopholes in the original specifications so that your company has not legally violated the specs.

The answer on the slide: C. Telling the customer is correct because it lets the customer decide what is in their best interest given new information. The slide admits this may be tough: your job may be on the line and your company's reputation may be at stake. It then names the two canons that justify the answer: avoid deceptive acts and act for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees.

Why the others fail, in marker language: A is a deceptive act by silence. B is a bargain that treats honesty as a trade and drags the customer into a cover-up. D is deception by technicality; it keeps the letter of the contract while betraying its purpose. Only C treats the customer as a person entitled to the facts. Note that the bolts function identically, so this case is not about safety. It is about honesty and the duty to a client, which is why it is a good example of canons 4 and 5 working without canon 1.

Important notes about the code (slide 35)

The slide makes four short points. Each is a possible short-answer or discussion statement.

  • It is not a legally binding document. The code is not a statute. Breaking it is not automatically a crime, although a professional body may discipline a member (t11 covers enforcement as a limitation). The law versus ethics contrast is in t06.
  • It is not something we want (or need) engineers to memorise. Reciting canons proves nothing.
  • It is something we want engineers to understand and be able to live by. The goal is conduct.
  • In the beginning, knowing the code is a guide to understanding how to apply it. A beginner needs the canons as a map, so you should know them until applying them becomes natural.

Watch out. The slide says memorising is not needed for real practice. It does not say you can skip learning the canons for the CAT. The exam asks you to list them, so learn them.

The Larom case (slides 36-38)

Setting. You were hired at Larom because of your promising research on catalysts as a student at SJSU. Your supervisor, Alex Smith, announces that your unit must make a recommendation within the next two days on which catalyst should be used in processing a major product.

The evidence. The overwhelming consensus of the engineers in your unit, based on many years of experience, is that catalyst A is best for the job. Your own research gives preliminary evidence that catalyst B might be more reliable, more efficient and considerably less costly.

The pressure. You ask whether the recommendation can be delayed a month to see if firmer evidence can be found. Alex asks you instead to write up the report leaving out the preliminary data about catalyst B. He says: "We've already taken too much time on this project. We have to be decisive, and we have to look decisive. Besides, we've had a lot of experience in this area."

Your position. You have no desire to challenge your colleagues. You do not necessarily disagree with them about which catalyst is best. But you wish you had been given more time to work on catalyst B, and you feel uncomfortable about leaving the preliminary data out of the report.

The task (slide 38). Discuss with a group: identify the issues, compare courses of action, identify the best course of action. One person reports out.

Worked analysis

beyond the slides The slides leave the answer open. Here is a model analysis in the template order (full template in t07).

Issues.

  • Honesty and deception. Omitting data that points the other way gives the readers a false picture. Canon: avoid deceptive acts; issue public statements only in an objective and truthful manner (applied to an internal report).
  • Duty to the employer. The company may spend money on a worse, costlier catalyst. Canon: faithful agents or trustees. Real loyalty means giving the employer the whole evidence.
  • Competence and uncertainty. The data is only preliminary, so it must not be overstated either. Being honest includes saying how firm the evidence is.
  • Pressure and conformity. Appearing decisive and relying on the experience of senior colleagues is not evidence.
  • Public safety and welfare. The case says catalyst B may be more reliable, which can matter for a process affecting a major product.

Courses of action.

  1. Write the report as ordered and leave the data out. Easy and obedient, but deceptive, and it breaks the canons above.
  2. Include the data, clearly labelled preliminary, and say it needs more testing. Honest and does not overclaim.
  3. Go to Alex first, explain the concern, and ask again for a short extension or for a line on catalyst B to be added.
  4. If Alex refuses, take it to a higher manager or the ethics channel, without making accusations.
  5. Refuse to write the report at all. Strong, but it gives up your chance to influence the outcome.

Best course. Combine 3 and 2, with 4 as a fallback. Talk to Alex first, propose adding the preliminary catalyst B results with an honest caveat about their limits, and keep the recommendation for A if that is what the evidence supports. Do not leave the data out. This respects Alex's need for a decision, keeps you honest, and gives the employer the facts. You do not have to say A is wrong. You only have to avoid hiding what you found.

The Atlanta Olympic stadium light tower

This is a classic "canon 1" case about public safety and communication.

2016 Q3C · 9 marksIn March 1995, the structural engineer for the Olympic Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia, discovered an error in his design of a steel light tower to be built as part of the stadium. He told the stadium's architect, sending along a sketch to repair the error. Supposing that work on the light tower was a month away, he treated the redesign as a routine change instead of an emergency order. In fact, construction was ahead of schedule and work on the light tower began ten days after he informed the architect of the error and the need for repair. The repairs had not been carried out by the time an ironworker fell fifty feet to his death when the canopy holding the lights broke. (i) What ethical issues, if any, does this incident raise? (ii) Is there anything the engineer should have done differently? Why? [reconstructed from garbled scan]

(i) Ethical issues.

  • Public safety, health and welfare: the first canon says to hold these paramount. A design error in a load-bearing structure endangers the workers on site and the public. A worker died.
  • Professional responsibility for one's own design: the engineer owned the error, so he owned the duty to see it fixed.
  • Negligence in communication: he treated an urgent safety repair as a routine change and so gave it the wrong priority.
  • Assuming instead of verifying: he assumed the work was a month away and did not check the construction schedule.
  • Lack of follow-up: after notifying the architect he did not confirm the repair was done before the work began.
  • Shared responsibility: the architect and the contractor also failed to act on the notice or to stop work, so responsibility is not his alone.

(ii) What he should have done. Yes. He should have:

  • marked the notice as an emergency, stated the danger in plain words and demanded that no work proceed on the tower until repaired;
  • checked the actual construction schedule instead of assuming it;
  • followed up in writing and in person to confirm receipt and the date of the repair;
  • if ignored, escalated to the project manager, the owner or the authorities, and recommended closing the area;
  • kept records of every notice.

Why: his duty is to hold the safety of the public paramount, and a notice that is not acted on has not discharged that duty. Competence means knowing the consequences of a structural error, so he should have recognised the urgency.

Two engineers, sealed bids

2015 Q3d · 7 marks (also 2011/12 paper)Two engineers submitted sealed bids to a prospective client for an engineering project. The client informed Engineer A of the amount that Engineer B had bid and invited Engineer A to resubmit a lower bid. Analyze this dilemma from the perspective of the client and Engineer A.

The dilemma. A sealed bid is meant to be secret and the same for everyone. The client has revealed one bidder's price to another, which turns a fair competition into price-shopping.

The client.

  • The client acted unfairly and broke confidentiality of Engineer B's bid. This is a deceptive act because B believes the bid is sealed.
  • The client may be trying to get the lowest cost, which is a legitimate aim, but the means (bid shopping) destroy trust and fair competition, and could lead to poor quality as bids are pushed down.
  • The client should have either kept bids sealed or opened the process to all bidders on equal terms.

Engineer A.

  • A must avoid deceptive acts and conduct himself honorably. Using B's secret price to undercut B benefits from a breach of fairness and could harm B.
  • A also owes the client faithful agent duties, and a lower price might genuinely serve the client.
  • A should decline to revise the bid on the basis of the leaked figure, and explain that a revised bid is acceptable only if every bidder, including B, is invited to resubmit on the same terms. A should also check that a lower price will not force him to cut safety or quality.
  • If the client insists, A can withdraw rather than take part in an unfair process.

Conclusion. The ethical course is for A to refuse to act on the leaked information and to insist on a fair process.

Personal versus organizational responsibility

beyond the slides Set 2 gives no definition for this pair, but it is a repeat question. Build the answer from the role-responsibility idea and general knowledge.

2015 Q1c · 8 marks (also 2011/12 paper)Distinguish between personal responsibility and organizational responsibility as far as morality is concerned.

Personal responsibility is the moral accountability of an individual for his or her own actions and their consequences. It rests on the person acting knowingly and freely. The individual is answerable, praised or blamed and cannot excuse a wrong act by saying "I was following orders". Example: the engineer who signs off a design he knows is unsafe.

Organizational responsibility is the moral accountability of a company or institution as a whole for the policies, structures and culture it creates and for the results of the group's decisions. It covers decisions taken collectively, safety systems, reward systems and whether employees can report concerns safely. Example: a firm that rewards speed over safety and punishes whistleblowers.

Differences.

PointPersonalOrganizational
BearerOne personThe company or body as a collective
BasisOwn intention, knowledge and choiceGroup decisions, policy and culture
RemedyIndividual blame, discipline, conscienceReform of policy, compensation, regulation

How they link. The two do not cancel out. Organizational responsibility does not remove personal responsibility, because each person must still obey the code. Equally, an organization must make it possible for individuals to act ethically. Note that engineers, like the Atlanta engineer above, remain personally accountable even where the architect and contractor share blame.

Four points about the code of ethics (slide 35).
It is not a legally binding document; we do not want (or need) engineers to memorize it; we want engineers to understand it and live by it; in the beginning, knowing the code is a guide to understanding how to apply it.

Ethics takes practice: knowledge versus behaviour (slide 39)

Unlike a robot, nobody can simply program you to be an ethical engineer who follows the codes. The slide makes three points.

  • No one can program you to follow the code.
  • It is possible to know the codes of ethics yet fail to follow them. Knowledge is not behaviour.
  • Ethical behaviour is about practice and virtue. It is about going beyond the codes and practising behaviour that leads to an ethical life.

This is the same idea as the note that the code need not be memorised: a person can recite all the canons and still lie in a report. What counts is the habit of acting well, and habits are built by practice.

The example of integrity (slide 40)

The slide uses an analogy from structures.

  • A building has structural integrity when it is designed so that it responds appropriately to the stresses and loads it is designed to carry.
  • A building can have poor integrity or good integrity, and so can a person.
  • A person has integrity when he or she can follow the codes he or she is supposed to follow under the stresses and loads of his or her role.

The loads on a person are things like the pressure to look decisive (Larom), the pressure of an urgent customer (bolts), or the fear of losing a job. A bridge that holds only on a calm day has no integrity; a person who follows the code only when it costs nothing has none either. The closing slide of the part (slide 58, which you will meet again in t05) says being ethical needs courage to do the right thing the situation calls for, and the integrity to withstand the pressures that push you in the wrong direction.

Key point. Integrity is the ability to follow the codes under pressure. Knowing the code is not enough. Courage and integrity are the practical side of ethics.

Marker words: knowledge, practice and integrity

Say it like this:

A person has integrity when he or she can follow the codes under the stresses and loads of his or her role, just as a building has structural integrity when it responds appropriately to the loads it is designed for.

Academic integrity and ethical conduct of research

~25 min to readMedium priority5 questions

Source: Set 2, slides 44-58; Set 3, slides 2-3. Research-misconduct material marked "beyond the slides" is added from general knowledge.

Students have a code of ethics too

Slide 44 opens "Part 2: Practicing ethics as an engineering student". The lecturer moves from the engineer's code of ethics to the student's own code. The idea is that you practise ethics now, as a student, so you are ready to practise it as an engineer.

The code used as the example is Senate Policy S07-2, the Academic Integrity Policy of San Jose State University (SJSU). It requires that each student:

  1. Knows the rules that preserve academic integrity and abides by them at all times. This includes learning and abiding by the rules for specific classes, exams and course assignments.
  2. Knows the consequences of violating the Academic Integrity Policy.
  3. Knows the appeal rights, and the procedures to be followed in the event of an appeal.
  4. Fosters academic integrity among peers.

Notice item 4. A student is not only asked to be honest personally. The student must also help others to be honest. This mirrors the engineering canons, where an engineer must also act against colleagues' unethical conduct.

The S07-2 preamble

The preamble gives the reason for the policy. In the slide's words:

  • The university emphasizes responsible citizenship and an awareness of the ethical choices inherent in human development.
  • Academic honesty and fairness foster ethical standards for all who depend upon the integrity of the university, its courses and its degrees.
  • University degrees are compromised and the public is defrauded if faculty members or students, knowingly or unwittingly, allow dishonest acts to be rewarded academically.

Two points to carry into an essay. First, the harm of cheating reaches beyond the cheater and the class: it reaches everyone who relies on the degree (employers, patients, the public). Second, even unwittingly allowing dishonesty to be rewarded is a failure. A lecturer or classmate who looks away shares in the damage.

Plagiarism and cheating: why competence is the issue

Slide 47 links cheating to the engineering codes of ethics. Its argument runs in four steps:

  1. Many components go into being a good engineering student.
  2. One of the most important, as reflected in the codes of ethics for engineers, is to be competent in your field. (Link to the principle of individual competence in the code of ethics section.)
  3. To be competent, you must actually know what you claim to know.
  4. Proving to others that you know what you are supposed to know requires certification through a degree.

So a degree is a public claim of competence. Cheating makes the claim false. That is why cheating is not a small school matter but an early breach of the same duty of competence you will owe as an engineer.

What students say: the statistics

Slide 48 gives three figures about how common cheating is:

  • 70% of American high school seniors admit to cheating on at least one test.
  • 95% of the students who said they cheated were never caught.
  • An average of 75% of college students report cheating sometime during their college career.

Use them to make the point that cheating is widespread and rarely punished, so the pressure to join in is real. That is exactly why the course ends the topic on courage and integrity (below). The figures are American; do not claim them for Uganda.

The four things S07-2 requires of each student.
1. Know the rules that preserve academic integrity and abide by them at all times. 2. Know the consequences of violating the policy. 3. Know the appeal rights and procedures. 4. Foster academic integrity among peers.
The three cheating statistics.
70% of American high school seniors admit to cheating on at least one test; 95% of those who cheated were never caught; an average of 75% of college students report cheating sometime in college.

Cheating defined, and the five SJSU types

Slide 49 gives the definition. At SJSU, cheating is the act of obtaining or attempting to obtain credit for academic work through the use of any dishonest, deceptive, or fraudulent means. Note "attempting": you do not have to succeed. Note "credit for academic work": the wrong is claiming a reward you did not earn.

SJSU defines five basic types of cheating. Each has its own slide, retold here.

TypeWhat the slide saysExample
1. CopyingCopying someone's work on a homework assignment, exam or paper. Submitting someone's work as your own.Copying a classmate's lab report.
2. Multiple submissionsSubmitting your own work from one class to another class, or submitting one piece of work to two distinct classes. A paper for one class is not a paper for another class.Handing in last semester's essay again for a new course.
3. Unauthorized sourcesUsing sources you are not allowed to use, as deemed by the instructor or the university as a whole.Solution manuals; a friend's text message with an exam answer.
4. Altering gradesAltering your grade in any way.Changing a C to a B+ on a marked paper.
5. Surrogate cheatingSomeone else does your homework, takes an exam for you, or writes your paper. Doing someone's work for them is also cheating.Paying someone to sit your exam or write your project.

Watch out. Plagiarism is not on the slide's list of five as a separate heading. It is a form of copying (submitting someone's work as your own). If asked about plagiarism, name it as copying and describe it that way.

Slides 49-56 · exam-style · 5 marksName and describe five types of cheating that a student can commit.

Cheating is obtaining or attempting to obtain credit for academic work through dishonest, deceptive or fraudulent means. Five types are:

  1. Copying: submitting someone else's work as your own, on homework, an exam or a paper.
  2. Multiple submissions: submitting work from one class to another, or one piece of work to two classes.
  3. Unauthorized sources: using sources the instructor or university forbids, such as solution manuals or an answer texted during an exam.
  4. Altering grades: changing a grade in any way, for example C to B+.
  5. Surrogate cheating: someone else does your homework, sits your exam or writes your paper.

Cheating versus teamwork, and free-riding

Slide 51 stops students from drawing the wrong conclusion. Working on a team for an assigned project is not cheating. Teamwork is important in engineering. But failing to do your assigned task on a team project is a form of cheating. It is called free-riding: benefiting from the work of others without doing any work of your own.

The slide's reason why free-riding is wrong is a universalization argument (compare Kant in the ethics foundations section): if everyone did it, nothing would get done. Say this when you explain it, because it is the justification the slide gives.

Why cheating is wrong

The slides give two separate harms.

1. It harms honest students (slide 50)

Cheating undermines the work of fellow students who are honest. When you cheat, all the students who did not cheat are penalized. They end up with lower grades, and as a consequence of lower grades they lose out on scholarships and recommendations. This works when marks are relative or ranked: a dishonest high score pushes honest scores down.

2. It undermines the credibility of the university and its degrees (slide 57)

If too many people cheat at the university, its degrees will not certify that its students are competent. So by cheating you not only hurt yourself, you also hurt others. This returns to the preamble: degrees are compromised and the public is defrauded.

3. Beyond the slides

beyond the slides A third argument is about the cheater. A cheater who graduates without the knowledge may later design something unsafe, which links to the engineer's duty to the public. A fourth is that cheating breaks the trust and honesty that make any profession work.

Key point. To "explain why cheating is wrong", give at least these: it penalizes honest students (lower grades, lost scholarships and recommendations); it undermines the credibility of the university and its degrees; it hurts the cheater as well as others; and, in a team, free-riding fails the "if everyone did it" test.

Ethics: courage and integrity

The last slide (58) says that, as the course will show more and more, being ethical requires two things:

  • Courage to do the right thing the situation calls for.
  • The integrity to withstand the pressures that push you in the wrong direction.

Knowing the rules is not enough. Given the statistics (95% never caught), the temptation is strong and the honest student needs these two qualities. They return later in whistleblowing and in cases such as the engineering code cases.

Marker words: student code, cheating and why it is wrong

Say it like this:

Cheating is the act of obtaining or attempting to obtain credit for academic work through any dishonest, deceptive, or fraudulent means. It is wrong because it undermines the credibility of the university and its degrees and penalizes honest students.

The hiring exercise and real cheating scandals

Set 3 opens with a review exercise from Lecture 1. You are an employer at a large multinational software firm. You advertise on Monster.com for software engineers to design a new product. Many applications arrive, but two stand out because of their internships and their communication skills in interviews.

  • Applicant 1 has almost all A grades, but comes from a university where several cheating scandals have been reported in the newspapers.
  • Applicant 2 has mostly B grades, but comes from a university well known for strictly enforcing integrity.

The question: who would you hire? The slide does not give the answer. It is designed to show that a degree is only as good as the integrity behind it.

Set 3 slide 2 · discussionYou must choose between an applicant with almost all A grades from a university with reported cheating scandals, and an applicant with mostly B grades from a university known for strictly enforcing integrity. Who would you hire, and why?

I would hire the second applicant (mostly B grades, strict-integrity university), on the assumption that the interviews and internships were equal.

  1. Credibility of the degree: where cheating is tolerated, the A grades no longer certify that the student is competent. At the strict university, the B grades can be trusted.
  2. Competence: the engineer must actually know what he claims to know. Because I cannot tell whether Applicant 1 earned the A grades, hiring him risks an incompetent engineer designing my product.
  3. Integrity: a firm needs engineers who will be honest in test results and reports. A graduate of an integrity-enforcing university is more likely to have those habits.
  4. Fairness to honest students: choosing on dishonest-looking grades rewards the cheating that penalizes honest students.

Caution: a university's reputation does not prove that this individual cheated, so I would check references and test his skills in interview rather than reject him unfairly.

Marker words: the hiring exercise

Say it like this:

Where cheating is tolerated, grades no longer certify that the student is competent, so I weigh the credibility of the degree and the applicant's integrity above the raw grade.

  • "Insider: UNC tolerated cheating", Charlotte Observer, 18 November 2012.
  • U.S. News strips George Washington University of its ranking for cheating, 15 November 2012.
  • Cheating scandal rocks Harvard University, NECN.com, 31 August 2012.

The ranking and tolerance cases show a university's credibility being lost, with consequences for every student who holds its degree. Note that the cheating here is not limited to students: staff and institutions cheat too. The Jenny case (cheating allowed at job exams) is worked in the dilemmas section.

Ethical conduct of research

beyond the slides The slides teach academic integrity through cheating and plagiarism. Exams ask a research version: "identify and explain three practices that violate ethical conduct of research". The same values apply (honesty, credit to others, accuracy) but to research and reports such as a final-year project. Practices to choose from:

  1. Plagiarism: presenting other people's words, data or ideas as your own, without quotation marks and citation. This is the slides' copying applied to a report.
  2. Fabrication: inventing data or results that were never collected.
  3. Falsification: changing, omitting or manipulating data, equipment or processes so the research does not truly represent what was found.
  4. Selective use of data: keeping only results that support your hypothesis and hiding the rest.
  5. Authorship abuse: leaving out people who contributed, listing people who did not (gift authorship), or claiming credit for a student's or colleague's work.
  6. Multiple or duplicate submission: publishing or submitting the same work twice as new (the slides' multiple submissions).
  7. Breach of participant rights: collecting data without informed consent or breaking confidentiality.

The first two or three are the safest to choose, since they connect directly to the slides' definition of cheating as dishonest, deceptive, or fraudulent means.

Past papers 2011-2015 · 6 marksIdentify and explain three (3) practices that violate ethical conduct of research.

Ethical research must be honest, accurate and give credit to the source. Three practices that violate it are:

  1. Plagiarism: using other authors' sentences, data or ideas as if they were one's own, without quotation marks or citations. It is a form of copying, which is cheating because it obtains credit through dishonest or deceptive means, and it steals the original author's credit.
  2. Fabrication: inventing data or results that were never collected, for example writing survey figures one did not gather. The findings are false and anyone relying on them, such as an engineer or a client, can be harmed.
  3. Falsification or selective use of data: altering data or hiding results that do not support the hypothesis. This misrepresents the findings and undermines the credibility of the researcher and of the institution.

Other practices are authorship abuse (crediting those who did no work, or omitting those who did) and duplicate submission of the same work.

The Mildred case

This case appears in the 2015, 2013/14 and 2011/12 papers with identical wording. The questions on it are: (i) Describe Mildred's ethical dilemma (2 marks); (ii) Is Mildred's final project report a product of ethical conduct of research? Justify (3 marks). Retold:

Mildred is a fourth-year undergraduate student in the Faculty of Technology (CEDAT) preparing her Final Year Project Report. Her project needs a survey among three mobile telephone service providers in Uganda. A few weeks before her final examinations she realizes she cannot get data from two of the three companies. She draws similar statistics from a report by the Uganda Communications Commission to fill the gap. To get her work ready for her supervisor, she then puts whole sentences and paragraphs, word for word, from several published papers and the internet into her report. She uses no quotation marks or footnotes to show the other authors consulted.

Reading the case

  • Pressure: time (only a few weeks left), missing data, and a supervisor waiting.
  • Substituted data: statistics from the UCC report were used in place of data she was meant to collect. Using them is not wrong by itself. Presenting them as results of her own survey, or not saying that two of the three companies were not surveyed, would be misrepresentation. The case does not say whether she disclosed it.
  • Plagiarism: verbatim sentences and paragraphs with no quotation marks or footnotes. This is copying (slide 52): submitting someone's work as your own.
  • Honest options she had: tell her supervisor early, narrow the project to the one company she could survey, state the limitation, cite the UCC report openly, and quote and reference every source.
Past papers 2015 / 2013-14 / 2011-12 · 2 marks(d)(i) Describe Mildred's ethical dilemma.

Mildred faces a conflict between academic honesty and the pressure to finish. She must choose between (a) reporting honestly to her supervisor that she could not get the data from two companies and acknowledging all sources, risking delay or a weaker project, and (b) filling the gap with other people's statistics and copied text so that her report is ready on time. Her duty of integrity and her wish to graduate pull in opposite directions.

Past papers 2015 / 2013-14 / 2011-12 · 3 marks(d)(ii) Is Mildred's final project report a product of ethical conduct of research? Justify.

No. The report is not a product of ethical conduct of research.

  1. Plagiarism: she copied whole sentences and paragraphs verbatim from published papers and the internet with no quotation marks or footnotes. This is copying, submitting someone's work as her own, which is cheating: obtaining credit through dishonest, deceptive means.
  2. Misrepresentation of data: she filled the gap with UCC statistics in place of the survey data she was meant to collect. Unless she states clearly that the data came from UCC and that two companies were not surveyed, the report presents second-hand data as her own findings. That is deception.
  3. Lost credibility: the report's findings and her degree can no longer be trusted as certifying that she is competent. She should have disclosed the problem to her supervisor and acknowledged every source.

Marker words: ethical conduct of research and plagiarism

Say it like this:

Plagiarism is submitting someone else's work as your own without quotation marks or citation. It violates ethical conduct of research because it is dishonest, so the report is not a product of ethical research.

Part 3

Law, dilemmas and case analysis

3 sections, about 2 h 30 min of reading.

Law versus ethics, and resolving ethical dilemmas

~40 min to readHigh priority11 questions

Source: Set 4, slides 2-10; Set 3, slides 4-12; Set 2, slides 41-43

The nature of ethics

Set 4 opens with its aims. The lecture sets out to teach the fundamental principles and canons of engineering ethics, to clarify the nature of ethics, to give a process for resolving ethical dilemmas, to cover the professional bodies' model rules of conduct and the code of ethics, and to use case studies so that you examine problems from a second-person perspective (you advise or judge someone else's choice). The first two of those aims are what this section covers. For the model rules and codes see t09 and t11.

The slide on the nature of ethics makes two statements.

  • Ethics is generally concerned with rules or guidelines for morals and/or socially approved conduct.
  • Ethical standards generally apply to conduct that can or does have a substantial effect on people's lives.

The second point matters for engineers. A badly chosen bolt or a hidden software flaw touches many lives, so engineering conduct falls squarely inside the field of ethics. Notice that the first statement says "morals and/or socially approved conduct". Ethics is not only private conscience (morals); it also covers what a group or society approves of. That is why professional codes count as ethical standards.

Fuller definitions of ethics, morals, values and law, and the theories, are in t01.

Law versus ethics

The slides (taken from a CSUN senior ethics lecture) set law and ethics side by side. Both guide conduct, but they work differently.

LawEthics
Creates rules to guide conductOffers guidance on conduct
Balances competing valuesAddresses situations in which competing values clash
Punishes conduct that is "illegal" through formal structures (courts, police, penalties)Incentives and disincentives may be created by a "group", formal or informal (a professional body, an employer, peers, society)

Read the table row by row and you have the answer to "what is the difference between ethics and law".

  • Source and form. Law is a set of rules made by an authority (the state). Ethics is guidance, not a command backed by the state.
  • Handling of values. Law tries to balance competing values and settle them into a rule. Ethics deals with the moment when those values clash and no rule has settled the matter.
  • Enforcement. Law punishes through formal structures: courts, fines, imprisonment. Ethics is enforced by groups, either formally (a professional body can discipline a member) or informally (loss of reputation, social disapproval). The rewards and penalties are incentives and disincentives, not sentences.

beyond the slides Other differences students usually add: law is written, public and applies to everyone in a territory, while ethics may be unwritten and differs between people and cultures; law often sets a minimum standard, ethics a higher one; and law can change by amendment while ethical convictions change slowly.

Key point. Law punishes illegal conduct through formal structures. Ethics offers guidance where competing values clash, and its incentives and disincentives come from a group, formal or informal.

QB E3 · 7 marksWhat is the difference between ethics and law?

Definitions. Law is a body of rules created to guide conduct, made by the state. Ethics is concerned with rules or guidelines for morals and socially approved conduct.

1. Purpose. Law creates rules to guide conduct; ethics only offers guidance on conduct.

2. Values. Law balances competing values and settles them in a rule. Ethics addresses situations in which competing values clash, for example loyalty to an employer against duty to the public.

3. Enforcement. Law punishes illegal conduct through formal structures such as courts and penalties. Ethics has incentives and disincentives created by a group, formal (a professional body) or informal (peer disapproval).

4. Coverage. The law does not address all ethical dilemmas, so something can be legal but unethical.

5. Conflict. Where the two conflict, legal standards must give way to ethical standards.

Example. Owning a slave before the American Civil War was legal but immoral; parking in a no-parking zone to help an injured person is illegal but moral.

Is "legal" the same as "ethical"?

The slides give both sides of the argument.

YES, legal is ethicalNO, legal is not the same as ethical
Law defines duties, rights and "allowable conduct".Law does not address all ethical dilemmas.
This is the compliance approach to business ethics: fulfil legally recognised duties, and do not go further.Legal duties may not meet the standard of ethical conduct.
This is the "beyond compliance" approach: fulfil legally recognised duties, but do not stop there.

The slide ends with the conclusion you should memorise: in case of conflicts, it is generally held that legal standards must give way to ethical standards.

A company on the compliance approach asks "Is it allowed?". A company on the beyond-compliance approach asks "Is it right?". An engineer who follows only the minimum the law demands can still harm people, for instance by meeting a legal emission limit while knowing a cheap fix would cut the harm further.

Watch out. Do not write that law and ethics are the same, or that they are unrelated. They overlap (murder is both illegal and unethical) but neither contains the other. Say that law does not cover everything and that ethics wins in a conflict.

Law versus morality: the four categories

Set 2 warns "don't confuse the two". It first asks a clicker question: which of the following ensure that behaviour is ethical? I. Following the law. II. Acting in the best interest of society. III. Following non-legal standards for socially appropriate conduct. The options are all of the above, II and III only, none of the above, or I only. The answer is II and III only beyond the slides (the slide prints the question only; the answer follows from the categories on the next slides). Following the law alone does not guarantee ethical conduct, but acting in society's best interest and following non-legal standards of socially appropriate conduct do.

Then it crosses legal/illegal with moral/immoral to get four categories and one example each.

CategoryExample from the slides
Legal and moralDesigning a system to be safe.
Legal and immoralOwning a slave before the American Civil War (slavery was lawful then).
Illegal and moralParking in a no-parking zone to come to the aid of an injured person.
Illegal and immoralKilling an innocent person.

The two off-diagonal cells prove law and morality are different things. A law can be immoral (slavery), and an illegal act can be the moral one (breaking a parking rule to save a life). When you need an example "where the two differ", use one of those two.

Set 2 clickerWhich of the following ensure that behaviour is ethical? I. Following the law. II. Acting in the best interest of society. III. Following non-legal standards for socially appropriate conduct.

II and III only. Acting in the best interest of society and following non-legal standards for socially appropriate conduct ensure ethical behaviour. Following the law alone does not, because legal duties may not meet the standard of ethical conduct (slavery was once legal).

2017 Q3D · 6 marks (also 2021-22 exam Q2B)Explain the difference between moral and legal responsibility (mention two points of difference). Illustrate your explanation with an example where the two differ.

Moral responsibility is the obligation to act according to ethical principles, based on conscience, personal values and socially approved conduct. Legal responsibility is the obligation to obey rules made by the state, defined as duties, rights and allowable conduct.

Point 1: enforcement. Legal responsibility is enforced through formal structures (courts) and breach is punished by penalties or sanctions. Moral responsibility is enforced only by incentives and disincentives from a group, formal or informal, and by conscience.

Point 2: coverage. The law does not address all ethical dilemmas, so moral responsibility reaches further than legal responsibility. Legal duties may not meet the standard of ethical conduct.

Example where they differ. Parking in a no-parking zone to help an injured person is illegal but moral. Owning a slave before the American Civil War was legal but immoral. Where they conflict, legal standards must give way to ethical standards.

Marker words: ethics versus law

Say it like this:

Law creates rules to guide conduct, balances competing values and punishes illegal conduct through formal structures. Ethics offers guidance on conduct and addresses situations in which competing values clash, with incentives and disincentives created by a group. Where they conflict, legal standards must give way to ethical standards.

Consider this: "You and Al"

This is the lecture's running example. You are the manager of Big-Mart, a large discount retailer. You recently fired Al, a sales clerk, after Al punched a customer during a dispute in the store. Al admitted it after the customer complained. A manager at a competitor, Mega-Mart, phones you. Al has applied for a job there, and the manager asks whether Al is "good with customers". The slide asks one thing: what do you do?

The later slide "Legal vs. Ethical: You and Al" turns this into a grid. Across the top are Legal and Illegal; down the side are Ethical and Unethical. Reading the slide:

LegalIllegal
Ethical?Tell the truth: "Al admitted to punching a customer."Contact another store, X-Mart, to warn about Al.
Unethical?"No comment."Say "He is great with customers."

The slide gives only these four example replies. Its row labels carry question marks ("Ethical?", "Unethical?"), so it invites class discussion rather than stating verdicts.

beyond the slides A likely reading of the grid: telling the truth about a fact Al himself admitted is lawful and honest. Warning a store that did not ask goes beyond the request, and a negative reference without proper basis can be open to a legal claim, even though the motive (protecting customers) is good. "No comment" is lawful because nothing false is said, but it may ignore a possible harm to Mega-Mart's customers. Saying "He is great with customers" is dishonest and could create liability for misrepresentation.

The point of the example is that there are several defensible answers, each protecting some value (honesty, fairness to Al, safety of customers, protection of your own firm) at the expense of another. That clash is what makes it a dilemma. Compare your own reply with the eight steps and the evaluation theories below.

beyond the slides The slides do not say how a reference should be handled. A reasonable approach is to stay with facts, state only what is documented, follow the company's reference policy and, if asked directly about conduct, avoid opinion while not hiding the incident.

Set 4 slide 6 · caseYou are the manager at Big-Mart. You fired Al, a sales clerk, after he punched a customer. A Mega-Mart manager phones and asks if Al is "good with customers". What do you do? Use the steps for resolving a dilemma.

Facts. Al punched a customer and admitted it; I fired him; Mega-Mart is asking for a reference.

Issues. Honesty against fairness to Al; safety of Mega-Mart's customers against Al's chance of a new job; my firm's legal exposure.

Primary stakeholders. Al, Mega-Mart and its customers, Big-Mart and me.

Possible solutions. (a) Say "no comment". (b) Say Al is great with customers. (c) Say truthfully that Al was dismissed after an incident with a customer. (d) Refer the caller to HR for a factual reference.

Evaluation. Under utilitarian theory (greatest good to the greatest number) truth protects many future customers. Under rights theory Al has a right to fair treatment and Mega-Mart's customers a right to safety. Under the categorical imperative, "what if everyone lied about dismissed staff?" shows option (b) fails. The front page test rules out (b) outright.

Decision. Option (d), or (c) if policy allows: a factual, documented statement with no opinion. Action. Do it, and record what was said.

What is an ethical dilemma?

Set 4 asks "An ethical dilemma?" and lists its features.

  • A choice has to be made.
  • It implicates competing values, rights and goals.
  • There is potential harm to the decision maker.
  • There is potential harm to others.
  • There is a "ripple effect": the decision has long-term, far-reaching implications.

Set 3 gives the classic definition: a dilemma is a problem offering two possibilities, neither of which is practically acceptable. Combine the two and you have a good answer: an ethical dilemma is a situation in which a choice must be made between options that implicate competing values, rights and goals, where each option carries potential harm to the decision maker or to others and may have a ripple effect.

Example in engineering terms: a manager tells you to approve a design that meets the budget but is not fully safe. Approving breaks your duty to the public; refusing risks your job and your colleagues' jobs. Neither is practically acceptable, and either choice has consequences beyond today. The slides' bridge and nuclear-reactor cases, covered in t07, are examples of the same thing.

CAT 2021-22 Q2d (also 2020-21 paper)Briefly describe how ethical dilemmas arise in the practice of the Engineering profession.

An ethical dilemma arises when a choice must be made between options that implicate competing values, rights and goals, so that either choice brings potential harm to the decision maker or to others. In engineering this happens in several ways.

1. Safety against cost. A manager or client wants a design that meets the budget and deadline but is not fully safe. Approving it breaks the duty to hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public; refusing risks the engineer's job (the bridge case in t07).

2. Loyalty against duty to the public. The engineer owes loyalty to the employer or client and also a duty to society, and the two clash when the employer wants a flaw hidden.

3. Truth against obedience. The engineer is asked to say or sign something untrue, as in the nuclear-reactor case where a public statement could be shaped by a government.

4. Conflict of interest. Personal or financial interests interfere with professional obligations, for example favouring a client over the public (t09).

5. Competing canons. The code itself can pull two ways at once, for example confidentiality to a client against the public's safety (t11).

beyond the slides The solution files add: conflicting priorities between deadlines, budget and client demands; environmental impact against development goals; and new technology that the law and codes have not caught up with.

Each case is a dilemma because the engineer cannot satisfy every value at once and the decision has a ripple effect on others.

The Pentium case and "going beyond the code"

Set 3 reviews the Pentium case from the previous lecture and asks three questions. The slides do not retell the case, so here it is.

beyond the slides In 1994 a mathematician found that Intel's Pentium processor sometimes gave slightly wrong answers in floating-point division. Intel had found the flaw itself and judged it so rare that it would affect almost nobody, and at first it said it would replace chips only for users who could prove they needed accuracy. Customers, the press and large buyers such as IBM reacted angrily, and the company's reputation suffered. Intel then offered to replace the chip for anyone who asked, at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars.

The three discussion questions and a way to answer each:

  1. What could Intel have done to satisfy customers and minimise negative publicity? Disclose the flaw promptly and honestly, say how rare it is and who is affected, and offer replacement or a fix up front rather than after public pressure.
  2. A warning such as "This product may contain unexpected flaws and might not operate correctly under all conditions". Does this solve the ethical problems for the company? The slide's clicker offers Yes, Sort of or No and says there is no right answer. The strongest reasoning is that it does not: a blanket warning is not honest disclosure of a known flaw, it shifts risk to the buyer, and it does not remove the duty to be truthful and protect users' interests.
  3. Was there really an ethical dilemma? If so, what was it? Yes: Intel's duty to be honest and to treat customers fairly against the cost of recalling and replacing every chip. Both options (hide the flaw, or pay for a full recall) were costly, and neither was practically acceptable. That is the definition of a dilemma on the slide.

Next the lecture moves "from codes to cases". The code of ethics for engineers gives a good set of guides to follow. But knowing what the codes say and knowing exactly what to do in a given situation is not always obvious. The primary reason is that really hard ethical situations require moral reasoning and conflict resolution. So the lecture starts with cases and practises a form of moral reasoning, which involves three things:

  • taking note of which codes of engineering ethics apply;
  • identifying conflicts;
  • making a choice of what to do.

All of this leads to a discussion of moral considerations and moral reasoning, which becomes the case-analysis method in t07.

Set 3 slides 6-7 · discussionA manufacturer prints in the product literature: "This product may contain unexpected flaws and might not operate correctly under all conditions." Does this solve the ethical problems for the company?

No. A blanket warning is not honest disclosure of a flaw the company already knows about, and it moves the risk onto the customer. Engineers must be objective and truthful and must safeguard public welfare. The company still has to tell users what the specific flaw is, how likely it is and what it will do about it (fix or replace). A general disclaimer protects the company's image, not the user, and users who learn of a hidden flaw will lose trust, as happened to Intel.

Set 3 slide 8 · PentiumWas there really an ethical dilemma in the Pentium case? If so, what was it?

Yes. A dilemma is a problem offering two possibilities, neither of which is practically acceptable. Intel could stay silent or play down the flaw and protect its profit and image, which is dishonest and unfair to customers, or disclose and replace every chip, which is honest but very costly. The competing values were honesty and customer welfare against company cost and reputation. The decision also had a ripple effect on trust in the whole company.

Define a dilemma (Set 3).
A problem offering two possibilities, neither of which is practically acceptable.
The five features of an ethical dilemma (Set 4).
A choice to be made; competing values, rights and goals; potential harm to the decision maker; potential harm to others; "ripple effect" (long-term, far-reaching implications).

Taking note of which codes of engineering ethics apply; identifying conflicts; making a choice of what to do.

How to resolve ethical dilemmas: the eight steps

Set 4 gives eight steps, in order. Learn them as a list and be able to explain each in a line.

  1. Identify relevant facts. Establish what actually happened and what is known, separating fact from assumption. Who, what, when, what has been agreed or promised.
  2. Identify relevant issue(s). Name the ethical issues and the conflict, such as safety against cost or loyalty against honesty.
  3. Identify primary stakeholders. List the people and groups affected by the decision (public, client, employer, colleagues, yourself).
  4. Identify possible solutions. List the realistic options, including a middle path.
  5. Evaluate each possible solution. Test every option against ethical theories and tests (next section).
  6. Compare and assess consequences. Weigh the likely outcomes, short and long term, for each stakeholder, including harm and the ripple effect.
  7. Decide on solution. Choose the best option and be able to justify it.
  8. Take action. Carry the decision out. A dilemma is not resolved until you act on the choice.

The steps run in a fixed sequence: understand (steps 1 to 3), generate and test options (4 to 6), then choose and act (7 and 8). In an exam, use the step names as headings. The full 7-step analysis template used for long cases is in t07.

How to evaluate solutions: five theories and tests

Step 5 asks you to evaluate each possible solution. Set 4 offers these lenses.

LensThe question it asks
Stakeholder / utilitarian theoryWhich option brings the greatest good to the greatest number?
Rights theoryWhich option respects and protects individual rights to fair and equal treatment, privacy, freedom to advance, and so on?
Justice theoryWhich option gives a fair distribution of benefits and burdens? Can harm to an individual be justifiable?
Categorical imperative"What if everyone took such action?"
"Front page test"What if my decision was reported on the front page of the number one daily newspaper (or on social media)?

The first four are theories; the front page test is a practical check on conscience and public reputation. If you would be ashamed to see the decision in the news, that is a warning. The categorical imperative is Kant's universalisation test (see t01).

The five ethical frameworks (Set 3)

Set 3 lists a different set of five approaches, each phrased as a question. These are the lenses to use in the Set 3 style of case analysis.

ApproachQuestion
Rights approachWhich option best respects the rights of all who have a stake?
Utilitarian approachWhich option will produce the most good and do the least harm?
Justice approachWhich option treats people as I want to be treated?
Ethic of care approachWhich option is best for those most in need?
Virtue approachWhich option leads me to act as a responsible person?

Comparing the two lists: rights, utilitarian and justice appear in both. Set 4 adds the categorical imperative and the front page test; Set 3 adds the ethic of care (look after those most in need) and the virtue approach (act as a responsible person). Note that Set 3 words justice as "treat people as I want to be treated", while Set 4 words it as fair distribution of benefits and burdens. Quote whichever slide you are answering from, or give both.

Key point. No single lens always gives the answer. Apply two or three, say where they agree, and decide. When the lenses disagree, explain which one you give priority to and why.

ethics-cat-1 Q3a · 2 marks; also asked as a 2-mark "define" in the 2011/12 and 2014/15 papersExplain with the aid of examples what you understand by the term ethical dilemma.

An ethical dilemma is a situation in which a choice must be made between options that involve competing values, rights and goals, where each option brings potential harm to the decision maker or to others, and neither is practically acceptable.

Example. An engineer is told to approve a bridge that meets the budget but may fail in an earthquake. Approving breaks the duty to protect public safety; refusing risks the engineer's job and colleagues' jobs. The same applies to the manager in "You and Al", who must choose between honesty about a sacked employee and fairness to him.

ethics-cat-1 Q3b · 6 marksBriefly describe the steps a given professional would take while attempting to resolve ethical dilemmas.

1. Identify relevant facts: establish what has happened and what is known.

2. Identify relevant issue(s): name the conflict of values, for example safety against cost.

3. Identify primary stakeholders: those affected, such as the public, client, employer and the professional.

4. Identify possible solutions: list the realistic options.

5. Evaluate each possible solution using theories: utilitarian (greatest good to the greatest number), rights, justice, the categorical imperative ("what if everyone took such action?") and the front page test.

6. Compare and assess consequences for each stakeholder, short and long term.

7. Decide on solution: choose the best option and justify it.

8. Take action: implement the decision.

CAT 2 2015 · 12 marksJenny recently completed her master's degree and was hired for her dream job with the local county government. In her first year she noticed that grant funds were being mismanaged and misallocated, and that coworkers used county-owned materials, including cars, for personal business. She was most shocked by the hiring practices. Applicants had to take exams proctored by government employees, and the results decided whether they were hired and for what. The proctors were letting applicants cheat because the applicants had already been chosen, many of them friends of current employees. Jenny reported this to Matt, the department's business manager and second-in-command, who said: "You heard nothing, you saw nothing; you say nothing." Jenny felt trapped. She needed the job to pay off graduate-school loans and loved the work. She also feared that leaving her first job in under a year would look bad and harm her future chances in government. But she was very uncomfortable in a culture of corruption. Describe Jenny's ethical dilemma and explain what she should do as a young professional in her circumstances.

Jenny's ethical dilemma

This is an ethical dilemma because a choice must be made between competing values: honesty and integrity, and her duty to the public who fund the county, against her own job security, her loan repayments and her career. Both obvious options are costly. If she stays silent she becomes complicit in corruption. If she reports it she risks retaliation or dismissal. There is potential harm to the decision maker (loss of job, bad record, loans) and potential harm to others (honest applicants denied jobs, taxpayers, the public). The decision has a ripple effect on her future career.

What she should do (steps)

Facts. Misallocated grants, personal use of county property, rigged exams. She has told her superior, who ordered silence.

Issues. Corruption and fraud, unfair hiring, a superior who is part of the cover-up, her own livelihood.

Stakeholders. Jenny, honest applicants, the department head, Matt, the county and taxpayers.

Options. (a) Stay silent. (b) Resign quietly. (c) Document the evidence and report it above Matt to the department head or the county's audit or anti-corruption body. (d) Report outside (for example to the Inspectorate of Government) if internal channels fail.

Evaluation. Option (a) fails the categorical imperative ("what if everyone kept quiet about corruption?"), the justice test (honest applicants lose) and the front page test. It does the greatest harm to the greatest number under the utilitarian view. Option (c) protects public rights and justice, and also her integrity.

Decision and action. Jenny should take action by keeping dated notes and copies of evidence, reporting first to a higher authority in the department than Matt, and escalating to an external body if nothing is done, using the proper channels and not leaks to the press. She should also seek advice from a trusted mentor or lawyer and check what whistleblower protection exists. Her duty to the public welfare and to honesty outweighs the temporary inconvenience to her career. See whistleblowing in t21.

CAT 2 2014 Q1c · 3 + 3 marksPhillip, a trainee telecommunications engineer working for a local Internet Service Provider's Technical Department, one morning discovers that Keith, one of the company's staff, is reading e-mails to Super Dip, one of the company's clients. It is clear that this employee has been peering into hundreds of e-mails for over six months to obtain confidential details about Super Dip Ltd. Phillip has only worked 2 months at this company following his graduation. Describe Phillip's ethical dilemma. What should Phillip as a young professional do in these circumstances? [reconstructed from garbled scan]

The dilemma (3 marks)

Phillip must choose between competing values: his duty to report a serious breach of the client's privacy and confidentiality, which is also against company policy and the law, and his own position as a new junior who has worked only two months and may face hostility or loss of the job if he accuses an established colleague. He also owes loyalty to a colleague and to the employer. Staying silent lets the harm continue to Super Dip and damages the ISP's integrity; speaking up risks harm to the decision maker.

What he should do (3 marks)

1. Identify the facts and secure evidence (what, how long) without joining in or tampering. 2. Report it to his immediate supervisor or the head of department through the company's proper internal channel, and not gossip. 3. If management ignores it, escalate to a higher authority such as the compliance officer or the regulator. 4. He should not confront Keith alone or tell Super Dip on his own. Reasoning: this is a breach of confidentiality and of the duty to protect the client's rights (rights theory), and keeping silent would fail the front page test.
