Case analysis and the 7-step template

~1 h 00 min to readHigh priority9 questions

Source: Set 3, slides 13-23 (bridge case and nuclear-reactor case); the 7-step ethical analysis template (appendix); question bank A1(i), C2; 2017 paper Q4; 2015 paper Q6

Why this section matters. Whenever an exam gives you a story and says "analyse", "identify the ethical issues" or "using the template as a guide", the marker is checking that you went through the seven steps in order and that you named one ethical theory and used its own vocabulary. The question bank sets two 12-mark questions of exactly this kind (Simon and Aggie). The ethical theories themselves (Kantianism, utilitarianism, social contract) are taught in section t01 and section t02. The steps for resolving a dilemma and the Pentium case are in section t06. The four group cases are in section t08.

The 7-step ethical analysis template

The template is a table with two columns. The left column is the step. The right column lists possible questions you can ask yourself at that step. You do not have to answer every question. You use them as prompts so that nothing is missed. The wording below is copied exactly from the template.

StepWhat to doPossible questions
1Set out the facts in a fair and balanced wayProvide a short summary of the ethical scenario
2List the main stakeholders Who is the instigator of the problem? In this scenario did someone identify there was an ethical issue? (Not always explicit in all scenarios)
Who are the stakeholders directly involved?
Who are the stakeholders indirectly implicated?
Who is affected by this scenario?
3Record the major ideals and the rights that you see having a role in the decision. Select one of two ideals/rights that you see as central to the situation Has a person's/stakeholders trust been broken?
Ideals: Do the ideals of fairness/honesty/equality/duty of care have a role in the ethical decision?
Rights: Does this scenario include: The right to know? The right to privacy? The right to property?
4What obligations are there? To whom and to what is an obligation owed and what sort of obligation is it? Laws
Engineering Code of Ethics
Obligations: To the profession and industry; To avoid misleading people; To produce a sound and safe product; To owners and shareholders; To foster professionalism
What kind of ethical infringement has occurred for each stakeholder?
Are there any laws that have been broken?
5What are the likely consequences for each stakeholder? (major, short term, long term?)Who benefits from the action?
Who is harmed by the action?
6Ethical theoriesSocial Contract Theory
OR
Utilitarianism
OR
Kantianism
7Summary. What is the best action? What should be done?Highlight the fact that there is often no definitive right or wrong

How to use each step in an answer

  1. Facts. Two or three sentences. Say only what the case says. Do not argue yet. "Fair and balanced" means do not take a side while stating facts.
  2. Stakeholders. Split them into directly involved and indirectly implicated, and name the instigator of the problem (the person or party who set the issue in motion). If a character noticed the issue (for example Simon in the social-media case), say so.
  3. Ideals and rights. Ideals are values such as fairness, honesty, equality and duty of care. Rights are the right to know, the right to privacy and the right to property. Say whether someone's trust has been broken. Then pick the one or two ideals or rights that are central, and say why.
  4. Obligations. Say who owes what to whom. Use the template list: to the profession and industry, to avoid misleading people, to produce a sound and safe product, to owners and shareholders, to foster professionalism. Then state the infringement (which obligation was broken, for which stakeholder) and any law broken.
  5. Consequences. For each stakeholder: major, short-term and long-term effects. End with who benefits and who is harmed.
  6. Ethical theory. Choose one of social contract, utilitarianism or Kantianism. Name it, define it in one line with its marker words, and apply it to the case. Optionally add one criticism of the theory.
  7. Summary. State the best action in one or two sentences. Then add that there is often no definitive right or wrong, so you are giving the best-justified answer.

Watch out. Question A1(i) and C2 both say "using the ethical analysis template as a guide, identify the ethical issues at play and conduct an ethical analysis using an ethical theory of your choice (12 marks)". That is two jobs: (1) the issues, which come out of steps 1 to 5, and (2) the analysis with one named theory, which is step 6, ending with step 7. Do not skip the theory. It carries the marks that students lose.

Which theory to pick, with its marker words from Set 1

TheorySay it like this (Set 1 wording)Apply it by askingOne criticism to add
Kantianism (Immanuel Kant, 1724-1804)Focus on the rightness of moral rules (good will); disregard emotional feelings and consequences. Founded on the view that all people are fundamentally rational beings who can derive moral rules from the logic of the situation.Can the rule be universally applied to everyone? Does the rule treat people as ends, not means?It allows no exceptions to moral rules; sometimes no rule adequately characterises an action; there is no way to resolve a conflict between rules.
UtilitarianismA consequentialist theory. It decides whether an act or rule is right depending on whether it results in the increase of the aggregate happiness (utilities). Act utilitarianism judges the benefits of a single act. Rule utilitarianism judges the benefits of all actions that follow the rule.Who would benefit? Who would be harmed? Do the benefits exceed the costs (or does harm outweigh benefit)?It requires aggregating all consequences on a single scale; it does not recognise or respect individual rights (a minority could be sacrificed for the majority).
Social contract theoryIndividuals implicitly accept a social contract on the condition that others follow the rules as well. Individuals act within a sphere of freedom as long as the rules are respected. The rules exist to enable everyone the benefits of social living and centre on respecting natural rights to life, liberty and property (John Locke).Whose rights are involved? Negative rights (liberties) are the right to act without interference. Positive rights (claim-rights) are an obligation of some people to provide certain things for others. Did someone break the rules everyone implicitly accepts?Conflicting rights problem; it may be unjust to people who are incapable of following the rules.

Rule of thumb for choosing. Use social contract when the case is about rights such as privacy, property or the right to know. Use utilitarianism when you can count benefits and harms to many people. Use Kantianism when the case is about a duty such as telling the truth, keeping a promise or not using people as a tool. The model answers below use all three so that you see each in action.

Case 1: protecting the safety of society (the bridge)

The case, retold

Your employer asks you to design a bridge that must not cost more than $1 million to build. After a study you find three things.

  • An ideal bridge can be built for $1.5 million.
  • Given the design constraints, a bridge built for $1 million will collapse in a moderate earthquake.
  • A bridge built for $1.25 million will survive a moderate earthquake but will collapse in an infrequent extreme earthquake.

Then your employer says: "If we don't build the bridge for $1 million, then we are going to have to lay off half of the staff, including you." He asks you to go ahead with the next stage of the project. What do you do?

What is the conflict?

The class was asked to pick the primary conflict from four options. The answer is the second: your duty to society versus your loyalty to your own career.

  • The code of ethics for engineers requires you to take the safety of society as being of paramount importance.
  • But you also feel a personal sense of loyalty to your company and fellow workers. You do not want anyone to lose their job.
  • So the conflict is between your duty to society and your loyalty to your own career and the welfare of your fellow employees.

The other options were wrong. Duty to fellow employees versus duty to the boss is a side issue. Uncertainty about the largest earthquake is a technical problem, not the conflict. Honesty to clients versus finishing the project does not capture the safety danger.

What is more important?

The conflict sets your future employment and the employment of others in your company against the welfare of society. The slide gives a firm ruling: in a case like this the welfare of society comes first. Your duty to protect the public is greater than your duty to your own career and that of your fellow employees.

Key point. The reason society wins is the engineering code: safety of the public is paramount, which means it ranks above loyalty to an employer or colleagues. Loyalty is real but secondary. State it in that order.

Set 3 case 1 · template practiceYour employer asks you to design a bridge costing no more than $1 million. A $1m bridge collapses in a moderate earthquake; a $1.25m bridge survives it but collapses in an extreme one; the ideal bridge costs $1.5m. Your employer threatens to lay off half the staff, including you, unless you proceed at $1m. Analyse the case using the ethical analysis template and one ethical theory.

Step 1. Facts

I am asked to design a bridge for not more than $1 million. My study shows that $1m gives a bridge that fails in a moderate earthquake, $1.25m a bridge that fails only in an infrequent extreme earthquake, and $1.5m an ideal bridge. My employer says that unless the bridge is built for $1m, half the staff including me will be laid off, and he asks me to go ahead.

Step 2. Stakeholders

Instigator: the employer, whose budget limit and threat create the problem. I identified the ethical issue through my study. Directly involved: me, the employer, my fellow employees. Indirectly implicated: the future users of the bridge and the surrounding community, the families of the staff, the engineering profession. Affected: everyone who crosses or lives near the bridge.

Step 3. Ideals and rights

Trust would be broken if the public relied on a bridge I knew to be weak. Ideals: duty of care, honesty and fairness to those who cannot see the design. Rights: the users' right to know the risk and their right to life and safety. The central one is the duty of care to the public.

Step 4. Obligations

The code of ethics requires me to treat the safety of society as paramount, and to produce a sound and safe product. I also owe loyalty to my employer and colleagues, but that is a lower obligation. Building the $1m bridge and staying silent would be an infringement of the code towards the public. Any law on negligence or building standards could also be broken beyond the slides.

Step 5. Consequences

If I build at $1m: short term, jobs are saved and the budget is met; long term, a moderate earthquake could collapse the bridge, causing deaths, lawsuits, loss of my licence and the end of the firm. If I refuse or raise the issue: short term, I may be laid off and some staff may lose jobs; long term, the public is safe and the firm keeps its reputation. Benefit from the $1m bridge: the firm and staff for a time. Harmed: the public and, eventually, the firm.

Step 6. Ethical theory: utilitarianism

Utilitarianism is a consequentialist theory that judges an act by whether it increases the aggregate happiness. The benefit of the $1m choice is jobs for half a company's staff. The harm is possible death and injury to many members of the public, plus the later collapse of the firm itself. Under rule utilitarianism the rule "build bridges that fail in a moderate earthquake to save jobs" would, if everyone followed it, destroy public trust in all bridges. The harm outweighs the benefit, so the $1m bridge is wrong. A weakness is that probabilities of earthquakes are uncertain and all consequences must be put on one scale.

Step 7. Summary

The welfare of society comes first. I should not proceed with the $1m design. I should explain the risk in writing to my employer and propose alternatives (a larger budget, a cheaper but safe design, or the $1.25m option with the extreme-earthquake risk disclosed to the client). If my employer still insists, I should refuse and escalate. There is often no definitive right or wrong, but a duty to the public outranks loyalty to my own career.

Case 2: telling the truth in public statements (the nuclear reactor)

The case, retold

The government asks you to verify that a nuclear reactor will not leak toxic substances into the neighbouring ocean. After your study you find that:

  • the reactor will likely leak within the coming 8 years, but there is significant uncertainty;
  • the reactor cannot be evaluated more carefully unless it is shut down immediately;
  • both the ocean and the neighbouring community are at risk.

Government officials receive your report and ask you to modify it so that it says the facility is actually safe. They claim that altering the report will protect the public, preventing panic while the government tries to shut down and fix the facility. What do you do?

What is the conflict?

The code requires you to safeguard the public's welfare. It also requires you to tell the truth when making public statements concerning your area of engineering. To solve the conflict you must (1) correctly understand what each code requirement is telling you and (2) choose to act on the obligation that is of priority.

  • "Protecting the public" means making sure they are safe.
  • "Issue public statements in an objective and truthful manner" means telling the public the reactor may not be safe while outlining the uncertainties.
  • The government asks you to alter the report in order to protect the public. So the two duties seem to pull apart.

Your obligation as an engineer is to safeguard public safety and tell the truth. That means you cannot alter data and you must tell the truth about the reactor. The government is calling on you as a citizen to alter documents as a way of protecting fellow citizens. So the conflict is between your obligations as an engineer and your obligations as a citizen. This is a role conflict. (Role responsibilities such as engineer, employee and citizen are introduced in t04.)

What is more important?

The slide says role conflicts are hard and there is no easy answer. This is where other moral considerations matter.

  • The public's right to know. The people near the reactor are the ones at risk. They have a right to know what the engineer found. A false "safe" report takes that right away from them.
  • The government's obligation to tell the truth. The government owes honesty to its citizens. It cannot ask an engineer to do what it should not do itself.

The ruling: your duty as an engineer to tell the truth when making public statements trumps your civic duty to be loyal to your government.

Key point. Both cases end the same way: a duty that comes from the engineering code (safety, truthfulness) ranks above a loyalty (to an employer, to a government). Say "role conflict" for the engineer-versus-citizen case and "welfare of society comes first" for the bridge.

Set 3 case 2 · template practiceYou are asked by the government to verify that a nuclear reactor will not leak toxic substances into the ocean. You find it will likely leak within 8 years (with significant uncertainty), that it cannot be evaluated more carefully unless shut down, and that the ocean and community are at risk. Officials ask you to change your report to say it is safe, to prevent panic. Analyse the case with the ethical analysis template and one ethical theory.

Step 1. Facts

My study shows the reactor likely will leak within 8 years, with significant uncertainty. It cannot be examined more closely unless shut down at once. The ocean and the neighbouring community are at risk. The government, which commissioned the report, asks me to rewrite it as "safe" to avoid panic while it arranges a shutdown and repair.

Step 2. Stakeholders

Instigator: the government officials who ask for the change (the reactor's possible defect is the underlying problem). I identified the ethical issue. Directly involved: me as engineer, the government officials, the reactor operator. Indirectly implicated: the profession, other engineers who rely on honest reports. Affected: the neighbouring community, the ocean and the people and industries that depend on it.

Step 3. Ideals and rights

Trust would be broken between the public and the government, and between the public and engineers, if a false report came out. Ideals: honesty, fairness and duty of care. Rights: the community's right to know and its right to life and health. Central: honesty and the public's right to know.

Step 4. Obligations

The code requires me to safeguard the public's welfare and to issue public statements in an objective and truthful manner. As an engineer I may not alter data. As a citizen I am asked to be loyal to the government. The government has an obligation to be truthful to citizens. Altering the report would be an infringement of the obligation to avoid misleading people, and it may be a legal offence beyond the slides.

Step 5. Consequences

If I alter the report: short term, no panic; long term, a leak harms the community and ocean while people are unaware, and my deception comes out, ending my career and the trust in engineers. If I report truthfully with the uncertainties: short term, possible fear and political anger toward me; long term, the facility is inspected and fixed, people can protect themselves, and trust is kept. Benefit from the false report: the government for a short time. Harmed: the community, the ocean, the public's trust.

Step 6. Ethical theory: Kantianism

Kantianism focuses on the rightness of moral rules, disregarding feelings and consequences, and asks whether a rule can be universally applied to everyone and whether it treats people as ends, not means. The rule "an engineer may alter a report when told it prevents panic" cannot be universalised: if every engineer did it, no report could be believed, which defeats the purpose of a report (the same logic as the false-promise example, where universalising makes promises unbelievable). The rule is flawed. Altering the report also treats the public as a means to the government's calm, instead of as rational people who can decide for themselves. "Do not lie" is a valid rule. A weakness is that Kantianism allows no exceptions, so it cannot weigh the argument that panic could cause harm.

Step 7. Summary

I should not alter the report. I should issue a truthful report that states the likely leak and its uncertainties, and recommend that the reactor be shut down so it can be evaluated. My duty as an engineer to tell the truth trumps my civic duty to be loyal to the government. If officials refuse to release it, I should take the matter higher. There is no easy answer in a role conflict, but this is the best-justified action.

Marker words: role conflicts and priority of duties

Say it like this:

The code requires the engineer to take the safety of society as paramount, so in a conflict between duty to society and loyalty to an employer, the welfare of society comes first. Where the conflict is between obligations as an engineer and obligations as a citizen, the duty to tell the truth in public statements wins.

Question bank A1(i): Simon and the social-media data

QB A1(i) · 12 marksSimon is working as a Social Media Consultant for a multi-national corporation. One day he gets a call from the CIO requesting him to collect personal data on the staff in the IT department via Facebook and LinkedIn. Simon is very concerned whether it is an ethical thing to do. Using the ethical analysis template (in appendix) as a guide, identify the ethical issues at play and conduct an ethical analysis using an ethical theory of your choice.

Theory chosen: social contract theory. A1(ii) of the same question (how ethical or legal it is for the CIO to use social media in HR monitoring) is answered in section t20.

Step 1. Facts

Simon is a social media consultant at a multinational. The CIO has asked him to collect personal data on the IT staff through Facebook and LinkedIn. The question does not say whether the staff were told or what the purpose is; I assume they were not told and that no purpose was given. Simon doubts it is ethical.

Step 2. Stakeholders

Instigator: the CIO. Simon is the one who identified the ethical issue. Directly involved: Simon, the CIO, the IT staff whose data is collected. Indirectly implicated: the HR department, other employees who may fear they are next, shareholders and the company's reputation, the social-media platforms and the profession of consultants. Affected: mainly the IT staff.

Step 3. Ideals and rights

The staff's trust in the employer would be broken if they found out. Ideals: honesty (collecting data in secret), fairness (only IT staff are targeted) and duty of care. Rights: the staff's right to privacy and their right to know that and why data is being collected; their personal data is also their property. Central: the right to privacy and the right to know. Against this is the company's right to protect its property and reputation.

Step 4. Obligations

Simon owes obligations to his employer (to carry out lawful instructions), to the staff (to avoid misleading people and respect their dignity), to the profession (confidentiality and integrity) and to the company's owners (not to expose it to legal risk). The infringement: collecting personal data without notice or consent breaches the staff's privacy and his professional integrity. Laws: data protection and privacy laws that require consent, a stated purpose and limits on use may be broken beyond the slides.

Step 5. Consequences

If Simon collects the data: short term, the CIO is satisfied and the company gets information; long term, loss of staff trust, a hostile workplace, possible lawsuits and fines, bad press, and Simon's own reputation damaged. Data could be misused for unfair treatment (profiling). If Simon objects: the CIO may be annoyed and Simon may be pressured, but staff privacy and the company's legal position are protected. Benefits: the CIO and, narrowly, the company. Harmed: the IT staff, and later the company.

Step 6. Ethical theory: social contract

In social contract theory, individuals implicitly accept a social contract on condition that others follow the rules as well. Individuals act within a sphere of freedom as long as the rules are respected, and the rules centre on natural rights to life, liberty and property. Employment is such a contract. Staff accept work rules and fair monitoring in return for respect for their private life. Collecting personal data from their private social-media spaces, in secret and without a stated purpose, goes beyond what they agreed to and breaks the contract. Their negative right (the right to act without interference) is violated. The company's competing right to protect its property is real (the conflicting rights problem in this theory), but it can be served by open, limited measures. So Simon should not do it secretly.

Step 7. Summary

Simon should not collect the data in the way requested. He should ask the CIO the purpose, explain the privacy and legal risks, and propose a transparent route: a written policy that staff know, consent, limits to public and job-relevant information, and HR and legal review. If the CIO insists on a secret and unlimited collection, Simon should refuse and escalate. There is often no definitive right or wrong, but this action best respects the staff's rights.

Question bank C2: Aggie and the weed killer

QB C2 · 12 marksAggie's pride and joy is her garden. One day she notices weeds growing through the gaps between the pavers in her garden. She decides to buy some weed killer to kill the weeds. She selects the "Knuck-Em-Dead" weed killer spray manufactured by Knock Dead Pty Ltd. There are no instructions for application nor warnings about side effects. It turned out inhaling fumes from the weed killer causes allergic reactions in some people. The company knew this but did not put instructions or warnings for its consumers. At home Aggie sprays what she thinks is enough weed killer to kill off the weeds. That night she falls violently ill and has to be hospitalised. Doctors find she has suffered a severe allergic reaction inhaling fumes from the weed killer. She has to pay $1,000 in hospital bills. Using the ethical analysis template (in appendix) as a guide, identify the ethical issues at play and conduct an ethical analysis using an ethical theory of your choice. [wording reconstructed from garbled scan]

Theory chosen: Kantianism.

Step 1. Facts

Aggie buys "Knuck-Em-Dead" weed killer from Knock Dead Pty Ltd. The product has no instructions and no warning about side effects. The company knew that the fumes cause allergic reactions in some people, but said nothing. Aggie sprays it, falls violently ill, is hospitalised and pays $1,000.

Step 2. Stakeholders

Instigator: Knock Dead Pty Ltd, which sold the product without warnings. In this scenario nobody raised the ethical issue; it is not explicit, and we identify it from the harm. Directly involved: Aggie and the company. Indirectly implicated: its managers and engineers or chemists, shareholders and owners, the retailer, the doctors and hospital, other buyers, regulators and the profession. Affected: Aggie, and every other customer at risk.

Step 3. Ideals and rights

Aggie's trust that a product on a shop shelf is safe to use was broken. Ideals: honesty (hiding a known danger), fairness and duty of care. Rights: the consumer's right to know the risks, her right to health and safety, and her right to property (she lost $1,000). Central: the right to know and the company's duty of care.

Step 4. Obligations

The company owed Aggie and other consumers an obligation to produce a sound and safe product and to avoid misleading people; leaving out a warning it knew was needed misleads by omission. It also owes owners and shareholders a lawful, sustainable business, and the profession a standard of integrity. The infringement against Aggie is clear. Laws such as product liability, negligence and consumer protection have probably been broken beyond the slides.

Step 5. Consequences

For Aggie: illness, hospital bills of $1,000, lost trust. For the company: short term, it saved the cost of testing and labelling and perhaps sold more; long term, lawsuits, compensation, a recall, loss of reputation. For other customers: risk of the same illness, perhaps worse for some. Benefits: the company, in the short term. Harmed: Aggie and other users, and finally the company.

Step 6. Ethical theory: Kantianism

Kantianism judges the rightness of moral rules and disregards consequences. Kant asks two questions. First, can the rule be universally applied to everyone? The company's rule was "sell a product that I know harms some users without telling them". If everyone did this, no consumer could trust any product, which contradicts the company's own wish to be trusted by buyers. It fails. Second, does the rule treat people as ends, not means? Aggie was used as a means to profit and was given no chance to decide whether to take the risk. She was not treated as a rational person. "Do not lie" and "do not harm" are valid rules and the company broke both. A known criticism of Kantianism is that it allows no exceptions, but nothing here would justify an exception.

Step 7. Summary

The company acted wrongly. It should have tested the product, put clear instructions and warnings on the label, and, once the hazard was known, recalled it. It should compensate Aggie for the $1,000 and her suffering and fix the labelling. Aggie should read the label and use safely, but with no label she cannot be blamed. There is often no definitive right or wrong, but a known risk hidden from the consumer is clearly an ethical failure.

Marker words: applying a theory in a case answer

Say it like this:

Using Kantianism, the rule must be universally applied to everyone and must treat people as ends, not means. Using utilitarianism, the right act is the one that increases the aggregate happiness, so the benefits must outweigh the harm. Using social contract theory, people accept rules on condition that others do, so we must respect natural rights to life, liberty and property.

Locke's three natural rights.
Life, liberty and property.
Negative rights (liberties).
The right to act without interference.

An obligation of some people to provide certain things for others.

Three arguments against Kantianism.
It allows no exceptions to moral rules; sometimes no rule adequately characterises an action; there is no way to resolve a conflict between rules.
Two arguments against utilitarianism.
It requires aggregating all consequences on a single scale; it does not recognise or respect individual rights (a minority could be sacrificed for the greater happiness of the majority).

BART case (2017 paper, question 4)

The case. In March 1972 three engineers, Holger Hjortsvang, Max Blankenzee and Robert Bruder, were working on the Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) project in California, United States. They were responsible for the design and creation of an automatic guided train system. They had been expressing doubts about the system's safety through internal memos to their managers since 1969. The managers' response was "don't make trouble". In March 1972 the three engineers were dismissed. (Part C, the four principles of the code, is in section t11. Part E, problems of law in engineering, is in section t10. Whistleblowing in detail is in section t21.)

A short template pass first, so you can see the facts that parts A, B and D use.

2017 Q4 · template walk-throughAnalyse the BART case using the seven-step template.

Step 1. Facts

Three engineers on the BART automatic train project raised safety doubts in internal memos from 1969. Managers answered "don't make trouble". The engineers were dismissed in 1972.

Step 2. Stakeholders

Instigator: the managers who ignored the warnings. Directly involved: the three engineers and the managers. Indirectly implicated: BART, the company, the transit authority and funders, the future passengers, the profession. Affected: passengers.

Step 3. Ideals and rights

The engineers' trust in management was broken. Ideals: honesty, duty of care and fairness (to employees who spoke up). Rights: passengers' right to know and right to life; the engineers' right to fair treatment. Central: the public's safety and right to know.

Step 4. Obligations

The code makes public safety paramount, to produce a sound and safe product. The engineers owe loyalty to the employer, but the duty to the public is higher. The managers' infringement: ignoring safety warnings and punishing people who raised them. Possible legal breach: unfair dismissal and negligence beyond the slides.

Step 5. Consequences

If the engineers stay silent: short term, they keep jobs; long term, a possible accident and passenger deaths. If they act: short term, dismissal (which has already happened); long term, safety checked, the profession's integrity upheld. Benefit from silence: managers and schedule. Harm: passengers, and the engineers.

Step 6. Ethical theory

See answers A, B and D below, which apply deontological ethics, consequentialist ethics, utilitarianism and social contract.

Step 7. Summary

The engineers should keep documenting the danger and take it above their managers, and, if that fails and the evidence is good, make it known outside the company. There is often no definitive right or wrong, but the safety of passengers outweighs obedience.

2017 Q4A · 6 marksWhat would you advise Holger Hjortsvang, Max Blankenzee and Robert Bruder to do after the response by the managers? Apply two out of the following three ethical theories (deontological ethics, consequentialist ethics and virtue ethics) to decide how to act.

Advice: do not drop the matter. Escalate beyond the immediate managers, keep written evidence, and if internal channels still fail, make the danger known to an outside body.

Deontological ethics. Deontological ethics judges an act by duty and the rightness of moral rules, not by the consequences. The engineering code makes the safety of the public paramount, so the engineers have a duty to ensure the train system is safe and to speak out. The test of universalisation shows the managers' rule "do not make trouble about safety" cannot be applied to everyone. Passengers must be treated as ends, not means. So the engineers have a duty to go further.

Consequentialist ethics. Consequentialism judges an act by whether the result gives the greatest good. If they stay silent, a failure could kill many passengers and destroy the project; if they speak out, the cost is their jobs and annoyance for the managers. The harm to many outweighs the cost to a few, so they should speak out, beginning with higher management and then, if needed, outside.

Advice, brief: (1) document the risks, (2) go to higher management or the board, (3) if ignored and the danger is serious, report externally to the professional body, the regulator or the public.

2017 Q4B · 4 marksIf the two theories come to different answers, explain why you think the outcome of one theory should prevail over the outcome of the other.

Here both theories agree, but suppose they differ. For example consequentialism says "keep silent: the chance of failure is small and many jobs depend on the project", while deontology says "speak out".

I would let the deontological answer prevail for three reasons.

  • Safety is a duty in the code. The code makes public safety paramount; it is not to be traded against jobs or schedule.
  • Consequences are uncertain. Consequentialism needs us to predict the chances and size of an accident and put all consequences on one scale, which is unreliable. A duty does not depend on a guess.
  • Individual rights. A consequentialist sum can sacrifice a minority (a few passengers) for a majority's happiness. Deontology protects each person's right to life.

The deontological answer is also the one that treats passengers as ends, not means. (A reasoned argument the other way, for example that consequentialism is comprehensive and handles exceptions, can also earn marks if it is justified.)

2017 Q4D · 6 marksUse two different ethical theories to explain or justify the actions of a whistle-blower.

A whistle-blower is an employee who makes a danger or wrongdoing in the organisation known, internally or externally, usually after the organisation has ignored it. The BART engineers are an example.

1. Utilitarianism. Utilitarianism is a consequentialist theory: an act is right if it increases the aggregate happiness. The whistle-blower's action prevents harm (deaths, injuries, losses) to many members of the public, at a cost mostly to himself (job, relationships) and to the organisation's image. The benefit to many exceeds the harm to a few, so the act is justified.

2. Social contract theory. In social contract theory people accept rules on condition that others follow them, and the rules protect natural rights to life, liberty and property. The public has the right to life and the right to know about a danger. The organisation broke the contract by hiding or ignoring it. The whistle-blower, as an engineer holding professional knowledge, upholds the contract by informing those at risk.

beyond the slides Alternative: Kantianism or virtue ethics also justify it. Kantianism: the rule "report a serious hidden danger" can be universalised. Virtue ethics: honesty, integrity and courage are virtues of a responsible person (the virtue approach in Set 3 asks "which option leads me to act as a responsible person?").

Marker words: advising the BART engineers and justifying a whistle-blower

Say it like this:

Deontological ethics judges an act by duty and the rightness of moral rules, not consequences, so the engineers must put public safety first. Consequentialist ethics judges by results, and the harm to many outweighs the cost to a few. A whistle-blower is justified because the benefit to the public exceeds the harm to the whistle-blower.

Pacemaker and transistor case (2015 paper, question 6)

2015 Q6 · 20 marksThe heart pacemaker is a modern wonder. The device has a timer that resets itself every time the patient's heart beats. If the heart does not beat on schedule (say, within 1.2 seconds), the pacemaker gives a stimulus that causes a heartbeat. It is 1975, and you are on the board of directors of a company that makes transistors. Among the many companies with whom you have a contract is one that makes heart pacemakers. Pacemaker technology is in its infancy. When doctors implant a pacemaker, the patient's normal heartbeat is disabled, and he or she relies entirely on the device. If it fails, the patient's heart stops. Doctors are not very adept at installing the pacemakers, which are extremely delicate: there is even a story of a person yawning deeply, pulling the pacemaker wire in his chest, and dying. After that and many similar incidents, the board begins to reconsider whether your company should sell to the pacemaker company. Members of the board feel this situation is a major lawsuit just waiting to happen, and your company, as well as the company you supply, will be liable. In addition, you feel the specs the pacemaker company uses to test the transistors are not very strong. You and the board decide to get out of the business before it is too late. You tell the pacemaker company representatives about your conclusion, and they respond: "You can't stop selling us transistors. You are the sole remaining supplier for us. Everyone else has backed out for the same reasons you're giving. If you don't sell us the product, we'll go out of business. Pretty soon no one will be making heart pacemakers, and many people need them. Without pacemakers, people don't even have a chance." You take that information back to the board. People have different opinions. One says, "This is a bad deal, and it isn't our problem. We don't make enough on this sale to make the risk worthwhile." Another says, "We don't know how other companies use the transistors we sell them. Why should we be concerned about this one? What about that baby who died when the transistor in the incubator failed? We didn't know that company was using the transistor." Another says, "I think the real issue here: don't we have an ethical obligation to sell the product to the pacemaker company? What will happen if we don't sell to them?" Another says, "Give me a break. Our only obligation is to our shareholders. And how did we get so stupid that we're the last source? I'm telling you, we don't need this." Finally the chair of the board says, "OK, let's make a decision." What do you do? (a) Analyse the factual, conceptual and moral issues in the case. (b) What conclusion do you come to about the ethically correct choice that should have been made? [wording reconstructed from garbled scan]

Part (a): factual, conceptual and moral issues

Factual issues are questions about what is the case and can be settled by evidence. Here:

  • How likely is it that the transistors fail, and is the cause the transistor, the weak test specs, or the doctors' poor installation?
  • Is our company really the sole remaining supplier, and would the pacemaker company really go out of business?
  • Would we really be liable in law, and how large is the risk against the profit?
  • How many people depend on pacemakers and what happens to them without the device? We do not know how other companies use our transistors (as in the incubator death).

Conceptual issues are questions about what a key term means.

  • What does obligation mean? Is a supplier obliged to sell a product when it is the last source? A duty to help versus a duty not to harm.
  • What is responsibility and liability? Do we answer for how others use a part we make, and what is the difference between legal liability and moral responsibility?
  • What counts as a safe or acceptable risk for a life-critical device in an infant technology?
  • What is the extent of our obligation to shareholders: is "our only obligation is to our shareholders" a correct understanding?

Moral issues are the conflicts of values and duties.

  • The lives of present and future patients: harm from a failing device versus harm from having no pacemakers at all.
  • Duty to shareholders and the company's profit and survival versus duty to the public.
  • Our duty to the pacemaker company (contract, fairness, reliance on us) versus our duty not to contribute to deaths.
  • Honesty and informed consent: patients and doctors are unaware of the weak test specs.
  • Fairness: other suppliers left; why should we alone carry the risk?

Part (b): the template, conclusion and theory

Step 1. Facts

We supply transistors used in pacemakers. Pacemakers are new and delicate, and a failure stops the patient's heart. The pacemaker company's tests are weak. We fear lawsuits and decided to stop selling. They say we are the last supplier and that without us the industry will collapse and patients will lose a needed device. The board is divided.

Step 2. Stakeholders

Instigator: our company and board, which raised the issue by deciding to withdraw. The weak testing by the pacemaker company is the cause. Directly involved: the board, our shareholders, the pacemaker company, and patients who have or need pacemakers. Indirectly implicated: doctors and hospitals, patients' families, other transistor suppliers, regulators, the engineering profession. Affected: all patients with heart conditions.

Step 3. Ideals and rights

Trust of patients and doctors in the device would be broken by a failure. Ideals: duty of care, honesty and fairness. Rights: the patients' right to life and right to know the risk; the shareholders' right to property. Central: patients' right to life and the duty of care.

Step 4. Obligations

To the public: to produce a sound and safe product. To the pacemaker company: honour the contract and give fair notice. To shareholders: protect the investment. To the profession: foster professionalism and refuse to put an unsafe part into a life-critical device. The infringement we risk: selling a part we believe is not adequately tested. If it fails, we may be liable in law beyond the slides.

Step 5. Consequences

If we stop: short term, we avoid liability; the pacemaker company may fail, and patients who need devices go without. Long term, the industry may return with better suppliers, but some patients die. If we continue unchanged: we keep revenue but risk deaths from failures and a lawsuit. If we continue on conditions: safety improves and patients keep access. Benefits and harms thus fall on the patients, our shareholders and the pacemaker company.

Step 6. Ethical theory: utilitarianism

Utilitarianism is a consequentialist theory that chooses the action that increases the aggregate happiness: compare who benefits and who is harmed. Pacemakers have a large benefit (many lives saved) and a smaller probability of failure; withdrawing would remove that benefit from many people. But continuing without any change leaves an avoidable risk caused by weak testing. The greatest good is reached by a third option: continue supply and raise the safety of the transistor and testing. (Under rule utilitarianism, the rule "supply life-critical parts only with adequate testing" is good for all.) The criticism that utilitarianism does not respect individual rights applies: those who die from a failed device must not be treated as an acceptable cost. A Kantian note: the shareholder-only view uses patients as means and fails.

Step 7. Summary and conclusion

The ethically correct choice is neither to walk away at once nor to carry on as before. Our company should (1) tell the pacemaker company in writing that it will keep supplying for a limited period only if the transistor test specifications are strengthened, (2) test its own transistors to a higher standard and share the data, (3) warn doctors and regulators about the risk, and (4) stop supplying if the pacemaker company will not improve safety. This respects the patients' right to life and their right to know, honours our contract, and answers the shareholders' interest in the long term (a failure would cost far more than the profit). The claim that "our only obligation is to our shareholders" is rejected because the professional code puts the safety of the public first. There is often no definitive right or wrong, but this action is best supported.

Marker words: factual, conceptual and moral issues

Say it like this:

Factual issues are about what the facts are and whether they can be checked. Conceptual issues are about the meaning of key terms such as obligation, responsibility and risk. Moral issues are the conflicts between values, rights and duties.

The four group cases

~50 min to readMedium priority4 questions

Source: Set 4, slides 33-38 (group exercise, Cases 1 to 4, lecture recap and homework)

Why this section matters. These four cases are the lecturer's own homework ("Assignments: Cases 1, 2, 3 and 4"). No past paper asks about them by name, but each one is a typical exam scenario: a short story, a question such as "what should the engineer do?", and a marker looking for the template steps, a clause from the code and one named theory. Practise each case until you can answer it in 15 minutes. The template steps are set out in full in section t07; this section uses the same seven step names. The theories are taught in section t01 and section t02. The clauses quoted come from the ASME canons and the UIPE/ERB model rules, which are taught in section t09 and section t11.

The group exercise and how to use it

Slide 33 sets the exercise. Each group must discuss one case and prepare a solution in PowerPoint. The group then has 15 minutes to present to the class and answer questions. Group 1 takes Case 1, Group 2 takes Case 2, Group 3 takes Case 3 and Group 4 takes Case 4. The slide adds one instruction: the cases are designed as problems for you, so seek resolutions that you personally can live with. That means the lecturer wants a decision you are willing to defend as your own, not a list of options.

Slide 38, the recap, repeats two ideas that every answer below relies on:

  • Ethics is generally concerned with rules or guidelines for morals and/or socially approved conduct.
  • Ethical standards generally apply to conduct that can or does have a substantial effect on people's lives.

The slide also sets the homework: do all four cases.

The seven template headings used for every case below

The names are the same as in the template table in t07.

  1. Set out the facts in a fair and balanced way.
  2. List the main stakeholders (directly involved, indirectly implicated, who is affected, the instigator of the problem).
  3. Record the major ideals and rights (fairness, honesty, equality, duty of care; right to know, right to privacy, right to property).
  4. What obligations are there? (laws, code of ethics, the obligations list).
  5. Likely consequences for each stakeholder (short term, long term; who benefits, who is harmed).
  6. Ethical theories (social contract, utilitarianism or Kantianism).
  7. Summary: what is the best action, what should be done? (there is often no definitive right or wrong).

Watch out. The model resolutions below are written in compact note form so you can learn the pattern. Under exam conditions you can merge steps 1 and 2 into one short paragraph if time is short, but keep the other headings visible. Each model uses one theory only, because the template says choose one. Where a second theory is mentioned it is a one-line contrast to show you understand the theory.

Case 1: safety shortcuts on presses and stamping machines

The case retold

You have just been hired as a production engineer. On the shop floor you find a possible problem. The workers are routinely ignoring some of the government-mandated safety regulations that cover the presses and stamping machines.

They do this in two ways. First, they override safety features such as guards, which are designed to make it impossible to insert a hand or arm into a machine. Second, they rig up "convenience" controls so that they can operate a machine while standing close to it, instead of using the approved safety switches. The approved switches need more movement or more operating steps.

The workers' reason, or excuse, is that following the safety features strictly would make production difficult, tiring and inefficient. They believe their shortcut is still adequately safe and gives better efficiency and worker satisfaction.

The slide asks three questions:

  1. Should you immediately insist on full compliance with all the safety regulations, or do the workers have enough of a case that you would be tempted to ignore the violations?
  2. If you are tempted to ignore them, how would you justify that to your boss?
  3. How much weight should you give the workers' clear preference for not following the regulations? Ethically, can safety standards be relaxed if the people they apply to want them relaxed?

Model resolution using the seven template headings

StepModel content
1. FactsA newly hired production engineer finds workers bypassing guards and approved switches on presses and stamping machines, which breaks government safety regulations. The workers say compliance makes work hard and slow and that their shortcut is safe enough. The engineer has not yet acted.
2. StakeholdersDirectly involved: the workers (who run the risk of losing a hand or arm), the production engineer, the supervisor and the boss. The instigator of the problem is the workers' habit, which management has tolerated. Indirectly implicated: the owners and shareholders, the workers' families, the regulator (government inspectors), customers who wait for products, and insurers. Everyone who works near the machines is affected.
3. Ideals and rightsTrust has been broken: the regulator trusts the company to enforce the rules, and workers trust the company to keep them safe. Ideals: duty of care and honesty. The worker's right to life and bodily safety is central, and so is the employer's duty of care. The workers' preference for efficiency is a preference about a risk that falls on them, but it does not remove the duty of care.
4. ObligationsLaws: the safety regulations are mandatory, so the violation is already an offence. Code: ASME canon "Engineers shall hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public in the performance of their professional duties". UIPE/ERB model rule "While performing services, the engineer's foremost responsibility is to the public welfare". Obligations list: to produce a sound and safe product and workplace; to the profession and industry; to owners and shareholders (whose firm faces fines and claims). Ethical infringement: the company is failing in its duty of care to the workers, and the engineer would fail if he or she looked away.
5. ConsequencesIf you ignore the violation: short term, higher output and happier workers; long term, a likely amputation or death, compensation claims, fines, closure of the plant and loss of your licence. If you insist on compliance: short term, resentment, lower output and some cost; long term, safer workers, a legal and reputable firm. Who benefits from compliance: workers, owners, regulator, you. Who is harmed: only the short-term output and convenience.
6. TheoryUtilitarianism, a consequentialist theory that decides whether an act is right by whether it increases the aggregate happiness (utilities). Compare benefits and harms: the gain in speed and comfort is small and spread thinly, while the harm (a crushed hand or a death) is severe and irreversible, and the long-run cost to the firm is large. The harm outweighs the benefit, so compliance is right. As rule utilitarianism: the rule "obey safety regulations" produces more happiness over all cases than "obey them unless workers prefer otherwise".
7. SummaryDo not ignore the violation. First talk to the workers and supervisor, listen to the efficiency problem, then insist on the guards and approved switches. Report to your boss and propose redesigning the workstation (for example, two-hand controls or light curtains that are safe and fast) so that safety and efficiency are both met. If management refuses, take the matter to the safety authority. There is often no definitive right or wrong, but this is the best-justified action and one I can live with.

The three questions answered directly

  • Insist or ignore? Insist. The workers' case is about convenience, and convenience cannot outweigh risk to life.
  • How would you justify ignoring it to your boss? You could not. A justification would have to say "the risk is small", but you cannot show that, and you would become responsible if someone was hurt. The honest thing to say to your boss is that you found a violation and propose a fix.
  • Can safety standards be relaxed because those they apply to want it? No, for four reasons. The workers may not understand the risk fully or may be under pressure to produce (consent is not fully free). The standard also protects others: the employer, the family and the public. A regulation is a legal requirement and cannot be waived by the people it covers. And the engineer's duty is to the public welfare, which is not owned by the workers. This links to the idea of voluntary risk in section t16: a risk is only voluntary when the person knows it and freely accepts it.

If the exam asks this

Answer skeleton. (1) State the facts in two lines. (2) Name the stakeholders: workers, engineer, boss, owners, regulator. (3) Name the central right (right to life and safety) and ideal (duty of care) and say trust has been broken. (4) Quote the canon "hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public" and the model rule "foremost responsibility is to the public welfare"; say the regulation is law. (5) Compare short-term and long-term consequences; who benefits, who is harmed. (6) Apply utilitarianism: harm outweighs benefit. (7) Conclude: insist on compliance, redesign for efficiency, escalate if refused; add that there is often no definitive right or wrong.

Practice · 12 marksWorkers at a plant remove machine guards to work faster, and they say they are happy to take the risk. As the new production engineer, using the ethical analysis template as a guide, analyse the case using an ethical theory of your choice and state what you should do.

Facts. Workers override safety features on presses and stamping machines, which is against government-mandated safety regulations, to work faster. They accept the risk.

Stakeholders. Directly involved: the workers, the production engineer, the boss. Indirectly implicated: owners and shareholders, the regulator, the workers' families. The workers are the instigators of the shortcut.

Ideals and rights. Duty of care and honesty; the right to life and safety. The regulator's trust has been broken.

Obligations. The law requires the guards. The code says engineers shall hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public, and the model rule puts the foremost responsibility to the public welfare. I owe a sound and safe workplace to the workers and to owners.

Consequences. Short term: faster output. Long term: injury or death, fines, plant closure. Who benefits from the shortcut: nobody for long; who is harmed: the workers and the firm.

Theory. Utilitarianism judges an act by whether it increases the aggregate happiness. A small gain in speed is outweighed by a severe, irreversible harm, so compliance is right.

Summary. Insist on compliance, redesign the controls to be safe and efficient, and report to management; go to the regulator if management refuses. There is often no definitive right or wrong, but this is the best-justified action.

Case 2: toxic liquid waste slightly over the legal limit

The case retold

You and an engineer colleague work closely on designing and carrying out procedures for the proper disposal of various waste materials in an industrial plant. He is responsible for liquid wastes, which are discharged into local rivers.

In your regular discussions you notice that he habitually allows the levels of some toxic liquid-waste chemicals to be slightly higher than the law permits for those chemicals. You tell him you have noticed. He replies that, because the levels are only slightly above the legal limit, any ethical or safety issue is trivial and not worth the trouble and expense of correcting.

The slide asks:

  1. Do you agree with your colleague?
  2. If not, should you try to get him to correct the excess levels, or is this none of your business since he, not you, is responsible for liquid wastes?
  3. If he refuses to correct the problem, should you report it to your boss or higher management?
  4. If no one in the company will do anything, should you be prepared to go over their heads and report to government inspectors or regulators directly? Or should one do that only when a much more serious risk to public health and safety is involved?

Model resolution using the seven template headings

StepModel content
1. FactsTwo engineers share waste-disposal design in a plant. The colleague, who is responsible for liquid waste, habitually lets toxic chemical levels run slightly above the legal limit before discharge into local rivers. He says the excess is trivial and correction is not worth the cost. You have told him; he has not changed.
2. StakeholdersDirectly involved: you, the colleague, your boss and higher management. The colleague is the instigator of the problem; you are the one who identified the issue. Indirectly implicated: owners and shareholders, the environment regulator. Affected: people who drink, fish or farm with river water downstream, children, wildlife, and the plant's reputation.
3. Ideals and rightsTrust broken: the public and the regulator trust the company to respect the limit. Ideals: honesty (the plant reports compliance but is not compliant), fairness (downstream people carry the risk, the company keeps the savings) and duty of care. Rights: the community's right to know what is in its water, and its right to life and health. The company has a right to property, but not to use the river as a free dump beyond the licence.
4. ObligationsLaw: the limit is set by law, so an exceedance, however small, is a breach. Code: canon "Engineers shall hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public"; model rule 3 on whistle blowing: "If an engineer's professional judgment is overruled resulting in danger to the life, health, welfare, or property of the public, the engineer shall notify his/her employer or client and any appropriate authority"; model rule 8, the final obligation to society: "Engineers who have knowledge of possible violation of any of the rules ... shall provide pertinent information and assist the state board in reaching final determination". Obligations list: to avoid misleading people, to produce a sound and safe product, to the profession. Ethical infringement: a breach of the duty to society; and the habit means it is not a one-off mistake.
5. ConsequencesIf you do nothing: short term, the company saves money; long term, toxins build up in the river and food chain (small excesses accumulate), people become ill, the company is fined or closed, and you share the blame because you knew. If you act: short term, conflict with a colleague, cost of treatment equipment, possible retaliation for you; long term, safe water, legal compliance, a firm that can defend its record. Who benefits from action: the community, the environment, the firm in the long run. Who is harmed: your relationship with the colleague and the short-term budget.
6. TheoryKantianism, which focuses on the rightness of moral rules and disregards consequences and feelings. Universalise the colleague's rule: "It is acceptable to exceed the legal limit when the excess is small." If everyone adopted it, limits would mean nothing and every plant would drift upward; the rule cannot be universally applied to everyone and so is wrong. Also, the downstream people are treated as a means to the company's savings, not as ends. The "it is his department" rule fails the same test, because if every engineer ignored wrongdoing by colleagues, no wrong would ever be checked.
7. SummaryDisagree with the colleague. It is your business because the harm falls on the public and the code obliges you to act. Escalate in steps: talk to the colleague again with the data and offer to help find a cheap fix; if he refuses, report to your boss and higher management in writing; if the company does nothing, report to the regulator. Do not wait for a much more serious risk: the code does not set a size threshold for a legal violation that endangers public health, although the stronger the danger, the stronger the duty. There is often no definitive right or wrong, but this is the best-justified course.

The slide's questions answered in one place

  • Do you agree that it is trivial? No. A legal limit is a decision by society about safe levels. "Slightly over" is the colleague's opinion, and he gives no data. The excess is habitual, so it accumulates.
  • Is it your business? Yes. The canon is about the safety, health and welfare of the public, not about whose department it is. The model rule on the final obligation to society speaks of any engineer with knowledge of a possible violation.
  • Go to the boss? Yes, once the colleague refuses. This is the internal route and it comes first.
  • Go over their heads? Yes if no one in the company acts. Model rule 3 names "any appropriate authority". The more serious the danger and the clearer the evidence, the more clearly you must do so. External whistle blowing is discussed fully in section t21.

If the exam asks this

Answer skeleton. (1) Facts. (2) Stakeholders: you, colleague, boss, owners, regulator, downstream community; colleague is instigator. (3) Trust broken; honesty, fairness, duty of care; right to health and right to know. (4) Law breached; canon "hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public"; rule 3 "notify his/her employer or client and any appropriate authority"; rule 8 final obligation. (5) Short- and long-term consequences, who benefits, who is harmed. (6) Kantianism: universalise the rule "slight excess is fine". (7) Escalate: colleague, boss, regulator; no definitive right or wrong.

Practice · 8 marksA colleague who handles effluent discharge tells you that exceeding the legal limit by a small margin is "not worth correcting". State your view and explain, with reference to the code of ethics, the steps you would take if he refuses to change.

I disagree. The law sets the limit to protect public health, and a habitual excess accumulates in the river. Engineers shall hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public, so it is my business even if the discharge is his responsibility.

Using Kantianism, his rule "a small excess of the legal limit is acceptable" cannot be universally applied to everyone, because limits would then mean nothing; and downstream residents are being treated as a means, not ends.

Steps: (1) Talk to him again with data and offer help to find a low-cost fix. (2) If he refuses, report to my boss and higher management in writing, as the model rule says the engineer shall notify his/her employer or client. (3) If the company does nothing, report to the appropriate authority, the environment regulator, because engineers with knowledge of a possible violation must assist the board. Keep records throughout.

Case 3: recycled-composite wall sections and whether to tell customers

The case retold

Your company has for some time supplied prefabricated wall sections, which you designed, to construction companies. One day you have a new idea: the sections could be made more cheaply from composites of recycled waste materials.

Pilot runs of the new technique are very successful, so the company decides to switch entirely to it for all future production runs. But there are management debates about how, or whether, to tell the customers about the change.

The supply contracts were written in terms of specifications and function. The load-bearing capacity and longevity of the wall sections were specified (the slide text says "love bearing", which reads as a typing error for load bearing), but no particular materials or fabrication techniques are named. So the changeover could be made without breaching any current contract.

On the other hand, the new method brings significant cost savings. The slide asks:

  1. Does your company have an ethical obligation to tell the customers, and perhaps to renegotiate supply at a reduced price so that the customers also share the benefit?
  2. More specifically, as a professional engineer and the designer of the new technique, do you have a special duty to be an advocate inside your company for fully informing customers about the technique and the savings?

Model resolution using the seven template headings

StepModel content
1. FactsYou designed prefabricated wall sections. You invent a cheaper recycled-composite method; pilots succeed; management will switch all production. Contracts specify load-bearing capacity and longevity but not materials or methods, so no contract is breached by the switch. Management is unsure whether to tell customers. The savings are significant.
2. StakeholdersDirectly involved: you (inventor and designer), management, the customers (construction companies). You are the person who identified the issue. Indirectly implicated: the occupants and users of the buildings, the building inspectors and regulators, owners and shareholders, other wall-section suppliers, and the recycling and environment sector. Affected: anyone who will live or work in a building that uses the sections.
3. Ideals and rightsHonesty (disclosure of a material change), fairness (sharing the savings) and duty of care. The customers' right to know what they are buying; the company's right to property in its invention. Trust: customers trust the supplier to deliver what they expected when they signed, and silence on a change they would care about risks that trust.
4. ObligationsLaw: no contract breach, but the contract is only a minimum (the letter of the contract is met; the spirit may not be, see section t10 on letter versus spirit). Code: ASME canon "Engineers shall act in professional matters for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees"; the canon "Engineers shall issue public statements only in an objective and truthful manner"; model rule 4 "Engineers shall be objective and truthful in professional reports, statements, or testimonies and shall provide all pertinent supporting information"; the duty of full disclosure. Competence canon: "perform services only in the areas of their competence" means the new material must be tested and proved for load and longevity. Obligation list: to avoid misleading people, to produce a sound and safe product, to owners and shareholders, to foster professionalism.
5. ConsequencesIf you tell the customers: short term, some may ask for lower prices or reject the product, and the company earns less per unit; long term, trust and reputation, repeat business, and a track record for the recycled material. If you do not tell: short term, higher profit; long term, if customers discover it (or a defect appears) they lose trust, may sue, and the company may be blamed; the recycled technique itself may be discredited. Who benefits from disclosure: customers, end users, the company's reputation, the recycling industry. Who is harmed: short-term profit margins.
6. TheorySocial contract theory. Individuals implicitly accept a social contract on the condition that others follow the rules as well; the rules exist so that everyone has the benefits of social living. Business depends on that implicit contract: customers deal on the assumption that suppliers do not hide material changes. Hiding a cost-saving change breaks the implicit rules of fair dealing even if it is within the written contract. The customers' rights (the right to know, the right to property in what they paid for) therefore require disclosure. A contrasting view: a utilitarian count could also favour disclosure because trust yields greater long-term benefit.
7. SummaryThe company should tell the customers about the change, with test evidence that load-bearing capacity and longevity are met, and should be willing to negotiate a share of the savings. As the designer, I have a special duty to advocate this inside the company because I know the technique better than anyone and the code binds me personally as a faithful agent and a truthful reporter. If management refuses, I should state my objection in writing; I should not tell customers anything false. There is often no definitive right or wrong about price-sharing, but disclosure of a material change is the best-justified action.

The slide's two questions answered separately

  • Is there an ethical obligation to inform and perhaps to share savings? To inform: yes, because the change is material and silence misleads by omission. To renegotiate the price: it is not strictly required by law or by the code, so it is an ethical ideal (fairness) rather than a duty. It is wise business to offer some benefit, because it builds trust. Say clearly which part is a duty and which part is good practice.
  • Special duty as designer? Yes. Engineers have a personal professional duty that is not removed by the company's decision. See personal versus organisational responsibility in section t04. The designer is the one who can vouch that the new material meets the specification, so the designer should push for disclosure and insist on proper testing before delivery.

beyond the slides A practical point examiners like: check that building codes or standards do not name approved materials. If they do, a change of material may need regulatory approval, and that makes disclosure to the buyer and the authority a legal duty too.

If the exam asks this

Answer skeleton. (1) Facts: cheaper recycled method, contracts silent on materials. (2) Stakeholders: you, management, customers, end users, regulators. (3) Honesty, fairness, duty of care; right to know; trust. (4) Cite canon "faithful agents or trustees" and "objective and truthful"; model rule 4 "provide all pertinent supporting information"; letter versus spirit of the contract. (5) Short and long term for each party. (6) Social contract: implicit rules of fair dealing. (7) Inform customers with test evidence, offer a fair share of savings, advocate inside the company; no definitive right or wrong on price-sharing.

Practice · 8 marksYour company wants to change the material of a product without telling customers, because the contract does not name materials. Discuss whether this is ethical, using one ethical theory and one clause from a code of ethics.

It is legal but not ethical. The contract specifies function only, so the letter is met, but the change is material and silence misleads the customers by omission.

Code: engineers shall be objective and truthful in professional statements and shall provide all pertinent supporting information; they also act for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees. Hiding a cost-saving change breaks both.

Theory: under social contract theory, individuals implicitly accept a social contract on the condition that others follow the rules as well. Customers contract assuming suppliers will not conceal significant changes. Concealment breaks that implicit contract and violates the customers' right to know.

Conclusion: tell the customers, show test evidence, and offer a fair share of the savings. There is often no definitive right or wrong, but disclosure is the best-justified action.

Marker words: Case 3, recycled-composite wall sections

Say it like this:

A change that is within the letter of a contract can still breach its spirit; engineers must act as faithful agents or trustees, be objective and truthful, and under social contract theory the customers' right to know requires disclosure.
