Case 4: security systems, surveillance and biometrics

The case retold

Your company makes security systems. Until now these raised few ethical problems, because the products were traditional: armed guards, locks, reinforced alloys that are hard to cut or drill, and similar methods.

As a design engineer you realise that modern technology allows much more comprehensive security packages. These could include extensive video and audio surveillance equipment and biometric monitoring devices for employees or other people seeking entry to secure areas. Biometric devices use highly personal data such as fingerprints, retinal patterns or voice patterns.

A literature search shows many ethical concerns about collecting and using such personal data. High-tech surveillance could easily become spying carried out without the knowledge of employees, and it would violate their privacy. The data gathered for security could also be sold or used outside legitimate workplace contexts by unscrupulous customers of your systems.

Your boss wants as much of this advanced technology as possible in future systems, because customers like the features and will pay well. You are concerned. The slide asks: as an engineer, do you have an ethical responsibility not to include such questionable technologies in products you design and sell, or to include them only in forms that are difficult to misuse? Or is misuse an ethical problem only for the customers who buy the equipment, and not your responsibility as an engineer?

Overlap with privacy. This case is a privacy case in engineering clothing. The right to privacy, the privacy-versus-security trade-off and surveillance by governments are taught in section t18. Workplace monitoring, data mining, facial recognition and the "nothing to fear" argument are in section t20. Use their vocabulary here.

Model resolution using the seven template headings

StepModel content
1. FactsA security-systems maker could add video and audio surveillance and biometric entry devices (fingerprints, retina, voice) to its products. These bring risk of covert spying and of sale or misuse of the data by customers. The boss wants the features because they sell. The design engineer is concerned.
2. StakeholdersDirectly involved: you (the design engineer), your boss and the company, the customers who buy the systems (employers). The instigator of the issue is the boss's push for features, and you identified the ethical problem. Indirectly implicated: employees and visitors who are monitored, regulators and data-protection authorities, owners and shareholders, and criminals or third parties who might buy or steal the data. Affected: everyone whose body data is collected.
3. Ideals and rightsRight to privacy (central) and the right to know that one is being monitored; honesty and fairness (secret monitoring is unfair); duty of care for the data. Trust: employees trust the employer, and the customer trusts the maker, to use the data only for security. The company has a right to property in its products and customers have a right to protect their premises, so rights conflict.
4. ObligationsLaw: privacy and data-protection law applies to the collection and use of personal data (see t18 and t20). Code: canon "hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public"; canon "perform services only in the areas of their competence"; canon "build their professional reputations on the merit of their services"; the preamble purpose "to safeguard life, health, and property, to promote the public welfare". Obligations list: to produce a sound and safe product, to avoid misleading people, to the profession and industry, to owners and shareholders. Ethical infringement: designing a product that makes spying easy, with no safeguard, would shift harm onto people who never agreed to it.
5. ConsequencesIf you include everything without safeguards: short term, strong sales and happy customers; long term, privacy violations, data leaks and sale of personal data, lawsuits, regulation, loss of reputation, and identity-based crimes because fingerprints and retina cannot be changed once stolen. If you include nothing: you lose sales and competitiveness, and customers may buy from a less careful maker. If you include the technology with safeguards (privacy by design): sales continue, harm is much reduced. Who benefits: the company, customers, security of premises. Who is harmed: monitored people if the data is abused.
6. TheorySocial contract theory (rights-based). Individuals implicitly accept a social contract on the condition that others follow the rules as well, and the rules centre on respecting natural rights to life, liberty and property. Employees accept monitoring at work within a sphere of freedom, and only for the stated security purpose. Covert or unlimited collection goes beyond that implicit agreement and breaks the rule of respecting the right to privacy. The maker who designs the tool shares responsibility for what it makes easy, so it must build in limits. (Utilitarianism would ask whether security gains exceed privacy harms; its weakness is that a minority's privacy can be traded away.)
7. SummaryDo not simply refuse and do not simply sell everything. As a design engineer I do have a responsibility, because designers decide what a product makes easy. I should propose including the technologies only in forms that are difficult to misuse: visible notice of monitoring, no hidden audio, encrypted storage of biometric templates (not raw images), access logs, limited retention, no export of data and a contract clause forbidding use outside security. If management insists on a version with no safeguards, I should record my objection and decline to design the covert features. Misuse by customers is partly their ethical problem, but this does not remove the maker's duty. There is often no definitive right or wrong, but this is the best-justified course.

Why the "it is only the customers' problem" view fails

  • Foreseeability. The case itself says misuse is easy and likely, so the harm is foreseeable. An engineer is responsible for foreseeable consequences of a design.
  • Design decides what is easy. A product built with no logs, no encryption and a hidden-recording mode makes abuse the default. Safeguards make abuse hard.
  • Public welfare. The canon and the preamble put the safety and welfare of the public (including monitored people) first, above the employer's preference.
  • The fair counter-point. A product is not responsible for every use. A lock can be used by a thief to protect stolen goods. So the duty is to take reasonable steps to prevent misuse, not to guarantee that no misuse can ever occur.

beyond the slides Designers call this privacy by design or data minimisation: collect only what is needed, keep it only as long as needed, and build the limits into the product rather than leaving them to customers' goodwill.

If the exam asks this

Answer skeleton. (1) Facts: surveillance and biometrics, boss wants them, risk of spying and data sale. (2) Stakeholders: you, boss, customers, monitored people, regulators. (3) Right to privacy central; honesty; trust. (4) Privacy law; canon "hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public"; preamble "safeguard life, health, and property, to promote the public welfare". (5) Short and long term, who benefits, who is harmed. (6) Social contract: sphere of freedom, implicit agreement, natural rights. (7) Include only in forms difficult to misuse; object in writing if refused; there is often no definitive right or wrong.

Practice · 8 marksA design engineer is asked to add fingerprint and voice recording to a security system, knowing buyers could use it to spy on staff. Does the engineer bear any ethical responsibility for misuse by customers? Argue for one view using an ethical theory.

Yes, the engineer shares responsibility. Misuse is foreseeable and the design determines how easy misuse is.

Using social contract theory: employees implicitly accept a social contract and act within a sphere of freedom only while the rules, including respect for the right to privacy, are followed. Covert audio and unlimited biometric data break that rule. The maker who builds the means of covert spying helps to break it.

The code says engineers shall hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public, which includes the people being monitored.

The responsibility is not to refuse all such technology but to include it only in forms difficult to misuse: visible notice, no hidden recording, encrypted templates, access logs and a limit on retention. If the employer wants covert spying, I should decline that part. There is often no definitive right or wrong, but this is the best-justified action.

Part 4

Professional bodies and codes

3 sections, about 1 h 55 min of reading.

Model rules: obligations to society, employers and engineers

~35 min to readHigh priority6 questions

Source: Set 4, slides 11-25 (UIPE and ERB Model Rules of Professional Conduct)

The model rules and their preamble

Slide 11 names the two Ugandan bodies whose model rules the lecturer uses. UIPE is the Uganda Institute of Professional Engineers. ERB is the Engineers' Registration Board. Their Model Rules of Professional Conduct say what a registered engineer must and must not do. The rules are grouped by the party the engineer owes the duty to. There are three groups, and a past question asks for exactly these three:

  1. Obligation to society (slides 13-15).
  2. Obligation to employers and clients (slides 16-22).
  3. Obligation to other engineers, which the exam calls "the engineering profession" (slides 23-25).

The preamble (slide 12)

The preamble states the purpose of the whole set of rules: to safeguard life, health, and property, to promote the public welfare, and to maintain a high standard of integrity and practice. Every later rule serves one of these three aims. When you answer an obligations question, you can open with this sentence and then name the three groups.

Key point. The slides number the rules separately inside each group (1, 2, 3 ... in society; 1, 2 ... in employers). Do not try to memorise a single rule number. Memorise the heading words, such as "whistle blowing", "clean hands" and "full disclosure", because those are the labels the lecturer gave.

Watch out. The past solution files answer "obligations to each stakeholder" with generic points (environmental impact, continuous learning, mentorship, community engagement). Those points are not in the slides. The slides contain specific rules, and the model answers below follow the slides. Where a solution-file point is useful but not on the slides, it is marked "beyond the slides".

Obligation to society

Slides 13-15 list eight rules under the heading "Obligation to Society". The slide itself gives the group a sub-heading for each cluster. The wording below is the slide wording.

Broad context of responsibility (rules 1 and 2)

  1. "While performing services, the engineer's foremost responsibility is to the public welfare."
  2. "Engineers shall approve only those designs that safeguard the life, health, welfare, and property of the public while conforming to accepted engineering standards."

Rule 1 sets the order of loyalty: public first, employer and client second. Rule 2 turns that into a test at the approval stage. An engineer signs off a design only if it protects the public and meets accepted standards. This is why a seal or signature carries ethical weight.

Whistle blowing (rule 3)

  1. "If an engineer's professional judgment is overruled resulting in danger to the life, health, welfare, or property of the public, the engineer shall notify his/her employer or client and any appropriate authority."

Read the trigger carefully. It has two parts: the engineer's professional judgment was overruled, and the result is danger to the public. Only then must the engineer notify two parties: first the employer or client, and also any appropriate authority. The slide does not say "go to the press". The word is "authority". For the theory of whistleblowing (conditions, internal versus external, effects on the whistleblower) see section t21.

Truth in duties (rules 4 and 5)

  1. "Engineers shall be objective and truthful in professional reports, statements, or testimonies and shall provide all pertinent supporting information relating to such items."
  2. "Engineers shall not express a professional opinion publicly unless it is based upon knowledge of the facts and a competent evaluation of the subject matter."

Rule 4 covers what the engineer writes or says in an official capacity: reports, statements and testimonies (for example in court). Two duties: be objective and truthful, and supply the supporting information, so nothing relevant is left out. Rule 5 covers public opinions. A public opinion is allowed only when two conditions are met: knowledge of the facts, and a competent evaluation.

The duty of full disclosure (rule 6)

  1. "Engineers shall not express professional opinion on subject matters for which they are motivated or paid, unless they explicitly identify the parties on whose behalf they are expressing the opinion and reveal the parties' interest in the matters."

This is about hidden sponsors. If you are paid or motivated to speak on a matter, the audience must be told on whose behalf you speak and what that party stands to gain. Example (beyond the slides): an engineer paid by a cement company who praises that company's product on radio must say that the company is paying.

The "clean hands" rule (rule 7)

  1. "Engineers shall not enter business ventures or permit their names or their firm's names to be used by any persons or firm which is engaging in dishonest, fraudulent, or illegal business practice."

The engineer keeps clean hands in two ways: by not joining such ventures, and by not lending a personal or firm name to them. A respected name gives a dishonest business credibility, and the rule forbids that.

Final obligation to society (rule 8)

  1. "Engineers who have knowledge of possible violation of any of the rules listed in this and the following two parts shall provide pertinent information and assist the state board in reaching final determination of the possible violation."

"This and the following two parts" means society, employers and clients, and other engineers. If you know of a possible breach of any of them, you must give the information and help the board decide. In Uganda the board is the ERB (the slide says "state board", from the model it was taken from). This makes the profession self-policing.

QB B4(i) · 3 marksDescribe a registered engineer's obligation to the following stakeholder group: (i) Society.

Under the UIPE/ERB model rules, the engineer's foremost responsibility is to the public welfare. The rules are meant to safeguard life, health, and property.

1. Approve only safe designs. The engineer approves only designs that safeguard the life, health, welfare and property of the public and conform to accepted engineering standards.

2. Whistle blowing. If the engineer's judgment is overruled and the public is in danger, the engineer must notify the employer or client and any appropriate authority.

3. Truth in duties. Reports, statements and testimonies must be objective and truthful, with all pertinent supporting information. Public opinion must rest on knowledge of the facts and competent evaluation.

Further duties: full disclosure of the party on whose behalf one speaks, the "clean hands" rule against dishonest, fraudulent or illegal ventures, and helping the state board with possible violations.

Obligation to employers and clients

Slides 16-22 give the engineer's duties to the people who hire or pay them. Slides 16 and 17 are the same slide repeated, so there are six headings: professional competence, validity of approvals, confidentiality, conflict of interest, full disclosure, and government conflicts of interest.

Professional competence (slides 16-17)

  1. "Engineers shall not undertake technical assignments for which they are not qualified."
  2. "Engineers shall approve or seal only those plans or designs that deal with subjects in which they are competent and which have been prepared under their direct control and supervision."

Rule 1 stops an engineer accepting work outside their training. Rule 2 is about the seal. Two conditions must both hold before sealing: the subject is within the engineer's competence, and the work was prepared under the engineer's direct control and supervision. Sealing a junior's drawings without supervising them breaks the rule. (This links to the individual competence principle in section t04.)

The validity of approvals (slide 18)

"Engineers may coordinate an entire project provided that each design component is signed or sealed by the engineer responsible for that design component."

A project manager-engineer may lead a big project made of many disciplines. The project is valid only when each part carries the signature or seal of the engineer who is responsible for that part. The coordinator does not seal what they are not competent in. Example (beyond the slides): on a building, the structural engineer seals the structure and the electrical engineer seals the wiring, and the coordinator seals neither on their behalf.

Confidentiality requirement (slide 19)

"Engineers shall not reveal professional information without the employer's or client's prior consent except as authorized or required by law."

Two points. The default is silence, and the way out is the prior consent of the employer or client, not consent given afterwards. The one exception is where the law authorizes or requires disclosure, for example a court order.

Conflict of interest (slide 20)

  1. "Engineers shall not solicit or accept direct or indirect considerations, financial or otherwise, from contractors, their agents, or other parties while performing work for employers or clients."
  2. "Engineers shall disclose to their employers or clients potential conflicts of interest or any other circumstances that could influence or appear to influence their professional judgment or their service quality."

Rule 1 bans taking benefits (gifts, money, favours) from contractors or others while working for an employer or client. "Direct or indirect" closes the loophole of benefits passed through a relative or agent. Rule 2 is a duty to disclose. Note the words "potential" and "appear to influence": the engineer must disclose even when no harm has happened and even when the influence is only apparent. Theory of conflict of interest (actual versus potential, situations, cases) is in section t21.

Full disclosure (slide 21)

"An engineer shall not accept financial or other compensation from more than one party for services rendered on one project unless the details are fully disclosed and agreed by all parties."

Being paid twice for one project creates divided loyalty. It is allowed only if two things happen: full disclosure of the details and the agreement of every party. Do not confuse this "full disclosure" with the society-group "duty of full disclosure" (rule 6, about naming the party you speak for). The words are the same but the rules are different.

Government conflicts of interest (slide 22)

"To avoid conflicts of interest, engineers shall not solicit or accept a professional contract from a governmental body on which a principal or officer of their firm serves as a member. An engineer who is a principal or employee of a private firm and who serves as a member of a governmental body shall not participate in decisions relating to the professional services solicited or provided by the firm to the governmental body."

There are two limbs. First, the firm must not seek or take a contract from a government body where one of the firm's principals or officers is a member. Second, an engineer who sits on a government body while working for a private firm must stay out of any decision about that firm's services to that body. Example (beyond the slides): an engineer who sits on a district tender board must leave the room when the board considers a bid from his own firm.

QB B4(ii) · 3 marksDescribe a registered engineer's obligation to the following stakeholder group: (ii) Employers and clients.

1. Professional competence. The engineer must not undertake technical assignments for which they are not qualified, and must approve or seal only plans prepared under their direct control and supervision.

2. Confidentiality. The engineer must not reveal professional information without the employer's or client's prior consent, except as authorized or required by law.

3. Conflict of interest. The engineer must not solicit or accept direct or indirect considerations from contractors while working for the employer or client, and must disclose potential conflicts that could influence, or appear to influence, professional judgment.

Also: validity of approvals (each component sealed by the responsible engineer), full disclosure (no compensation from more than one party on one project unless fully disclosed and agreed by all), and the rule on government conflicts of interest. Beyond the slides: the CAT solution files describe this duty as acting as a "faithful agent or trustee", a phrase from the canons that you can add.

Obligations to other engineers

Slides 23-25 cover how engineers must treat each other and the market for work. This is the group the exam calls "the engineering profession". It has three headings: obligation to potential employers, conflicts of interest, and reputations of other engineers.

Obligation to potential employers (slide 23)

"Engineers shall not misrepresent or permit misrepresentation of their or any of their associate's academic or professional qualifications. They shall not misrepresent their level of responsibility or the complexity of prior assignments. Pertinent facts relating to employers, employees, associates, joint ventures, or past accomplishments shall not be misrepresented when soliciting employment or business."

This is honesty in CVs and bids. Four things must not be misrepresented: qualifications (yours and your associates'), your level of responsibility, the complexity of past jobs, and facts about employers, employees, associates, joint ventures or past achievements. The words "or permit" matter: staying silent while someone else exaggerates for you is also a breach.

Conflicts of interest (slide 24)

"Engineers shall not directly or indirectly give, solicit, or receive any gift or commission, or other valuable consideration, in order to obtain work, and shall not make contribution to any political body with intent of influencing the award of contract by governmental body."

Work must be won on merit. Three acts are banned: giving, soliciting or receiving gifts, commissions or other valuable consideration to get work; doing so directly or indirectly; and making political contributions meant to influence a government contract. A gift to a tender official, or a "facilitation fee" to win a bid, is the typical breach (example beyond the slides).

Reputations of other engineers (slide 25)

  1. "Engineers shall not attempt to injure, maliciously or falsely, directly or indirectly, the professional reputations, prospects, practice or employment of other engineers, nor indiscriminately criticize the work of other engineers."
  2. "Criticize cautiously and objectively with respect to the person's professional status."

The rule does not ban criticism. It bans malicious or false injury and indiscriminate criticism. Where criticism is justified (for example, you find a design fault in a colleague's work) it must be cautious, objective, and mindful of the person's professional status. Compare rule 8 in the society group: if you know of a possible violation you must also help the state board, so criticism through the proper channel is allowed.

Key point. Slides 20, 22 and 24 all deal with conflicts of interest, in three different settings. Slide 20: gifts and double pay while working for an employer or client. Slide 22: government bodies and your own firm. Slide 24: gifts, commissions and political contributions to win work. A question on "conflict of interest clauses in the model rules" wants all three, each with its wording. The deeper theory is in section t21.

QB B4(iii) · 3 marksDescribe a registered engineer's obligation to the following stakeholder group: (iii) The engineering profession.

The model rules call this the obligation to other engineers.

1. No misrepresentation. The engineer must not misrepresent, or permit misrepresentation of, academic or professional qualifications, level of responsibility or the complexity of prior assignments when soliciting employment or business.

2. No improper inducements. The engineer must not directly or indirectly give, solicit or receive any gift or commission in order to obtain work, nor make political contributions to influence the award of a government contract.

3. Protect reputations. The engineer must not maliciously or falsely injure the reputation, prospects, practice or employment of other engineers, nor indiscriminately criticize their work, and must criticize cautiously and objectively.

CAT 1 (ethics-cat-1) Q1c · 2 marks eachDescribe the obligations of a registered engineer to each of the following stakeholder groups: (i) society, (ii) employers and clients, (iii) the engineering profession.

(i) Society. The foremost responsibility is to the public welfare. The engineer approves only designs that safeguard life, health, welfare and property, and notifies the employer or client and any appropriate authority if overruled in a way that endangers the public.

(ii) Employers and clients. Professional competence (accept and seal only work they are qualified for and have supervised) and confidentiality (no revealing information without prior consent, unless the law requires it). The engineer must also avoid and disclose conflicts of interest.

(iii) The engineering profession. No misrepresentation of qualifications or past work, no gifts or commissions to win work, and no malicious or false injury to the reputations of other engineers; criticize cautiously and objectively.

2020-21 exam Q1D · marks not statedDescribe the obligations of a registered engineer to each of the following stakeholder groups: (i) Society, (ii) Employers and Clients, (iii) The Engineering Profession.

Answer exactly as in QB B4 (i-iii) and CAT 1 Q1c above. QB B4 reads: Describe a registered engineer's obligation to the following stakeholder groups: (i) Society (3 marks); (ii) Employers and clients (3 marks); (iii) The engineering profession (3 marks). The CAT 1 version asks the same three parts at 2 marks each. In one line each:

(i) Society. The foremost responsibility is to the public welfare: approve only designs that safeguard life, health, welfare and property, and notify the employer or client and the appropriate authority if overruled in a way that endangers the public.

(ii) Employers and clients. Competence, confidentiality and avoiding or disclosing conflicts of interest.

(iii) The profession. No misrepresentation of qualifications, no gifts or commissions to win work, and no malicious or false injury to the reputations of other engineers.

Size it to the marks and lead each point with its marker word. Generic points from the solution files (environmental impact, continuous learning, mentorship) are not in the slides and score less than the specific rules.

Slides 20, 22, 24 · practiceState the conflict-of-interest clauses in the UIPE/ERB model rules.

1. Employers and clients (considerations). Engineers shall not solicit or accept direct or indirect considerations, financial or otherwise, from contractors, their agents or other parties while performing work for employers or clients, and shall disclose potential conflicts of interest or circumstances that could influence or appear to influence their judgment or service quality.

2. Employers and clients (government). Engineers shall not solicit or accept a professional contract from a governmental body on which a principal or officer of their firm serves, and an engineer who sits on such a body shall not participate in decisions on the firm's services to it.

3. Other engineers. Engineers shall not directly or indirectly give, solicit or receive any gift or commission in order to obtain work, nor contribute to a political body to influence the award of a government contract.

Contract law and the problems of law in engineering

~25 min to readMedium priority3 questions

Source: Set 4, slides 26-29; Set 6, page 3 (second half) and page 4 (first half)

Contract law: what makes a contract

The slides place contract law under the heading "Engineering Ethics and Legal Issues". Engineers work through contracts all the time: with clients, employers, suppliers and subcontractors. So an engineer needs to know when a promise becomes legally binding. This links to the obligations to employers and clients in section t09.

The slide definition is short. A contract is a mutual agreement between two or more parties to engage in a transaction which provides benefits to each of them. Three elements are listed.

  1. Mutual consent. All parties agree to the same thing, freely and knowingly. There is a "meeting of minds". If one side is forced or misled, there is no real consent.
  2. Offer and acceptance. One party makes an offer with definite terms. The other accepts it. Acceptance must match the offer. If the other party changes the terms, that is a counter-offer, not an acceptance.
  3. Consideration. Each side gives or promises something of value to the other. A contract is an exchange, not a one-way gift. A promise to give something for nothing is normally not enforceable.

Key point. Three elements, in this order: mutual consent, offer and acceptance, consideration. If any one is missing, there is no legally enforceable contract.

Other contract issues

Slide 27 adds three points about when an agreement is legally enforceable.

  • It needs a definite promise by each party to do something specific. Vague statements such as "we will look after you" are not enough. The promise must say what will be done.
  • Each party must receive some benefit it did not have before. This is the slide's way of describing consideration.
  • The agreement does not have to be in writing to be valid. A spoken agreement can bind. Writing matters mainly as proof, not as a requirement. beyond the slides Some contracts, such as sale of land, do need writing by statute, but the slides do not cover this.

Breach of contract

Slide 28: a breach is an actual violation of the terms in the contract. It must really occur. A fear that the other side might fail is not a breach. The slide gives three points.

  1. Breach happens when items are not supplied, are supplied but of substandard quality, or are not supplied until long after a deadline.
  2. The party in breach is required to provide an equivalent value previously offered. The other side must be put in the position it was promised.
  3. If a party cannot fulfil the contract, it is under an ethical and legal imperative to do everything possible to provide equivalent value to the other party. Inability does not remove the duty. It changes it into a duty to make up the loss as far as possible.

Watch out. Point 3 joins ethics and law in one sentence: the imperative is "ethical and legal". Quote both words when you discuss breach in an ethics answer.

The letter versus the spirit of the law

Slide 29 gives one instruction: "read between the lines" in terms of the intent of the documents as understood by those who formulated them. The letter of a law or contract is its exact words. The spirit is the purpose its authors had. An ethical engineer follows the purpose, not only the wording. Someone who obeys the letter and defeats the spirit is acting like the "minimal compliance" described below. The difference between law and ethics is covered in section t06.

Case question: Madge and Harold

This is the contract question in the bank. Read it as a law problem first, then as an ethics problem.

QB C1 · 8 marksMadge's shop has been robbed. She says to Harold, a police officer: "If you find the thief, I will pay you $500." Harold, through the course of his police investigations, finds the thief, and the thief is convicted of the robbery. Madge refuses to pay. Advise Harold. [reconstructed from garbled scan]

Issue. Is Madge's promise a legally enforceable contract, so that Harold can make her pay the $500?

Rule. A contract is a mutual agreement between parties to a transaction that provides benefits to each. It needs mutual consent, offer and acceptance and consideration. It need not be in writing, so the spoken promise is not a problem by itself.

Application.

  1. Offer. Madge made a definite promise: $500 for finding the thief. It was addressed to Harold, and it is clear and specific. beyond the slides In common law such a reward is a unilateral offer, accepted by doing the act (the Carbolic Smoke Ball case). Harold does not need to say "I accept". Finding the thief is the acceptance.
  2. Mutual consent. Both sides understood the terms. Nothing suggests force or misleading.
  3. Consideration. This is the crux. Consideration needs each party to receive some benefit it did not have before. Madge gains the thief's capture. But Harold is a police officer, and finding thieves is already his public duty. He gave Madge nothing he was not already bound to give. beyond the slides The common-law rule is that performing a duty you already owe, here a duty to the public, is not good consideration for a new promise. English cases apply this: England v Davidson (1840), where a police officer could not claim a reward for doing his duty, and Collins v Godefroy (1831), where a witness already bound to attend court could not claim payment for attending.
  4. Exception. beyond the slides The rule changes if Harold did something clearly beyond his normal duty, such as working in his own time or doing extra work Madge asked for. The facts say he found the thief "through the course of his police investigations", so he did only his job.

Conclusion on the law. Probably no enforceable contract, so Harold would most likely lose in court. I would advise him that a claim is weak, and that the outcome depends on whether any part of his work went beyond his police duty.

Ethical advice. The law is not the end of the matter. Madge made a promise and Harold relied on it. She benefited, and refusing to pay is dishonest and unfair, because she gets what she asked for and keeps the money. Her conduct fails the spirit of the deal even if it passes the letter of contract law. Ethically she ought to pay. On Harold's side, a police officer may be barred by service rules from taking rewards for official work. beyond the slides The slides' conflict-of-interest rule says engineers must not accept considerations from other parties while doing work for their employers (section t09). Harold should check whether he may accept the money at all, and should report it to his superiors. Being unable to sue does not make Madge's refusal right.

Summary. Offer yes, consent yes, consideration no, because police duty already existed. No legal remedy likely, but a clear moral duty on Madge to pay.

Marker words: the Madge and Harold answer

Say it like this:

Madge's promise is an offer but there is no consideration, because Harold gave no benefit he did not have before: finding thieves is his existing public duty. So the promise is probably not legally enforceable, but refusing to pay breaches the spirit and is unethical.

Offer and acceptance: yes; mutual consent: yes; consideration: no (Harold was already bound by his police duty), so no binding contract.

The problems of law in engineering

Set 6 lists five problems. The first is called the greatest. Learn all five, because the question asks for any three.

  1. Minimal compliance. This is the greatest problem. Engineers and employers search for loopholes in the law, to barely keep to its letter while violating its spirit. Engineers also tend to copy standard readymade specifications instead of coming up with innovative ideas, because meeting the standard is enough to be safe from blame. Minimal compliance led to the tragedy of the Titanic.
    The Titanic. beyond the slides The ship met the regulations of its day, which set the number of lifeboats by the ship's tonnage and not by the number of passengers. It therefore carried far fewer lifeboats than people on board. The law was obeyed and over 1,500 people still died. Set 6 itself describes the disaster as an emergency (collision with an iceberg at night) plus unpreparedness: too few lifeboats, inadequate training, and warnings of icebergs unheeded.
  2. Constantly updated laws lag behind technology. Continually updating laws and regulations can be counter-productive. It makes the law always lag behind technology, and it overburdens the rules and the regulators.
  3. "Non-laws". Many laws are laws without enforceable sanctions. They serve only as window dressing and give the public a false sense of security.
  4. Burdening the law on purpose. Opponents of a law may deliberately load it with many unreasonable provisions, so that its repeal is not far off.
  5. Powerful organizations break the law. Very powerful bodies, such as the government, may violate the laws when they think they can get away with it, by inviting challengers to face them in lengthy and costly court proceedings. This creates frustration with the law.

Key point. For a "list any three" question, give minimal compliance first (with Titanic), then two more. Name each in a short phrase and add one sentence of explanation. The marks go to the named problems.

2017 Q4E · 5 marksList any three problems associated with application of the law in the field of Engineering.
  1. Minimal compliance. Engineers and employers look for loopholes to keep to the letter of the law while violating its spirit, and they rely on standard readymade specifications instead of innovating. This led to the Titanic tragedy.
  2. Law lags behind technology. Continually updating laws and regulations is counter-productive. The law always lags behind technology and the rules and regulators become overburdened.
  3. "Non-laws". Many laws have no enforceable sanctions. They are window dressing and give the public a false sense of security.

(Other valid problems: opponents burden a law with unreasonable provisions so it is repealed; powerful organizations such as the government break the law and draw challengers into lengthy, costly court proceedings.)

The role of law in engineering

After the problems, Set 6 insists that it is wrong to write off rule-making and rule-following as futile. Good laws, effectively enforced, clearly produce benefits. The slides give these roles.

  • Laws ensure reasonable minimum standards of professional conduct.
  • They give most people and corporations a self-interested motive to comply, because breaking the law costs them.
  • They are powerful support and defence for those who wish to act ethically in situations where ethical conduct might not be welcome. An engineer who refuses an unsafe shortcut can point to the law. Codes of ethics play a similar part (section t11).
  • Viewing engineering as social experimentation gives engineers a better perspective on laws and regulations.

Precise rules versus broad guidelines

The slides say which kind of rule fits which situation.

SituationKind of rule that fits
Misconduct that violates well established and regularly re-examined procedures whose purpose is the safety of the publicPrecise rules and enforceable sanctions
Areas of experimentation, where outcomes cannot be fully knownBroad based guidelines that hold the engineer accountable for his or her decisions. Rules must not try to cover all possible outcomes of an experiment, nor force a rigidly specified course of action.

The reason is practical. Where the procedure is settled and safety is at stake, a fixed rule is easy to check and punish. Where the work is new, a rigid rule would block good judgement or would be out of date quickly, which is problem 2 above.

Practice · 4 marksState two benefits of law to the engineering profession and say when precise rules suit better than broad guidelines. (Original practice question, not from the bank.)

Benefit 1: reasonable minimum standards. Good laws, effectively enforced, ensure reasonable minimum standards of professional conduct.

Benefit 2: support and defence. Law gives powerful support to engineers who want to act ethically where ethical conduct might not be welcome. It also gives people and corporations a self-interested motive to comply.

Precise rules with enforceable sanctions suit well established, regularly re-examined procedures meant to protect public safety. Broad guidelines that still hold the engineer accountable suit experimentation, where not all outcomes can be foreseen.

Codes of ethics: functions, limitations and canons

~55 min to readHigh priority16 questions

Source: Set 6, pages 1-3 (ABET principles and canons, functions, limitations); Set 4, slides 30-32 (ASME principles and canons); Set 2, slides 30, 31 and 35 (three components, NSPE canons, notes about the code). The "problems of law" and "role of law" material on Set 6 pages 3-4 is in section t10. How the model rules apply to society, employers and the profession is in section t09.

What a code of ethics is, and what it contains

A code of ethics is a written statement published by a professional society that sets out the standards of conduct its members are expected to keep. The slides never give a one-line definition, so the sentence below is general knowledge. beyond the slides Everything after it is from the slides.

The Set 2 slides open this topic by pointing out that engineering has many fields (civil, mechanical, electrical, software, industrial) and that the same ethical issues arise across all of them. So one code of ethics pertains to engineers of all kinds.

The three components of the Engineering Code of Ethics

  1. The Fundamental Canons. They articulate the basic components of ethical engineering.
  2. The Rules of Practice. They clarify and specify in detail the fundamental canons of ethics in engineering.
  3. Professional Obligations. They elaborate the obligations that engineers have.

So the canons are the short headline statements. The rules of practice spell each one out. The obligations (to society, employers and clients, and the profession) are covered in t09.

Important notes about the code (Set 2, slide 35)

  • It is not a legally binding document.
  • It is not something we want (or need) engineers to memorize.
  • It is something we want engineers to understand and be able to live by as engineers.
  • However, in the beginning, knowing the code is a guide to understanding how to apply it.

Watch out. The slide says the code need not be memorized, but your CAT asks you to list canons and principles. For the exam you must reproduce the wording. Learn it by understanding each line, then use the drills below.

Why engineers should follow the code (Set 2 clicker question)

The slide asks why engineers should follow their professional code and offers four options. The answer the slide is steering towards is the one in the middle: the code provides a clear definition of what the public has a right to expect from responsible engineers. The other options are weaker reasons. The public will trust engineers more if they know there is a code (true, but a by-product). It helps avoid legal problems (the code is not a law). It raises the image of the profession and so gets engineers more pay (a motive, not an ethical reason). beyond the slides The slide does not print the answer; this reading follows the notes on slide 35.

2016 Q2A · 4 marksWhat is a professional code of ethics?

A professional code of ethics is a written set of principles and canons issued by a professional society that states the standards of conduct expected of its members. The engineering code has three components: the fundamental canons, which articulate the basic components of ethical engineering; the rules of practice, which clarify and specify the canons in detail; and professional obligations, which elaborate the obligations engineers have.

It is not legally binding. It is meant to be understood and lived by, and it gives the public a clear idea of what to expect from a responsible engineer. Example: the first canon, hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public.

2017 Q3A · 4 marks · see also t21Describe what is meant by a Code of Ethics citing clear supporting examples.

A code of ethics is a formal statement of the standards of conduct that a professional body expects of its members. It articulates the fundamental canons and is backed by rules of practice and professional obligations.

Examples: the ABET code, which opens "Engineers shall uphold and advance the integrity, honor, and dignity of the engineering profession", and the canon "perform service only in areas of their competence". The NSPE code and the ASME code carry the same kind of statements. The code is not legally binding; it guides conduct.

2020-21 Q1A, QB B2 · 5 marksWhat is meant by a Code of Ethics (COE) and what are the known weaknesses of CoEs?

Meaning. A code of ethics is a written set of fundamental principles and canons published by a professional society to guide the conduct of its members. It is not legally binding and is meant to be understood and lived by.

Weaknesses (from the slides, see the limitations section below):

  1. General and vague wording, so it cannot be applied straight away to every situation.
  2. Clauses can conflict and the code gives no priority, creating moral dilemmas.
  3. It cannot be the final moral authority; treating it so is ethical conventionalism.
  4. Separate codes for different societies make ethics look more relative than it is.

The unofficial solution file lists "lack of enforcement", "subjectivity" and "cultural differences". Those are not in the slides. Lead with the slide four and add one of them only if you have marks to fill.

2017 Q3B · 6 marksGive four (4) reasons behind why these codes are important to society.

Each reason below is one of the functions of codes in the slides, restated from society's side.

  1. Support for engineers who want to act ethically: an engineer under pressure can cite a publicly proclaimed code, so problems are spoken about openly before the public is harmed.
  2. Deterrence and discipline: the code is the basis for investigating unethical conduct, and punishment deters others.
  3. Education and mutual understanding: it lets engineers, clients and the public discuss moral responsibilities.
  4. Public image: it presents engineering as an ethically committed profession, and it establishes an agreed minimum level of ethical conduct.

Also available: inspiration and guidance, through positive language. The first canon, paramount safety, health and welfare of the public, is the clearest benefit to society.

2015 Q1B · 2 marks · 2011/12What is the purpose of a Code of Ethics in engineering practice?

The purpose is to guide and support engineers in ethical conduct and to set an agreed minimum level of ethical conduct. It gives inspiration and guidance, supports engineers under pressure, deters misconduct, and shows the public the profession is ethically committed, which raises trust.

CAT 2021-22 Q1A (as worded in the solution file)What do you understand by a professional code of conduct and how is it important for any engineer?

A professional code of conduct is a set of principles and canons that states the expected standards for members of a profession. It is important to an engineer because it provides support when under pressure to act unethically, gives guidance on safety, competence and honesty, and gives the public a clear picture of what to expect. The code is not legally binding but is the standard against which conduct is judged.

What do the Professional Obligations do?
They elaborate the obligations that engineers have.

It is not a legally binding document; it is not something we want (or need) engineers to memorize; it is something we want engineers to understand and be able to live by; in the beginning, knowing the code is a guide to understanding how to apply it.

The fundamental principles: ABET and ASME

The slides give two codes with the same opening. ABET (Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology) is on the Set 6 notes. ASME is on Set 4, slide 30. Both begin: "Engineers shall uphold and advance the integrity, honor, and dignity of the engineering profession by:" and then list the principles. ABET has four. ASME has three. The ASME slide uses "Engineers uphold and advance", without "shall".

#ABET Fundamental Principles (4)ASME Fundamental Principles (3)
1using their knowledge and skill for the enhancement of the human raceusing their knowledge and skill for the enhancement of human welfare
2being honest and impartial and serving with fidelity the public, their employers, and clientsbeing honest and impartial, and serving with fidelity the public, their employers and clients

Key point. The only wording difference is "human race" (ABET) against "human welfare" (ASME). The only extra principle is the fourth, ABET's "supporting the professional and technical societies of their discipline". For a 4-mark "list four fundamental principles" answer, give the ABET four.

Read as a set, the four principles say: use your skill to benefit people; be honest, impartial and loyal to the public, employers and clients; raise the standing of the profession; back your professional societies.

2016 Q2D · 4 marks · 2017 Q4C · CAT 2021-22 Q1CList four fundamental principles of the Engineers' code of ethics (common to the different engineering society codes of ethics).

Engineers shall uphold and advance the integrity, honor, and dignity of the engineering profession by:

  1. using their knowledge and skill for the enhancement of the human race (human welfare);
  2. being honest and impartial and serving with fidelity the public, their employers, and clients;
  3. striving to increase the competence and prestige of the engineering profession;
  4. supporting the professional and technical societies of their discipline.

The first three also appear word for word in the ASME code. The solution file for CAT 2021-22 gives integrity, competence, respect for others and responsibility to society. That list is not in the slides; it is a reasonable paraphrase but the slide wording above is what the lecturer taught.

CAT 1 2015 Q2C · 5 marksHighlight any 5 points of the IEEE code of ethics.

The slides do not print the IEEE code, only the ABET, ASME and NSPE codes, which share the same canons. Five points that appear in all of them and that you can give safely, in slide wording:

  1. Hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public.
  2. Perform services only in areas of their competence.
  3. Issue public statements only in an objective and truthful manner.
  4. Act for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees, and avoid conflicts of interest.
  5. Continue their professional development throughout their careers and support the development of engineers under their supervision.

beyond the slides The IEEE code itself also commits members to disclose conflicts of interest, reject bribery, and avoid injuring others; say so only if you are sure.

The fundamental canons: ABET, ASME and NSPE

The slides carry three lists of canons. ABET (Set 6) has seven. ASME (Set 4, slides 31 and 32, split over two slides) has seven. NSPE (Set 2, slide 31) has six. Set 6 spells the heading "Fundamental Cannons"; the correct spelling is canons, and that is what you should write.

Key point. When the exam says "list the seven fundamental canons", give the ABET list below in this order. It includes the honor, integrity and dignity canon that most seven-canon lists use. The ASME seven (below) is also a valid slide list of exactly seven.

The seven canons, in slide wording (ABET, Set 6 page 1)

Engineers shall:

  1. hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public in the performance of their professional duties;
  2. perform service only in areas of their competence;
  3. issue public statements only in an objective and truthful manner;
  4. act in professional matters for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees, and shall avoid conflicts of interest;
  5. build their professional reputations on the merits of their services and shall not compete unfairly with others;
  6. act in such manner as to uphold and enhance the honor, integrity and dignity of the profession;
  7. continue their professional development throughout their careers, and shall provide opportunities for the professional development of those engineers under their supervision.

One memory hook, in order: public, competence, statements, employer, reputation, honor, development.

The ASME canons (Set 4, slides 31 and 32)

Slide 31 gives three and slide 32 gives four. The ASME list reorders the ABET canons and swaps one: it has no "honor, integrity and dignity" canon and adds "associate only with reputable persons or organizations".

  1. Engineers shall hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public in the performance of their professional duties.
  2. Engineers shall perform services only in the areas of their competence.
  3. Engineers shall continue their professional development throughout their careers and shall provide opportunities for the professional development of those engineers under their supervision.
  4. Engineers shall act in professional matters for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees, and shall avoid conflicts of interest.
  5. Engineers shall build their professional reputations on the merit of their services and shall not compete unfairly with others.
  6. Engineers shall associate only with reputable persons or organizations.
  7. Engineers shall issue public statements only in an objective and truthful manner.

The NSPE canons (Set 2, slide 31)

"Engineers, in the fulfillment of their professional duties, shall:"

  1. Hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public.
  2. Perform services only in areas of their competence.
  3. Issue public statements only in an objective and truthful manner.
  4. Act for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees.
  5. Avoid deceptive acts.
  6. Conduct themselves honorably, responsibly, ethically, and lawfully, so as to enhance the honor, reputation, and usefulness of the profession.

The Set 2 bolts exercise (a sub-contractor supplies foreign-made bolts where only U.S.-made parts are allowed) ties the answer "tell the customer" to two NSPE canons: "Avoid deceptive acts" and "Act for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees". Full retelling is in t04.

The seven functions of codes of ethics

Set 6 lists seven roles or functions. Six are the useful functions. The seventh is listed as a function but is actually a warning. In order:

1. Inspiration and guidance

  • Codes provide a positive stimulus for ethical conduct and helpful guidance by using positive language.
  • Codes should be brief to be effective, so they offer only general guidance.
  • A number of societies or professional bodies add supplementary statements or guidelines giving specific directions.

2. Support

  • Codes give positive support to those seeking to act ethically.
  • An engineer under pressure to act unethically can use one of the publicly proclaimed codes to get support for his stand on specific moral issues.
  • Codes also serve as legal support for engineers.

3. Deterrence and discipline

  • Codes can be used as a basis for conducting investigations on unethical conduct.
  • They also provide a deterrent for engineers to act immorally.
  • Engineers punished by professional societies for proven unethical behaviour, by revoking the right to practise as engineers, also suffer public ridicule and loss of respect from colleagues and the local community.
  • This helps produce ethical conduct, even though it can be viewed as a negative way of motivation.

4. Education and mutual understanding

Codes can be used for discussion and reflection on moral issues, and so improve the understanding of moral responsibilities among all engineers, clients, the public and good organizations.

5. Contributing to the profession's public image

Codes present the engineering profession as an ethically committed society in the eyes of the public, enhancing its image.

6. Protecting status quo

Codes establish ethical conventions, which can help promote an agreed upon minimum level of ethical conduct.

7. Promoting business interests

Codes can place unwarranted restraints of commerce on business dealings. This is a danger, not a benefit: a code written to protect members' business can limit honest competition.

Watch out. Functions 5 (preserving the profession's public image) and 6 (protecting the status quo) are the two the slide says have been abused: the worst abuse is using "preserving profession's public image" and "protecting status quo" to restrict honest moral effort. Function 7 is listed as a function but is itself a warning (unwarranted restraints of commerce). If a question says "list six roles", give 1 to 6 and say that 5 and 6 can be abused. Add 7 as a negative if asked for more.

2016 Q2B · 10 marks · 2011/12List any SIX roles/functions of professional codes of ethics.

At about one and a half marks each, give the name, then one line.

  1. Inspiration and guidance: gives a positive stimulus to ethical conduct through positive language; because codes are brief, the guidance is general and societies add supplementary guidelines.
  2. Support: an engineer under pressure to act unethically can point to a publicly proclaimed code; it is also legal support.
  3. Deterrence and discipline: the code is a basis for investigating unethical conduct and deters misconduct, since offenders can lose the right to practise and face public ridicule.
  4. Education and mutual understanding: it prompts discussion and reflection on moral responsibilities among engineers, clients and the public.
  5. Contributing to the profession's public image: it presents engineers as an ethically committed group.
  6. Protecting status quo: it sets ethical conventions and an agreed upon minimum level of ethical conduct.

Seventh, if asked for more: promoting business interests, which can place unwarranted restraints of commerce on business dealings.

Practice · 4 marksExplain how a code of ethics supports an engineer, and how it deters misconduct.

Support. A code gives positive support to an engineer who wants to act ethically. An engineer under pressure from a manager to cut safety corners can point to a publicly proclaimed code to defend his stand on the moral issue. It also serves as legal support.

Deterrence. The code is a basis for investigating unethical conduct. An engineer found guilty can lose the right to practise and suffers public ridicule and loss of respect. This is a negative way of motivation but it still produces ethical conduct.

The seven functions of codes of ethics (Set 6).
1 Inspiration and guidance; 2 Support; 3 Deterrence and discipline; 4 Education and mutual understanding; 5 Contributing to the profession's public image; 6 Protecting status quo; 7 Promoting business interests.
Function 6: protecting status quo.
Codes establish ethical conventions, which can help promote an agreed upon minimum level of ethical conduct.
Function 7: promoting business interests.
Codes can place unwarranted restraints of commerce on business dealings.
Function 5: contributing to the profession's public image.
Codes present the engineering profession as an ethically committed society in the eyes of the public, thus enhancing their image.
Function 4: education and mutual understanding.
The codes can be used for discussion and reflection on moral issues and thereby improve the understanding of moral responsibilities among all engineers, clients, public and good organizations.

The relative importance of the functions

Set 6 ranks the functions through the idea of engineering as social experimentation: a new project is an experiment on society, so the people running it must be free to say what the risks are.

  • Support is the primary function. Only this support enables engineers to speak out clearly and openly their views to those affected by engineering projects.
  • Inspiration and guidance and education are also important, in promoting mutual understanding and in motivating engineers to act with higher moral standards.
  • Discipline is of secondary importance. People with unethical conduct, when exposed, are subject to law. Building elaborate paralegal procedures inside professional societies duplicates a job the legal system does better. At best, codes should discipline engineers in areas not covered by law.
  • The worst abuse of codes has been to restrict honest moral effort in the name of "preserving the profession's public image" and "protecting status quo". The best way to increase trust is by encouraging and aiding engineers to speak freely and responsibly about public safety.

So the ranking is: support first; inspiration, guidance and education next; discipline second-tier; and the image and status quo functions are the ones most open to abuse. The link to the law is developed in t10.

Practice · 5 marksWhich function of codes of ethics is the most important, and which is the most open to abuse? Give reasons.

The primary function is support. Seeing engineering as social experimentation, engineers must be able to speak out clearly and openly to those affected by projects, and only the support of a public code makes that possible. Inspiration and guidance and education come next because they promote mutual understanding.

The disciplinary function is of secondary importance: unethical conduct is subject to law, and paralegal procedures in societies duplicate the legal system.

The worst abuse is using "protecting the public image" and "status quo" to restrict honest moral effort. Trust is better built by helping engineers speak freely and responsibly about public safety.

The four limitations of codes of ethics

1. General and vague wording

Codes are restricted to general and vague wording. They cannot be straightaway applied to all situations. It is impossible to foresee the full range of moral problems that can arise in a complex profession like engineering. Example: "hold paramount the safety of the public" does not tell you how much safety margin a given bridge needs.

2. Clauses can conflict

It is easy for different clauses to come into conflict with each other. Usually codes provide no guidance as to which clause should have priority, so they create moral dilemmas. Example: "act as faithful agents" to an employer against "hold paramount the safety of the public" when the employer wants a defect hidden.

3. Not the final moral authority

Codes cannot serve as the final moral authority for professional conduct. If a professional society's code is taken as the last word, we have adopted one particular set of conventions, that is ethical conventionalism. Ethical conventionalism is the view that what is right is simply what the accepted conventions say.

4. Separate codes make ethics look relative

Andrew Oldenquist and Edward Slowter pointed out that separate codes for different professional societies can give members the feeling that ethical conduct is more relative than it is, and can convey to the public the view that none is "really right". The slides close this limitation with a balanced line: the current codes are by no means perfect but are definitely steps in the right direction.

Key point. Always add the closing line. It shows the marker you are weighing limitations, not dismissing codes: "not perfect, but steps in the right direction".

2016 Q2C · 6 marks · 2017 Q3C · 4 marksDescribe any FOUR limitations of a professional code of ethics. (2017: Discuss two limitations associated with the use/application of professional codes or codes of conduct.)
  1. General and vague wording. Codes cannot be applied straight away to all situations, and it is impossible to foresee the full range of moral problems in a complex profession like engineering.
  2. Clauses can come into conflict. Codes give no guidance on which clause has priority, creating moral dilemmas. Example: loyalty to an employer against the safety of the public.
  3. Not the final moral authority. Taking the code as the last word is ethical conventionalism, accepting one set of conventions as right.
  4. Separate codes make ethics seem relative. Oldenquist and Slowter noted that different societies' codes can make members feel ethics is more relative than it is and make the public think none is really right.

For the 2017 two-limitation version, give limitations 1 and 2 in full. Close with: the codes are not perfect but steps in the right direction.

CAT 2021-22 Q1DDiscuss four limitations of the use of professional codes of conduct and use one of the ethical theories either to support or refute these limitations.

Limitation 1: general and vague wording. Codes cannot be applied straight away to every situation. It is impossible to foresee the full range of moral problems in a complex profession like engineering.

Limitation 2: clauses come into conflict. Codes give no guidance on which clause has priority, which creates moral dilemmas, for example loyalty to an employer against the safety of the public.

Limitation 3: not the final moral authority. Taking the code as the last word is ethical conventionalism, accepting one set of conventions as right.

Limitation 4: separate codes make ethics seem relative. Oldenquist and Slowter noted that different societies' codes can make members feel ethics is more relative than it is, and make the public think none is really right.

Now use one theory (Kantian ethics below, with a utilitarian partial refutation).

Using Kantian (duty) ethics to support limitations 2 and 3. For Kant, a rule is binding only if it can be willed as a universal law, and duties must not contradict each other. A code with clauses that conflict and gives no priority leaves the engineer without a clear duty, so the limitation holds. Kant also holds that moral authority comes from reason and the categorical imperative, not from the conventions of a society, so treating a code as the final moral authority is ethical conventionalism, which duty ethics rejects.

Using utilitarianism to refute limitation 1 in part. A utilitarian would say general wording is acceptable if the code, on balance, produces more good than harm: broad canons are applied by judging consequences in each case, so vagueness is a flexibility as well as a weakness.

Using Kantian ethics to support limitation 4. Separate codes for separate societies make ethics look relative, which Kant rejects: a universal law binds every rational being, so moral rules should not vary from one society or body to another.

The unofficial solution applies consequentialism to support all four limitations. Either approach is acceptable if you name the theory and link it to a specific limitation. Theory definitions are in t01.

Ethical conventionalism (in the context of codes).
Taking the code of a professional society as the last word, so we are getting into a particular set of conventions.
Who pointed out that separate codes make ethics seem relative, and what did they say?
Andrew Oldenquist and Edward Slowter: separate codes for different professional societies can give members the feeling that ethical conduct is more relative than it is, and can convey to the public the view that none is "really right".

Writing a code for a small high-tech firm

The 2014/15 paper (Q1d, 7 marks) asks you to act as president of a small high-technology firm that has grown to the point where employees need ethics guidelines. 2015 Q1D · 7 marksImagine you are the president of a small high technology firm. Your company has grown over the last years to the point where you feel that it is important that your employees have some guidelines regarding ethics. Start by deciding what type of code is appropriate for your company. Then finally write a code that incorporates these features.

Type of code. beyond the slides I would choose a short code of conduct that is mainly aspirational with some enforceable rules. It must be brief so staff will read it, with positive language to give inspiration and guidance, and a few precise rules because a small firm cannot run elaborate disciplinary procedures. It is built on the same three components as the engineering code: canons, rules of practice, and obligations.

Code of ethics of [Firm name]. Employees shall uphold and advance the integrity, honor and dignity of the company and the engineering profession by being honest and impartial. Employees shall:

  1. Hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public in everything we design, build and sell.
  2. Perform services only in areas of their competence, and say so when a task is outside it.
  3. Issue statements to customers and the public only in an objective and truthful manner, and avoid deceptive acts in marketing and testing.
  4. Act for the firm and each client as faithful agents or trustees and avoid conflicts of interest, including keeping client data confidential.
  5. Build reputations on the merits of our work and not compete unfairly.
  6. Continue professional development and give juniors the chance to develop.

Rules of practice and obligations. Staff may raise a safety or ethics concern to the president or an ethics contact without penalty. Conflicts of interest must be disclosed. Breaches are investigated under the code and can lead to warning or dismissal. The code is not a legally binding document beyond the staff contract; it is to be understood and lived by, and is reviewed each year.

Fundamental canons; rules of practice; professional obligations.

Part 5

Intellectual property

4 sections, about 2 h 25 min of reading.

IP, protection types, copyright and fair use

~40 min to readHigh priority8 questions

Source: Set 5, slides 1-9

The Set 5 deck opens with a title slide that lists its four parts: intellectual property, protecting intellectual property, copyright and fair use, and challenges. Its sources are Baase (A Gift of Fire) and Quinn (Ethics for the Information Age). This section covers the first three parts. The challenges (digital copying, lawsuits, DRM, landmark cases) are in section t13, copyright law and software protection in t14, and open source in t15.

What is intellectual property?

The slide defines intellectual property in one line: any unique product of the human intellect that has commercial value. Two ideas carry the definition. The thing must come from a person's mind (it is a creation, not a natural object). It must also be worth money, so that someone would pay to use or copy it.

The slide gives three groups of examples. Learn them, because examples earn marks in a 2-mark definition question.

  • Books, songs, movies.
  • Paintings, drawings.
  • Inventions, chemical formulas, computer programs.

The last line of the slide is a rule: intellectual property is not physical property. Physical (tangible) property is a thing you can touch, such as land, a car or a machine. Only one person can hold or use it at a time, and if it is stolen the owner no longer has it. Intellectual property is an idea or a creation. It can be copied without taking anything away from the owner, many people can use it at once, and the same song can sit on a million devices. What the owner owns is the right to control copying and use, not a physical object. Buying a CD gives you the disc but not the song's copyright.

PointTangible (physical) propertyIntellectual property
FormPhysical thing you can touch: land, buildings, machineryCreation of the mind: a song, a design, a program, a formula
Use by othersOne user at a time; use by one excludes othersMany can use at once; copying leaves the original intact
TheftThe owner loses the itemThe owner keeps the original but loses control and income
ProtectionProperty law, locks, ownership documentsTrade secret, trademark, patent, copyright law, for a limited time
QB D1 · 2 marksHow is intellectual property different from tangible property?

Intellectual property is any unique product of the human intellect that has commercial value, for example a song, an invention or a computer program. It is intangible: the owner owns the creation and the right to control its copying and use, not a physical object. It can be copied without the owner losing the original, and many people can use it at once.

Tangible property is physical property such as land, buildings, machinery or vehicles. It can be touched, only one person can use it at a time, and if it is taken the owner loses it.

CAT 1 · Q2a · 2 marksWhat do you understand by the term intellectual property?

Intellectual property is any unique product of the human intellect that has commercial value. Examples are books, songs and movies, paintings and drawings, and inventions, chemical formulas and computer programs. It is not physical property: the law gives the creator limited ownership rights over it, protected as a trade secret, trademark, patent or copyright.

Protecting IP: two competing goals

The slide says protection has to serve two competing goals.

  1. Benefiting society. Society wants new inventions and works to reach the public domain (free use by everyone) without delay. The sooner anyone can use a medicine formula or a program, the more people gain.
  2. Rewarding the creators. Creators must be paid for their work so that future inventions are promoted. If anyone could copy a work the day it appeared, no one would spend years creating it.

The goals pull against each other. Total secrecy and permanent ownership favour the creator and starve society. Instant free copying favours society now but kills the incentive to create. The slide gives the compromise: the government grants limited ownership rights to IP creators. "Limited" is the key word. The creator gets a monopoly for a fixed time (for example 20 years for a patent), and afterwards the work passes to the public domain.

The slide then names the protection types. It prints "Trade secrets, Trade secrets, Patents, and Copyrights", which is a typing slip. The four types are trade secrets, trademarks, patents and copyrights, and the next four headings follow that order.

Key point. When asked why governments protect IP, name both goals and the compromise: benefit society, reward creators, so government grants limited ownership rights. Naming only the reward side is half an answer.

Marker words: intellectual property and the two goals

Say it like this:

Intellectual property is any unique product of the human intellect that has commercial value, and it is not physical property. Because society wants benefit and creators want reward, the government grants limited ownership rights to creators.

Define intellectual property.
Any unique product of the human intellect that has commercial value.
The slide's examples of IP (three groups).
Books, songs, movies; paintings, drawings; inventions, chemical formulas, computer programs.
The two competing goals of IP protection.
Benefiting society (inventions reach the public domain without delay); rewarding the creators (promote future inventions).
The solution to the two competing goals.
The government grants limited ownership rights to IP creators.
The four protection types.
Trade secrets, trademarks, patents, copyrights.

Trade secrets

A trade secret is a confidential piece of IP that provides a company with a competitive advantage. It works only while it stays secret. Examples on the slide:

  • the formula for Coca-Cola syrup;
  • the internal design of a system;
  • customer lists.

The protection is unusual because the law does not do the work alone. The owner must take active measures to keep the secret from being discovered. The slide lists the measures:

  • Locked boxes (physical security for documents and samples).
  • Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) and non-compete clauses. An NDA binds an employee or partner not to reveal the secret. A non-compete clause stops a worker from joining a rival and using what they learned.
  • The Uniform Trade Secrets Act (UTSA). It imposes civil liability for misappropriation of trade secrets, meaning a person who steals or wrongly uses a secret can be sued for damages.

Unlike a patent, a trade secret has no filing, no fixed term and no public description. It lasts as long as it stays secret. If a rival works the formula out independently, or the owner is careless, protection is gone.

Trademarks

A trademark is a word, a logo, a sound, etc., that identifies a company or a product. Its job is to tell buyers who made the goods, so a customer can tell the real product from an imitation.

Protection: the company can sue for improper use of its trademark. There is a risk, though. If the trademark name becomes a common noun, the trademark may be lost, because the name no longer points to one company. The slide's examples are aspirin, escalator, thermos, xerox and yo-yo. These were once brand names and became ordinary words for the whole class of product.

Watch out. A trademark protects a name or sign, not an invention or a creative work. Do not write that a trademark protects a program's code. That is copyright.

Patents

A patent is a public document that provides a detailed description of an invention. In return for publishing the details, the owner gets an exclusive right to the invention. The owner can prevent others from making, using or selling the invention for 20 years. After 20 years the invention is in the public domain and anyone may use it.

This is the clearest case of the compromise in the two-goals slide. Society receives the full description of the invention immediately (it is public), and the inventor receives a monopoly for 20 years. Compare it with a trade secret: a patent is public and lasts 20 years, while a trade secret is hidden and can last forever.

beyond the slides To be patented an invention must normally be novel, non-obvious and useful, and the 20 years run from the date the application is filed. The past-paper solutions give these conditions.
