CAT 1 · Q2b · 6 marks; also 2017 Q2D · 6 marksDifferentiate between the different available methods of intellectual property protection.

The government grants limited ownership rights to creators through four methods.

1. Trade secrets. A trade secret is a confidential piece of IP that provides a company with a competitive advantage, for example the formula for Coca-Cola syrup or customer lists. The owner must take active measures to keep it secret, such as locked boxes, non-disclosure agreements and non-compete clauses. The Uniform Trade Secrets Act gives civil liability for misappropriation. It lasts only while the secret is kept.

2. Trademarks. A trademark is a word, logo or sound that identifies a company or a product. The company can sue for improper use, but it can lose the mark if the name becomes a common noun, as with aspirin or escalator.

3. Patents. A patent is a public document giving a detailed description of an invention. It gives the owner the exclusive right to prevent others from making, using or selling the invention for 20 years.

4. Copyrights. Copyright protects an original work such as a book, song or program and gives the owner five rights: reproduction, distribution, public display, public performance and production of derivative works. The length is set by copyright law.

Difference in short: trade secrets protect by secrecy, trademarks identify the source, patents protect inventions through a public document for 20 years, and copyright protects the expression of original works.

2014/15 Q5c; also 2011/12 and 2013/14 papers · 3 marksIdentify three (3) ways in which an engineer can protect intellectual property.

1. Patent the invention. This gives the engineer the exclusive right to stop others making, using or selling it for 20 years.

2. Claim copyright in original designs, drawings, reports and program code. This gives the five rights, including reproduction and derivative works.

3. Keep confidential designs and methods as trade secrets using non-disclosure agreements, non-compete clauses and locked storage.

Other acceptable ways: register a trademark for the product name or logo, and settle ownership of designs in the employment contract. beyond the slides

2016 Q4B · 6 marksWhat two forms of legal property protection are most frequently applied to software? List two or three of their key characteristics.

The two forms are copyright and patents.

Copyright.

  • It protects an original work (the program code) and gives the owner five rights: reproduction, distribution, public display, public performance and production of derivative works.
  • It arises automatically when the work is created, with no registration needed. beyond the slides
  • Its length is defined by copyright law (the slides in t14 teach the author's life plus 95 years; some past-paper solutions say life plus about 70, so give "a long period after the author's death" if unsure), after which the work enters the public domain.

Patents.

  • A patent is a public document that describes the invention in detail, so others can replicate it.
  • It gives an exclusive right: others cannot make, use or sell the invention for 20 years.
  • The invention must be novel, non-obvious and useful. beyond the slides

Whether software should be copyrighted or patented is itself debated: see t14.

Define a trade secret.
A confidential piece of IP that provides a company with a competitive advantage.
Three examples of trade secrets.
The formula for Coca-Cola syrup; the internal design of a system; customer lists.
Protections for a trade secret.
Owners must take active measures to keep it from being discovered: locked boxes; non-disclosure agreements (NDA) and non-compete clauses; the Uniform Trade Secrets Act (UTSA), which imposes civil liability for misappropriation.
Define a trademark.
A word, a logo, a sound, etc., that identifies a company or a product.
Trademark names that became common nouns.
Aspirin, escalator, thermos, xerox, yo-yo.
Define a patent, and what it gives the owner.
A public document that provides a detailed description of an invention. It gives the owner an exclusive right to the invention: the owner can prevent others from making, using, or selling it for 20 years.

Copyright and its five rights

Copyright provides the owner of an original work with five rights. Learn the list whole and in order, because it is a standard marker list.

  1. Reproduction (making copies).
  2. Distribution (selling, lending or giving out copies).
  3. Public display (showing the work in public, for example a painting or an image on a screen).
  4. Public performance (playing or performing the work in public, for example a song or a film).
  5. Production of derivative works (new works built on the original, such as a translation, a film of a novel or a modified version of a program).

The length of the protection is defined by copyright laws, and the slide adds that these laws have been expanded greatly over the years. The exact terms and the history of the extensions are in t14. beyond the slides Copyright protects the expression of an idea (the actual song, the actual code), not the idea itself, and it arises automatically when the work is created.

Anyone who does one of these five things without the owner's permission infringes the copyright, unless the use is a fair use.

CAT 1 2021-22 solution file · Q3c · marks not statedDescribe the key differences between intellectual property rights and copyrights.

Copyright is only one type of intellectual property right. IP is the whole family: trade secrets, trademarks, patents and copyrights.

  • Scope. IP rights cover inventions, names and logos, secrets and creative works. Copyright covers only original works such as books, songs, films and programs.
  • Rights given. Copyright gives five rights: reproduction, distribution, public display, public performance, derivative works. A patent gives the exclusive right to make, use or sell an invention for 20 years; a trademark lets the owner sue for improper use; a trade secret gives civil liability for misappropriation.
  • Duration. Copyright length is defined by copyright laws; a patent lasts 20 years; a trade secret lasts as long as it is kept secret.
  • Registration. Copyright arises automatically on creation, while patents need an application and registration. beyond the slides
Solution file · CAT 1 2021-22 Q4a · marks not statedWhat justifies the need of a copyright policy in the Engineering profession?

A copyright policy is justified by the two competing goals of IP protection: rewarding the creators and benefiting society. Five reasons:

  1. Protection of intellectual property. Engineers create original designs, drawings, reports and code. The five rights stop others reproducing, distributing or adapting them without permission.
  2. Incentive for innovation. Exclusive rights for a limited time reward the time and money put in, which promotes future inventions.
  3. Legal compliance. A policy tells staff what they may copy and use, so the firm and engineer avoid infringement and ownership disputes. Fair use limits are set out.
  4. Commercialisation. Ownership lets the engineer or firm earn from licensing, royalties and sales.
  5. Fair competition and professional integrity. It discourages plagiarism and unfair use of other people's work.

Fair use

Copyright does not give the owner total control. The slide says: under some circumstances it is legal to reproduce a copyrighted work without permission. This is fair use. It is how the law protects society's side of the two-goals trade-off, for example for teaching, criticism and research.

There is no fixed list of allowed copies. Courts consider four factors, and the slide gives a guide for each:

FactorWhat the court asksSlide guide
1. Purpose and character of useWhy was it copied? Teaching, criticism, private study, or profit?Educational use is generally OK
2. Nature of the workWhat kind of work was copied?Nonfiction and non-arts work are more permissible
3. Amount of the work being copiedHow much was taken?Small portions are more permissible
4. Effect on the commercial market for the workDoes the copy reduce sales or licence income of the original?Should have a negligible effect

Reading the guides the other way gives the factors against fair use: commercial use, creative or artistic works (a novel, a game, a film), copying a large portion or the heart of the work, and a copy that replaces a sale.

The slide's two examples

  • Journal articles on a class website (OK). A professor scans a few journal articles and posts them on his class website. Students in the class get in with a password. This is fair use: the purpose is educational, journal articles are non-fiction, only a few were copied, and the password keeps the audience to the class, so the market effect is negligible.
  • Painting slides (maybe not OK). An art professor photographs some paintings from a book as slides and uses them in her lectures. The use is educational, but the works are art (a creative work, so less permissible) and the copy might replace the sale or licence of the images. A court could go either way, which is why the slide says "maybe not OK".

Watch out. Fair use is a defence a court decides case by case on all four factors together. No single factor settles it, and "educational" alone does not guarantee a win.

Worked case: Mofonic, Bunten and Schaeffer (2016 Q6, 20 marks)

This question tests copyright, fair use and (beyond your slides) personality rights. Everything the slides cover is marked as such; the extra law is labelled. The answer is a memo to the judge in three parts, as the marks suggest: A claims (10), B defences (5), C remedies (5).

The facts, retold

  • The game. Mofonic Games made Stormcrasher, a fantasy epic about Thessia, a dragon trainer and mercenary. It runs only on the Degenatron console, has sold over 5 million copies and retails at $50. Players can customise every aspect of Thessia's looks, and the story cutscenes (short high-resolution videos) show Thessia as the player designed her.
  • Bunten. Roberta Bunten is the voice actress for Thessia. She worked six weeks, eight hours a day, in a studio Mofonic rented. Mofonic's producers directed her and chose the best take. She got a flat fee of $50,000 plus a $100,000 bonus when sales passed one million. Her contract says nothing about who owns the intellectual property.
  • The ending. Many players disliked the ending, in which Thessia dies. Fan Steve Schaeffer made a new ending. He designed his Thessia to look exactly like Bunten (an uncanny resemblance), then spliced game clips from all over the game, never more than two or three words from any one scene, to make a version where Thessia becomes Supreme Emperor and gets a birthday cake. He posted the video free on fan sites. Fans were split.
  • The sales. Schaeffer then offered "Stormcrasher: The Supreme Emperor Edition". A player sent him an original game disc and $10, and he mailed back a Degenatron disc carrying the game with his ending. He kept the originals and made coasters and wind chimes of them. He bought 500 blank discs for $1,000 and filled 300 orders, paying $4 postage each. Revenue was 300 x $10 = $3,000. Costs were $1,000 plus 300 x $4 = $1,200, so his profit was about $800.
  • Mofonic and Bunten have sued Schaeffer separately. You are law clerk writing the memo.
2016 Q6 · 20 marks (A 10, B 5, C 5)Write a memo to the judge explaining A. the intellectual property claims Mofonic and Bunten can bring (10 marks), B. any defenses Schaeffer can raise (5 marks), C. the remedies, if any, that Mofonic and Bunten might be entitled to (5 marks). [Facts as retold above; reconstructed from garbled scan.]

MEMORANDUM. To: the Judge. From: Law Clerk. Re: Mofonic Games and Bunten v. Schaeffer.

Summary. Mofonic has a strong copyright claim over the game discs Schaeffer copied and sold, a likely trademark claim, and a weaker claim over the free video. Schaeffer's best defence is fair use, which is strongest for the free video and weakest for the sold discs. Bunten has little or no copyright claim, but a plausible claim over the use of her likeness and voice. The recommended remedy is an injunction, destruction of the discs and an award of Schaeffer's profit.

A. Claims (10 marks)

Mofonic: copyright infringement. Stormcrasher is an original work (software, graphics, story, characters, sound), and Mofonic owns the copyright as the creator that paid for and directed it. Copyright gives the owner five rights, and Schaeffer exercised all five without permission. The four bullets below cover them, with public display and public performance taken together.

  • Reproduction. He copied whole game discs 300 times, and copied clips from many scenes to build the video.
  • Distribution. He mailed 300 copies to buyers.
  • Production of derivative works. The new ending changes the game's story and scenes. A new version of the work, fixed on a disc, is a derivative work.
  • Public display and public performance. He posted the video on popular fan sites, showing the clips publicly.

Mofonic's sales were not lost, since buyers already owned the game, but infringement does not require a lost sale.

Mofonic: other claims. beyond the slides (1) Trademark: the name "Stormcrasher: The Supreme Emperor Edition" uses Mofonic's mark to identify a product Mofonic did not make, so buyers may think it is an official edition. This is likely infringement or false designation of origin. (2) Breach of the game licence, if the game's terms forbid copying or modification, which the facts do not say.

Bunten: copyright. This claim is weak. She spoke lines in a studio Mofonic rented, directed by Mofonic's producers, for a flat fee and a bonus. A court will probably treat her performance as a work made for hire owned by Mofonic, or at least as licensed to Mofonic. The contract is silent, so she could argue she is a joint author of the voice performance, but courts are reluctant to give one performer separate copyright in her part of a finished audiovisual work. Even if she did own it, Schaeffer took only two or three words at a time.

Bunten: personality rights. beyond the slides This is her better claim. Schaeffer deliberately built a character with her exact face and used her recorded voice, then sold the result for $10. Many legal systems recognise a right of publicity (protection against commercial use of a person's identity without consent), and false endorsement (suggesting she approved the product). Her resemblance and voice are her own, and her contract with Mofonic does not license Schaeffer. She may also object that her words were re-arranged to say things she never said.

B. Defences (5 marks)

1. Fair use. Schaeffer can say that copying without permission is lawful. Courts weigh the four factors.

  • Purpose and character of use. For him: a fan wanting to give an alternative ending, a creative, transformative and critical purpose; the video was free. Against him: the discs were sold for $10, a commercial purpose that earned about $800 profit; and it is not educational.
  • Nature of the work. Against him: a game and its story are creative, imaginative works, which are less permissible than non-fiction.
  • Amount used. For him: from each scene he took only two or three words, small portions. Against him: on the discs he copied the entire game, and the ending he replaced is the part fans care about.
  • Effect on the market. For him: each buyer already owned the game and paid again for nothing Mofonic sold, so Mofonic lost no sale and he kept the originals. Against him: a market exists for licensed alternate endings and add-ons, and if every fan could copy and sell modified discs the effect would not be negligible.

Assessment. Fair use is likely to succeed for the free video and likely to fail for the sold discs.

2. First sale and owner's rights. beyond the slides Players may lawfully hand over their own discs, and he can say he simply swapped one disc for another. This fails because the doctrine lets an owner pass on a copy, not make new ones; he made 300 new copies and kept the originals.

3. Customisation and ideas. He can say that the player designs Thessia's look in this game, so appearance is the player's own choice, and that ideas such as "Thessia lives" are not protected, only the expression.

4. Against Bunten. She has no separate copyright (work for hire; she was paid $150,000 or more); the voice taken is tiny; and the work is fan commentary protected as free expression. Against trademark, he can say the edition was plainly a fan product, though the name works against him.

C. Remedies (5 marks)

  • Injunction. An order that Schaeffer stop copying and selling the discs and remove the video from the fan sites if it is held to infringe. This is the main remedy and it suits both claimants.
  • Impounding and destruction. beyond the slides The court can order the remaining blank and burned discs destroyed.
  • Damages and profits to Mofonic. beyond the slides Mofonic can recover its actual loss plus any profit of Schaeffer's attributable to the infringement, or statutory damages per work, which can be higher if the infringement was wilful. Actual loss is small because each customer already owned the game; Schaeffer's profit is about $3,000 revenue minus $2,200 costs = $800. The law allows him to deduct costs only if he proves them. Mofonic can also ask for its legal costs.
  • Remedies for Bunten. If her publicity claim succeeds: an injunction and damages equal to the commercial value of her identity, such as the licence fee she would have charged. If she proved joint authorship she could share income, but that would be claimed from Mofonic, not Schaeffer.
  • Limits. If fair use covers the video, no remedy for it. The court should avoid double recovery of the same $800 profit between the two claimants.

Recommendation. Find infringement of Mofonic's reproduction, distribution and derivative-work rights by the sold discs, grant an injunction and destruction order, award profit and costs, treat the free video as probable fair use, and hold Bunten's copyright claim weak but her likeness and voice claim open for trial.

Protection challenges, DRM and the landmark cases

~35 min to readHigh priority8 questions

Source: Set 5, slides 10-19. The definition of IP, the four protection types, copyright and fair use are in section t12. Copyright term history, the DMCA, software copyright and software patents are in section t14.

IP protection challenges: digital copies and peer-to-peer sharing

Copyright, patents and trade secrets were designed for a world of physical copies. Digital technology breaks the assumptions behind them. The slides list the challenges under the heading "IP Protection Challenges". The first is digital copies.

  • Easy to make perfect copies of CDs and DVDs. A photocopy or a cassette copy is worse than the original. A digital copy is identical to it, and a copy of a copy is identical too. Copying costs almost nothing.
  • Easy to download books, music and videos. Once content is digital, it travels over the network in seconds.
  • Peer-to-peer (p2p) networks allow strangers to share music and other data files. There is no shop, no publisher and no central owner in between. Any person with a connection can become a distributor.

The result is that the copyright owner's rights of reproduction and distribution (two of the five rights in t12) are exercised by millions of ordinary people, mostly without permission.

The RIAA lawsuits

The music industry body, the RIAA (Recording Industry Association of America), reacted by suing. The slides give these facts.

  • Since 2003 the RIAA has filed more than 26,000 lawsuits against individuals for illegal downloading.
  • Tanya Andersen: sued by the RIAA, and the case was dropped.
  • Jammie Thomas: fined $222K for sharing 24 songs.

The two names show both sides of the problem. One defendant was sued and the case was dropped. The other received a fine that looks far out of proportion to the value of 24 songs. Many people argue that suing individual users is an unfair and ineffective way to protect IP. It also does nothing about the people who run the sharing networks, which is why the network cases below matter.

beyond the slides Thomas was found liable for infringement at trial. The damages award was later changed on appeal and retrial. For the CAT, quote the slide figure of $222K for 24 songs and move on.

Fair use issues and the software protection question

The second group of challenges on slide 11 is posed as questions, not answers. Treat them as open debates.

  • Fair use issues. How do we draw the line between fair use and infringement? How do we protect the legal fair use right of ordinary users when owners add technical locks to content? (The four fair use factors are in t12.)
  • Software protection. Should software be copyrighted? Should software be patented? These two questions are answered in t14.

The three answers to the challenges: prevention, tracking, punishing

Slide 12 groups the responses into three words. Memorise them as a set of three, each with its example.

AnswerMeaningSlide example
PreventionMake copying technically hard or impossibleDigital IP protection techniques, for example DRMs
TrackingFind out who copied, and where a copy came fromDigital watermarking
PunishingMake infringement costly through the lawExtending copyright laws

Key point. The slide adds that this is an on-going process and that some of the changes are controversial. Use both phrases when you discuss the three answers.

Prevention is covered under DRM further down. Punishing is covered in t14 (longer terms, felonies, minimum damages, the DMCA). Tracking by digital watermark means hiding an identifying mark in the content so that a leaked copy can be traced.

ethics-cat-1 Q2c · 6 marksWith the aid of examples, briefly explain why intellectual property protection is much harder to enforce in this internet age.

Digital copies are perfect and cheap. A CD or DVD can be copied with no loss of quality and almost no cost, so each copy is as good as the original. Example: a song ripped from a CD is identical to the CD track.

Easy download and distribution. Books, music and videos can be downloaded in seconds, so the rights of reproduction and distribution are exercised by anyone. Example: a film uploaded once is downloaded by thousands.

Peer-to-peer networks let strangers share files directly with no central owner to control them. Example: Napster had 26 million registered users in two years, and Grokster ran a decentralized network.

Enforcement against individuals is difficult. The RIAA filed more than 26,000 lawsuits against individuals since 2003, yet sharing continues, and some cases were dropped (Tanya Andersen).

Technical protection (DRM) can be cracked. CSS on DVDs has a crack code, so the lock does not stop determined users.

Unclear fair use line. It is hard to separate legal copying such as time shifting or space shifting from infringement.

beyond the slides 7. Global reach: countries have different laws, so enforcement across borders is hard. 8. Anonymity: online users can hide their identity.

2017 Q2C · 5 marksBriefly analyze why intellectual property protection is that much harder to enforce in the internet age. Illustrate your positions with clear examples.

Perfect digital copies. Copying CDs, DVDs and files costs almost nothing and loses no quality. Example: a pirated DVD is identical to the original.

Easy download of books, music and videos. Content spreads worldwide at once. Example: an album leaked online.

Peer-to-peer file sharing lets strangers swap files without any intermediary. Example: Napster, which grew to 26 million users in two years.

Suing users does not scale. More than 26,000 individuals were sued since 2003, but millions still share.

DRM can be broken. The DVD encryption scheme CSS has been cracked, and the cracking code spread online.

beyond the slides 6. Global reach: countries have different laws, so enforcement across borders is hard. 7. Anonymity: online users can hide their identity.

Should software be copyrighted? Should software be patented?

Significant fair use cases: Sony and Diamond

Slide 13 gives two cases where the court decided that a form of private copying was fair use. They give the practical meaning of the fair use rule in t12.

Sony v. Universal City Studios [1976]

  • Issue: using a VCR to tape TV programmes for later viewing.
  • Verdict: time shifting is fair use. The US Supreme Court decided this by 5-4.

Time shifting means recording a broadcast you have a right to watch, so that you can watch it at a more convenient time. The viewer is not creating a new market for the programme. The date on the slide is 1976. beyond the slides That is when the suit began. The Supreme Court ruled in 1984, and the VCR in question was the Sony Betamax. Quote 1976 in the CAT as it is on your slides.

RIAA v. Diamond Multimedia Systems [1998]

  • Issue: transforming music CDs to MP3 format and playing them on the Rio player.
  • Verdict: space shifting is fair use.

Space shifting means moving content you already own from one medium or device to another, here from a CD to a portable MP3 player. The user has already paid for the music and uses it privately.

Watch out. Do not mix the two up. Sony is the VCR and time shifting. Diamond is the Rio MP3 player and space shifting. Both were decided in favour of the user.

Reverse engineering cases

Reverse engineering means taking a finished product apart to find out how it works. For software this means decompiling it, turning machine code back into readable form. The legal question is whether the copying made during decompiling breaks copyright. Slide 14 lists three cases and gives details for the first.

Sega v. Accolade [1992]

  • Issue: Accolade made video games to run on Sega game machines. To do so, it decompiled Sega's game engine.
  • Verdict: reverse engineering does not violate copyright if the intention is to make new creative works, not copy the original work.

Accolade wanted its own games to be compatible. It did not want to sell Sega's code, so the copying was a means to an end. This is the line to remember: new creative work is allowed, copying the original is not.

Atari v. Nintendo [1992] and Sony v. Connectix [2000]

The slides name these two cases as other significant reverse engineering cases but give no issue or verdict, so list them by name and date with Sega v. Accolade. beyond the slides In Atari v. Nintendo, Atari wanted to make games for the Nintendo console but lost, partly because it obtained Nintendo's program code in a way the court found improper. In Sony v. Connectix, Connectix reverse engineered the Sony PlayStation to build software that ran PlayStation games on a PC. The court held that the copying done in the process was fair use, which supports Accolade's result.

Practice · 4 marksDistinguish between time shifting and space shifting, naming the case in which each was held to be fair use.

Time shifting is recording a TV programme with a VCR to watch it later. The US Supreme Court held it to be fair use in Sony v. Universal City Studios by 5-4.

Space shifting is transforming music CDs to MP3 format to play on a portable player. It was held fair use in RIAA v. Diamond Multimedia Systems, the Rio player case.

In both, the user copies content they are entitled to use, for private use.

Practice · 4 marksWhat is reverse engineering of software, and when is it lawful? Name one case.

Reverse engineering is decompiling a product, such as a game engine, to learn how it works.

It is lawful when the intention is to make new creative works, not copy the original work. In Sega v. Accolade [1992] Accolade decompiled Sega's game engine to make games for Sega machines, and the court held that this did not violate copyright.

Say it like this:

In Sony v. Universal the Supreme Court held that time shifting is fair use, in RIAA v. Diamond that space shifting is fair use, and in Sega v. Accolade that reverse engineering is lawful if the aim is new creative works.

File sharing cases: Napster

RIAA v. Napster [2001]

  • Issue: a peer-to-peer music exchange network.
  • Verdict: web sites could be liable for users' actions if they took measures that deliberately encouraged users to do illegal things. This is called secondary infringement.

Background from the slide. Napster was started by a Northeastern student in the summer of 1999. In two years it had 26 million registered users. In court, Napster argued that it did not copy any files. It said it was merely providing a directory service, so the users, not Napster, were the ones copying.

The court did not accept that Napster could shelter behind its users. Secondary infringement means being held responsible for someone else's copying. The direct infringers are the users, and the secondary infringer is the service that helps and encourages them. beyond the slides Napster kept a central index of which user had which file, which made it easy to shut down and easy to prove it helped.

File sharing cases: Grokster

MGM v. Grokster [2005]

  • Issue: a decentralized p2p file-sharing network.
  • Verdict: in favour of MGM, by the Supreme Court.

The holding, which you should learn word for word:

"We hold that one who distributes a device with the object of promoting its use to infringe copyright, as shown by clear expression or other affirmative steps taken to foster infringement, is liable for the resulting acts of infringement by third parties."

Evidence in the case: Grokster advertised "an infringe use" of its service. That advertising was the "clear expression" of intent to promote infringement.

How Grokster differs from Napster: Grokster had no central directory. Its network was decentralized, so the Napster argument "we only run a directory" could not be used. The Supreme Court focused on intent, shown by what the company said and did. The words to underline in the quote are object of promoting, clear expression or other affirmative steps, and liable for third parties.

Watch out. The law does not punish a device just because it can be misused. It punishes distributing it with the object of promoting infringement. The Napster slide says the same idea: sites are liable if they deliberately encouraged illegal acts.

Practice · 6 marksExplain the Napster and Grokster cases and what they decided about the liability of file sharing services.

RIAA v. Napster [2001]: Napster was a peer-to-peer music exchange started in 1999 that reached 26 million registered users in two years. It argued it did not copy any files and only provided a directory service. The court held that web sites could be liable for users' actions if they deliberately encouraged illegal acts. This is secondary infringement.

MGM v. Grokster [2005]: Grokster ran a decentralized p2p network. The Supreme Court held for MGM: one who distributes a device with the object of promoting its use to infringe copyright, shown by clear expression or other affirmative steps, is liable for infringement by third parties. The evidence was that Grokster advertised an infringing use of its service.

Together the cases show that a service cannot escape liability by saying that users do the copying.

Under secondary infringement, a service is liable for the infringement of third parties if it distributes a device with the object of promoting its use to infringe copyright, as shown by clear expression or other affirmative steps.

DRM examples for CDs and DVDs

DRM stands for digital rights management. It is the main prevention technique from slide 12. It means technical methods built into media, devices or software to control how content is copied and used. Slides 17 and 18 give examples.

DRM for CDs (slide 17)

  • Exploiting a hardware difference. A CD-ROM drive in a computer and an ordinary CD player read discs differently. The slide calls these the "Yellow Book" (CD-ROM) and "Red Book" (audio CD) standards. A disc is made to play on a CD player but not to be read properly by a computer, so it cannot be copied easily.
  • Annoying sounds. Patterns are encoded into the audio so that, when the disc is decoded or copied, they turn into annoying sounds. The original plays cleanly and the copy does not.
  • Secure Digital Music Initiative (SDMI). This introduces a "digital watermarking" scheme. A watermark is hidden information in the music that identifies it as protected or marks its source. This is the tracking answer from slide 12.

DRM for DVDs (slide 18)

  • Content Scramble System (CSS). An encryption scheme for DVD contents. You need decryption keys to view a DVD. Status: in use, but a crack code exists.

The CSS case: Jon Johansen and 2600.com

The slide calls this "an important case".

  1. Jon Johansen wrote a decryption program for Linux. At the time there was no licensed DVD player for Linux, so he wrote one that could decrypt CSS.
  2. 2600.com published the code. The web site put the decryption program online.
  3. Motion picture studios sued 2600.com and won. The US courts ruled for the studios.
  4. Johansen was tried in Norway and found not guilty. Norway is where he lived and wrote the code.

The point of the case is that the same act, breaking CSS, was punished in one country (the site that published it) and not in another (the writer). beyond the slides The program is generally known as DeCSS. The US case against 2600.com relied on the DMCA anti-circumvention rule covered in t14.

Practice · 5 marksDescribe two examples of digital rights management used to protect CDs and DVDs, and the case that tested the DVD scheme.

CDs: DRM exploits the difference between CD-ROM drives in computers and CD players ("Yellow Book" vs "Red Book"), and some discs encode patterns into audio that turn into annoying sounds when decoded. The Secure Digital Music Initiative introduced digital watermarking.

DVDs: the Content Scramble System (CSS) is an encryption scheme that needs decryption keys to view a DVD. It is in use but a crack code exists.

Case: Jon Johansen wrote a CSS decryption program for Linux and 2600.com published it. The studios sued 2600.com and won, but Johansen was tried in Norway and found not guilty.

Marker words: DRM examples and the CSS case

Say it like this:

Digital rights management protects content through methods such as the Content Scramble System, an encryption scheme that needs decryption keys to view a DVD, but a crack code exists.

Criticisms of DRM

Slide 19 gives three criticisms and one closing remark.

  1. DRM undermines fair use. A lock cannot tell a legal copy (time shifting, space shifting, a quote for teaching) from an illegal one. It blocks both, so the user's legal fair use right is lost.
  2. Some DRM schemes track user information. To control use, some schemes record what you play, read or copy, which is a privacy problem.
  3. DRM protections never expire (unlike copyrights). A copyright ends after a fixed term and the work then enters the public domain. A technical lock stays on, so the work is never really free to use, even after the legal protection ends.

Closing remark. Many people believe that any technological "fix" is bound to fail, because determined people find ways around it. The crack for CSS is the evidence. The slide then asks "The alternative?", which leads to the discussion of tougher laws, open licensing and new business models, and the open questions are in t15.

Key point. DRM, tougher laws and the other answers come from the same two competing goals in t12: reward creators and benefit society. DRM leans too far toward creators. The fair use criticism is the way to say so.

Practice · 6 marksGive three criticisms of digital rights management.

DRM undermines fair use. It blocks legal copying such as time shifting and space shifting, along with illegal copying.

Some DRM schemes track user information. They record how people use content, which threatens privacy.

DRM protections never expire (unlike copyrights). Copyright ends after a limited time and the work enters the public domain, but the lock stays.

In addition, many people believe that any technological fix is bound to fail, as shown by the crack code for CSS.

Copyright law, software protection and the DMCA

~35 min to readHigh priority7 questions

Source: Set 5, slides 20-29

This section follows on from the basics of IP protection and fair use (t12) and the online protection challenges, DRM and landmark cases (t13). It covers how copyright law has grown over time, how punishments have become harsher, what the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) did, and the argument over how software should be protected. The open-source answer to that argument is in t15.

US copyright law: a history of expansion

The slides use the United States as the case study. The pattern is simple: each new law covered more kinds of work and lasted longer than the one before.

The first copyright law was passed in 1790. It gave 28 years of protection (two terms of 14 years: 14+14) and covered books only. After that, each subsequent revision broadened the scope of coverage and increased the protection period.

LawWhat it newly coveredLength of protection
1790 ActBooks28 years (14+14)
1831 ActPrints and sheet music42 years
1909 ActPhotos, recordings, movies56 years
1976 ActSoftware and databases75 years
1998 ActMusic broadcast over the InternetAuthor's lifetime + 95 years

Slide 21 is a picture (credited to Tom Bell on Wikipedia) that plots the length of copyright against time. The x-axis is the year a copyright term began (1790 to 2008) and the y-axis is the duration of the term in years (up to 120). Each Act is a coloured band that steps the term up: 28, 42, 56, 75, then about 95 years after the 1998 (Sonny Bono) Act. The legend also lists the 1962-74 Acts, short interim extensions that are not on the text slide. It adds nothing you need to memorise beyond the table.

Two things to notice. First, the 1976 Act is the one that brought software and databases into copyright; this is why the software-protection debate later in this section starts there. Second, the term changed from a fixed number of years to a period tied to the life of the author, which is a much longer period.

Watch out. The slide says "author's lifetime + 95 years" for the 1998 Act. Your solution files (and many textbooks) say "life of the author plus 70 years". beyond the slides In real US law, life plus 70 years applies to individual authors and 95 years from publication applies to corporate works, which probably explains the two numbers. If a question uses your lecturer's figures, use the slide's. If you want to be safe, write "the life of the author plus several decades (95 years in the slides)".

Criticisms of longer protection

The slides start from the purpose of copyright stated in the US Constitution (Article I, Section 8, Clause 8). Congress has the power:

"to promote the Progress of Science and useful Arts, by securing for limited times to Authors and Inventors the exclusive Right to their Respective Writings and Discoveries."

The key words are promote progress and limited times. Copyright exists to help society, and the owner's monopoly is meant to be temporary. This links straight back to the two competing goals of IP protection: benefit the society (get inventions to the public domain without delay) and reward the creators.

Critics say that making protection longer and longer works against that purpose. The slides give three criticisms.

  • It benefits only the few owners of franchises. The big winners are companies that own valuable old works. An author who is already dead cannot be encouraged to create anything by an extension.
  • The 1998 Act is called the "Mickey Mouse Protection Act". The nickname comes from the claim that it was pushed through to stop early Mickey Mouse works from falling out of copyright. beyond the slides The Act is formally the Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act.
  • It will shift progress of science and arts offshore, where copyrights would have expired. If a work is still locked up at home but free in another country, people in that country can build on it, adapt it and publish it. Creative and scientific progress then moves there.

Notice the shape of the argument: the critics accept that copyright is justified by progress, and then show that longer terms do not serve progress. That is a consequentialist (utilitarian) style of criticism.

Practice · 6 marksOutline the history of copyright law in the United States and give three criticisms of making the protection period longer.

History (3 marks). The first copyright law was passed in 1790 and gave 28 years (14+14) of protection for books. Each subsequent revision broadened coverage and increased the protection period: the 1831 Act added prints and sheet music (42 years), the 1909 Act added photos, recordings and movies (56 years), the 1976 Act added software and databases (75 years), and the 1998 Act added music broadcast over the Internet, with protection for the author's lifetime plus 95 years.

Criticisms (3 marks). The Constitution says copyright is meant to promote the progress of science and useful arts by securing exclusive rights for limited times. Longer protection works against this because:

  • it benefits only the few owners of franchises, not creators or the public;
  • the 1998 Act is nicknamed the "Mickey Mouse Protection Act", showing it served big corporate owners;
  • it will shift the progress of science and arts offshore, to countries where the copyrights would have expired.

Harsher punishments

The second way the law has changed is that punishments for infringement have become much harsher. This is one of the three "answers to the challenges" of digital copying listed in t13 (prevention through DRM, tracking through watermarking, punishing through extended copyright laws). The slides list three laws.

  • No Electronic Theft (NET) Act, 1997. Any unauthorised copying with a retail value of more than $1000 is covered. The important idea is that it applies even when the copier makes no profit: before this law, giving copies away free was hard to prosecute. beyond the slides
  • Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), 1998. Many copyright violations become felonies. A felony is a serious crime (as opposed to a civil wrong or a minor offence).
  • Digital Theft Deterrence and Copyright Damages Improvement Act, 1999. A minimum of $750 for each infringement, and up to 5 years in prison or a $500,000 fine for a first offence.

Put together, the trend runs: a low threshold for what counts as criminal copying (1997), felony status for many violations (1998), then fixed minimum damages and prison terms (1999). The RIAA lawsuits described in t13 (Jammie Thomas fined $222,000 for sharing 24 songs) are examples of what these laws allow.

The DMCA and its consequences

The Digital Millennium Copyright Act was passed in 1998 but is still controversial. Its heart is this rule: the DMCA makes circumventing copy control a felony, even if it is done for a fair-use purpose. "Circumventing copy control" means breaking or bypassing a technical protection such as DRM or the DVD scrambling scheme (CSS, see t13). The usual defence that "this was fair use" does not help once a protection was bypassed. That is why critics say the DMCA and DRM together undermine fair use (compare the DRM criticisms in t13 and the fair-use factors in t12).

The slides give four consequences.

  1. Inconsistency between media. Making a personal copy of a music CD is fair use, but it is illegal to do so for a movie DVD. The reason is that DVDs are protected by CSS, so copying means circumventing it, while music CDs have no such lock.
  2. It is illegal to play a DVD on a GNU/Linux machine. Early Linux had no licensed DVD player, so users had to use a decryption program, which counts as circumvention. This is the Jon Johansen story from t13.
  3. Online service providers (OSPs) may be held liable, and face severe penalties, for copyright violations by their users. A website or hosting service can be punished for what its users upload. This pushes providers to remove content quickly or to monitor users.
  4. The Viacom v. YouTube lawsuit is on-going. Viacom (a media company) sued YouTube for clips of its programmes uploaded by users. It is the test of how far an OSP is responsible. (The slide was written in 2010 when the case was still running.)

Key point. The DMCA protects the lock, not just the work. Even if your use of the work would be legal, breaking the lock is a felony. That is the sentence to remember when asked why the DMCA is controversial.

Practice · 6 marksExplain why the Digital Millennium Copyright Act is controversial. Give three consequences.

The DMCA was passed in 1998 and is still controversial because it makes circumventing copy control a felony, even if it is for a fair-use purpose. It therefore undermines fair use, and it makes many copyright violations felonies. Consequences:

  • Inconsistent rules: making a personal copy of a music CD is fair use, but doing the same for a movie DVD is illegal because the DVD's encryption would have to be circumvented.
  • It is illegal to play a DVD on a GNU/Linux machine, because the decryption program needed counts as circumvention.
  • Online service providers may be held liable, and face severe penalties, for copyright violations by their users. The Viacom v. YouTube lawsuit tests this.
Practice · 4 marksList the three US laws since 1997 that made punishments for copyright infringement harsher, and state what each provides.
  • No Electronic Theft Act (1997): any unauthorised copying with a retail value above $1000 is covered.
  • Digital Millennium Copyright Act (1998): many copyright violations become felonies.
  • Digital Theft Deterrence and Copyright Damages Improvement Act (1999): a minimum of $750 for each infringement, and up to 5 years in prison or a $500,000 fine for a first offence.

Software protection: the two arguments

Slide 11 of t13 asked "should software be copyrighted? should it be patented?". Slide 25 begins the answer by asking why software should be protected at all. It gives two kinds of argument, and the difference between them is the difference between the two big ethical theories (see t01).

Utilitarian arguments (consequences)

The slides give a chain of consequences, each one leading to the next:

  1. Copying software reduces software purchases.
  2. That leads to less income for software makers.
  3. That leads to lower production of new software.
  4. That leads to fewer benefits to society.

The conclusion is that copying should be illegal because the total good for society falls. The argument judges the law by its outcomes, so it is utilitarian (consequentialist).

Rights-based arguments (deontological)

  • Programming is hard work that only a few can do.
  • Programmers should be rewarded for their labour.
  • They ought to be able to own their programs.

This argument ignores outcomes. It says the programmer has a right to what their labour produced, whatever the effect on society. beyond the slides This is the same thought as the labour theory of property (a person owns what they mix their work into), and it is a duty or rights style of reasoning. Use the slide wording first and add the theory name as a bonus.

The basic dilemma

The slides do not use the word "dilemma" here, but your question bank asks for it. beyond the slides The dilemma is this: giving the programmer ownership and control rewards labour and encourages new software, but it also lets the owner restrict who may use, copy or improve the software. Software can be copied at almost no cost and without taking anything from the original owner. Ownership therefore keeps useful software away from people who could benefit, and it can give owners monopoly power and high prices. So society must balance the owner's rights and incentive against the public's access, affordability and progress. Your solution files phrase it as monopoly power and access and affordability.

QB D2 · 6 marksWhat is the consequentialist justification for laws that give ownership and control of software to individuals or corporations (proprietary software)? What is the basic dilemma in giving individuals the ownership and control of software they wrote?

Consequentialist justification (3 marks). A consequentialist judges a law by its consequences for society as a whole. The justification is a chain of consequences:

  • If copying is allowed, software purchases fall, so developers earn less income.
  • With less income and no incentive, there is lower production of new software.
  • This means fewer benefits to society. So laws giving ownership and control to the creator (copyright, patents, trade secrets) lead to the greatest good: they encourage innovation and investment, and so more and better software for everyone.

Basic dilemma (3 marks). Ownership and control of software that individuals or companies wrote:

  • rewards the programmer's labour and protects their right to own what they made (the rights-based side);
  • but it restricts access and can create monopoly power and high prices, even though software is easy to copy at almost no cost and copying does not take anything from the owner.

So the dilemma is how to balance proprietary rights with public access and affordability: too little protection kills the incentive to create, too much blocks the public from benefiting and from building on earlier work.

2016 Q4A · 8 marks; also CAT 1 2021-22 Q3b · utilitarian arguments on software property rightsThere are a number of arguments for and against strong property rights over computer software. Provide two utilitarian-style arguments for each side. [2016 wording reconstructed from garbled scan: "construct two utilitarian-style arguments supporting, and two opposing, strong property rights in software"]

For strong property rights (2 arguments).

  • Incentive for innovation: when developers know they can profit, they invest in new software. Copying reduces purchases, which means less income, lower production of new software and fewer benefits to society.
  • Economic growth and job creation: protected software creates a thriving industry with demand for skilled labour. beyond the slides

Against strong property rights (2 arguments).

  • Restricted access and innovation: high prices and licences keep useful software from people (for example schools and developing countries), and lock up knowledge others need to build new things. This reduces total benefit.
  • Monopoly and market control: owners can dominate markets, charge higher prices and reduce consumer choice. Critics also add that most software patents cover trivial inventions and that traditional copyright is enough (see the criticisms below).

Each argument is utilitarian because it is judged by the overall good for society, not by the owner's right alone. This question is also covered under utilitarianism in t01.

Marker words: why software should be protected

Say it like this:

The utilitarian argument is that copying software reduces software purchases, leading to less income for software makers, lower production of new software and fewer benefits to society. The rights-based argument is that programming is hard work and programmers should be rewarded for their labour and be able to own their programs.

Software copyrights

Software was brought into copyright by the 1976 revision. The slides explain what exactly is protected, using the copyright rule that applies to every work.

  • Expression of an idea, not the idea itself. You may not copy the way the program is written, but nobody owns the idea (for example "a program that sorts names"). Another programmer may write a different program that does the same job.
  • Object code, not source code. The copyright covers the machine-readable program that is sold. Companies treat source code as a trade secret (see trade secrets in t12) and keep it hidden, so the two protections work together.

Three examples of violations from the slides:

  1. Copying a program to give or sell to someone else.
  2. Preloading a program onto the hard disk of a computer being sold (a shop installs software on computers without a licence).
  3. Distributing a program over the Internet.

These all breach the owner's copyright rights of reproduction and distribution (see the five rights in t12). The question on the two forms of legal protection for software, 2016 Q4B (6 marks: What two forms of legal property protection are most frequently applied to software? List two or three of their key characteristics.), is answered in t12; here we add the debate over patents.

Software patents

The slides ask "software patents?" with a question mark because this is the most disputed form of software protection.

When is software patentable? The slide's rule: software is patentable if it contains a mathematical formula and implements it in a structure which performs a patentable function. Patents are not to be given for things that are obvious or already in common use. The trouble is that it is hard to determine what is "obvious", and the result is that some bad patents have been issued.

Examples of software patents (slide 28):

CategoryExamples
Data compression schemesGIF, JPEG, MP3, RSA
Internet toolsPay-per-click ads, the browser plug-in
User interfacesThe progress bar, force feedback (in game controllers)

Remember a patent lasts 20 years and requires a public, detailed description (t12). Ideas such as the progress bar were seen by many as obvious, which is the main complaint below.

Criticisms of software patents

Slide 29 gives four.

  1. The cost is too high. Getting and defending a patent is expensive, so small developers and individuals lose out to large firms with lawyers.
  2. Traditional copyright has provided sufficient protection. Software was already protected by copyright (and trade secrets) since 1976; a patent adds a second, stronger layer that is not needed.
  3. Most software patents cover trivial inventions or trivial extensions of existing technologies. This is the "obvious" problem again. Trivial patents let owners block others for 20 years without real invention.
  4. Lack of patent application disclosure: patent applications are published 18 months after they are filed. A patent exists to publish the invention, but in software the world moves so fast that 18 months of secrecy hides ideas while others unknowingly build the same thing and may then be accused of infringing.
2016 Q4C · 6 marks; also exam 2021-22 solution file Q5dIn a few sentences, explain why software poses a challenge to these traditional forms of intellectual ownership.

Traditional forms of ownership (copyright, patents and trade secrets) were designed for physical or printed things. Software challenges them because:

  • Digital copies are easy to make and perfect: software can be copied at almost no cost, so the owner cannot control reproduction and distribution. Copying also does not remove anything from the owner, unlike stealing a physical object.
  • The Internet and peer-to-peer networks let strangers share files globally and instantly, outside traditional distribution channels, which makes enforcement across borders very hard.
  • Software does not fit neatly into one form of protection. Copyright protects only the expression of an idea, not the idea, and the object code, not the source code. Patents are hard to apply because it is hard to decide what is "obvious", so some bad patents have been issued. Critics say traditional copyright has provided sufficient protection and patents are costly and cover trivial inventions.
  • Open-source and free software reject ownership altogether and share source code freely (see t15).

The result is a conflict between rewarding creators and giving the public access, so the law keeps being stretched (longer terms, DMCA) and remains controversial.

Open source and Creative Commons

~35 min to readMedium priority7 questions

Source: Set 5, slides 30-37

This section finishes the intellectual property topic. The earlier sections covered what IP is and how it is protected (IP, protection types, copyright and fair use), why protection is hard online and DRM (Protection challenges, DRM and the landmark cases), and copyright law, software copyright and patents (Copyright law, software protection and the DMCA). Those sections describe the proprietary model: the owner keeps control and the law enforces it. This section covers the opposite answer: giving rights away on purpose, using licences.

Open-source software and copyleft

The slides introduce open-source software as the opposite answer to proprietary software. Proprietary software is sold or licensed by an owner who keeps the source code secret and restricts copying, modifying and redistributing. Open-source software removes those restrictions. The slide lists four features:

  • No restrictions preventing others from selling or giving away the software. Anyone who has a copy may sell it or give it away.
  • Source code is included in the distribution. The human-readable instructions come with the program, not only the compiled version. This is what makes study and change possible.
  • No restrictions preventing others from modifying the source code. Users may fix bugs, add features or adapt the program.
  • No restrictions regarding how people can use the software. The licence does not limit the purpose, user or field of use.

The slide then adds copyleft, with the General Public Licence (GPL) as the example. Copyleft means: free to modify and redistribute, as long as the same rights apply to everyone receiving the software. The author does not give up copyright. The author uses copyright law to force every later user to pass on the same freedoms. If you take GPL code, improve it and distribute it, you must distribute your version under the same terms, with source code. Nobody can take the shared work and make it proprietary.

The word is a pun on copyright: copyright restricts, copyleft keeps the work free. Open source is therefore not the same as having no licence or no copyright. The code is still owned. The owner chooses a licence that grants broad permissions.

beyond the slides The Free Software Foundation (Richard Stallman, GNU project, 1980s) states the idea as four freedoms: to run the program for any purpose, to study and change it (needs source code), to redistribute copies, and to distribute modified versions. The four bullets on the slide match these. Famous examples are Linux, Apache, Firefox and LibreOffice. The Open Source Initiative later promoted the term "open source" with a business-friendly emphasis on practical benefits rather than on freedom as a moral aim. Not all open-source licences are copyleft: permissive licences such as MIT and BSD allow anyone to reuse the code, even inside proprietary products, without passing on the same terms. The GPL is the strong copyleft example the lecturer chose. "Free" here means freedom, not price: open-source software may be sold.

Key point. Open source works through copyright, not against it. The licence is a legal tool. Copyleft uses the owner's right to impose conditions, and the condition is "share alike".

Copyleft (for example the GPL) lets people modify and redistribute it as long as the same rights apply to everyone receiving the software.

Creative Commons licences

The slides say that in 2001 a group of professionals created the non-profit corporation Creative Commons to provide copyright licences free of charge. The idea is that an author, not the law's default, decides the extent of IP protection. Under normal copyright everything is "all rights reserved" automatically. A Creative Commons (CC) licence lets the author say "some rights reserved" without hiring a lawyer. The slide gives two examples:

  • Free to copy, modify and distribute, but no commercial use.
  • Free to copy and distribute, but no modification or commercial use.

It also notes that many Wikipedia pictures are protected by CC licences. Slides 32 and 33 are titled "Creative Commons (cont.)" and are two screenshots. Slide 32 lists the six Creative Commons 3.0 licences with their icons: Attribution; Attribution-NoDerivs; Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs; Attribution-NonCommercial; Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike; Attribution-ShareAlike. Slide 33 is the human-readable deed for Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported. It says: "You are free to Share (copy, distribute and transmit the work) and to Remix (adapt the work), under the conditions Attribution, Noncommercial and Share Alike." The meaning of each condition is in the table below, which is from general knowledge.

beyond the slides The four licence elements. Every CC licence is built from these:

ElementSymbolWhat it means
Attribution (BY)Person iconOthers may use the work only if they credit the author. Present in all six standard licences.
NonCommercial (NC)Crossed dollar signThe work may not be used for commercial purposes.
NoDerivatives (ND)Equals signThe work may be shared but not changed, remixed or adapted.
ShareAlike (SA)Circular arrowAdaptations must be released under the same licence. This is the copyleft idea applied to creative works.

beyond the slides The six standard licences, from most to least open:

LicenceCredit requiredCommercial useModificationSame licence on adaptations
CC BYYesAllowedAllowedNo
CC BY-SAYesAllowedAllowedYes
CC BY-NCYesNot allowedAllowedNo
CC BY-NC-SAYesNot allowedAllowedYes
CC BY-NDYesAllowedNot allowedNot applicable
CC BY-NC-NDYesNot allowedNot allowedNot applicable

The slide's first example (copy, modify, distribute, no commercial use) is CC BY-NC. The second (copy and distribute only, no modification, no commercial use) is CC BY-NC-ND. There is also CC0, a "public domain dedication" in which the author waives rights as far as the law allows. Each licence has three layers: a plain-language summary, the legal text, and machine-readable code so search engines can find CC-licensed work. CC licences apply to creative works such as text, photographs, music and video. They are not designed for software, where the GPL and similar licences are used.

Watch out. A CC licence does not abandon copyright. The author still owns the work and the licence is legally binding. If you break its terms, for example by using a NC image in an advert, you lose the permission and can be sued for infringement. The licence is also irrevocable for those who already received the work under it.

Benefits and criticisms of open source

Benefits (slide 34)

  • Programs belong to the entire community. No single firm owns the program or can withdraw it.
  • Eliminates the tension between obeying the law and helping others. Under proprietary licences, sharing a program with a friend is illegal copying. Under open source, sharing is legal and encouraged. This answers the dilemma of proprietary software, where the law forbids what feels like a neighbourly act.
  • Gives everyone the opportunity to improve the program. Anyone can read the code, find bugs and contribute fixes.
  • New versions appear more frequently. Many contributors work in parallel, so releases come faster.
  • Shifts focus from manufacturing to service. Copies are free, so firms earn from support, installation, training and customisation, not from selling copies. Red Hat is the standard beyond the slides example.

Criticisms (slide 35)

  • Without an "owner", incompatible versions may arise. Anyone may modify and redistribute, so the program can split into versions that do not work together (forking). No authority sets the standard.
  • Without a critical mass of developers, quality can be poor. The "many eyes" benefit only works for popular projects. Small projects can be abandoned or buggy.
  • Relatively weak graphical user interface. Volunteers like to build engines and tools. Polished, easy interfaces need designers and usability testing, which are costly.
  • Poor mechanism for stimulating innovation: no companies will spend billions on new programs. This is the consequentialist argument for proprietary software (covered in t14): without the chance to earn money from sales, big investments will not be made. Open source tends to copy and improve existing ideas.

beyond the slides Evidence is mixed. Linux, Apache and Android run much of the world's servers and phones, and big companies pay staff to work on open source. That weakens the "no innovation" claim. Security is also debated: public code can be audited, but attackers can read it too. For a student in Uganda, open source also means free tools and no licence bills, which is a strong practical benefit.

Marker words: benefits and criticisms of open source

Its weaknesses are incompatible versions, poor quality without a critical mass of developers, a weak interface and a poor mechanism for stimulating innovation.

Practice: open source, copyleft and Creative Commons

Practice · 6 marksWhat is open-source software? Explain the term copyleft.

Open-source software is the opposite answer to proprietary software. It has four features:

  • No restrictions preventing others from selling or giving away the software.
  • Source code is included in the distribution.
  • No restrictions preventing others from modifying the source code.
  • No restrictions regarding how people can use the software.

Copyleft, for example the General Public Licence (GPL), means the software is free to modify and redistribute as long as the same rights apply to everyone receiving the software. The author keeps copyright and uses it to make sure every later version stays free, so nobody can turn the shared work into proprietary software.

Practice · 9 marksOutline the benefits and the criticisms of open-source software.

Benefits.

  2. It eliminates the tension between obeying the law and helping others: sharing a program is legal.
  3. It gives everyone the opportunity to improve the program.
  4. New versions appear more frequently.
  5. It shifts focus from manufacturing to service: firms earn from support and customisation.

Criticisms.

  1. Without an owner, incompatible versions may arise.
  2. Without a critical mass of developers, quality can be poor.

  4. A poor mechanism for stimulating innovation: no company will spend billions on new programs without sales.
Practice · 4 marksWhat is Creative Commons? Give two examples of the licences it offers.

In 2001 a group of professionals created the non-profit corporation Creative Commons to provide copyright licences free of charge. The author decides the extent of IP protection, so "some rights reserved" replaces "all rights reserved".

  • Free to copy, modify and distribute, but no commercial use.
  • Free to copy and distribute, but no modification or commercial use.

Example of use: many Wikipedia pictures are protected by CC licences. beyond the slides The licences are built from four elements: Attribution, NonCommercial, NoDerivatives and ShareAlike.

Discussion questions with model answers

These four questions are on slides 36 and 37. They are discussion questions, so a good answer argues both sides and ends with a verdict. They are likely exam material because the lecturer asks "give arguments for each side".

Set 5 slide 36 · discussionA software service company A has a client C. C uses a software S made by company B. Company A made a copy of S, not to resell, but to provide service to C. Company B sued, and company A argues that the copying was a fair use. Give arguments for each side. Which side do you think should win?

The fair-use test. Courts apply four factors (see fair use in t12): purpose and character of use, nature of the work, amount of the work copied, and effect on the commercial market for the work.

Arguments for company A.

  • Purpose: A did not resell or distribute the copy. It used it only to service a client who already owns a legitimate copy of S. The aim was maintenance and support, not competition.
  • Effect on the market: C already paid B for S, so B lost no sale from this copy. A is not selling a rival product.
  • Without a working copy for testing and repair, service work on S would be very hard, and service companies benefit users and the wider economy. This is a consequentialist argument.

Arguments for company B.

  • Purpose: A is a commercial business. It earns money from servicing S, so its use is commercial, not educational. Commercial use weighs against fair use.
  • Amount: A copied the whole program. Copying all of a work weighs heavily against fair use.
  • Market effect: A's copy is an unlicensed extra copy. If every service firm copies S, B loses licence fees. B may also sell its own support, so A competes with B's service business.
  • Copyright gives the owner the exclusive right of reproduction. The licence C bought probably covers C only, and C cannot give A rights that C does not have.

Verdict. Company B should win. Of the four factors, A's use is commercial, the whole work was copied, and the unlicensed copy deprives B of a licence fee. Only the "no resale" point favours A. The fair solution is for A to obtain a licence from B, or to use the client's copy under the client's licence if the licence permits it. If the copy is made only as temporary backup or for repair of a legal copy, some laws allow it, but that is a narrow exception. This is my judgement, and A's argument is not frivolous.

Set 5 slide 36 · discussionConsider applying the fair-use guidelines to making a video of oneself lip-synching to a popular song and posting the video on a social-networking site. Do you think it is ethical to do this?

Apply the four factors.

  • Purpose and character: the video is personal, not for profit, and shows creativity (a performance). This favours fair use. But posting to a public site is distribution, not private use. Monetised accounts or adverts push it towards commercial use.
  • Nature of the work: a popular song is a creative, artistic work. Creative works get stronger protection than factual ones. This weighs against fair use.
  • Amount: lip-synching normally uses the whole song or a large part. This weighs against fair use, unless only a short clip is used.
  • Effect on the market: one amateur video does not replace buying the song. It often advertises the song. This favours fair use, but millions of such videos might change the picture.

Legal position. The score is mixed, about two factors each way. The result is uncertain. In practice, platforms hold licences from music companies or use filters, and rights-holders often tolerate such videos because they promote the music. A transformative element (parody, commentary, a new performance) strengthens the fair-use claim.

Ethical position. For: no one is harmed, the artist may gain publicity, it is non-commercial and creative (utilitarian argument: much pleasure, little harm). Against: the artist did not give permission and may be unpaid; a person who wants to respect copyright should ask or use licensed material (duty argument: respect for the owner's rights).

Verdict. It is generally ethical provided it is non-commercial, uses a limited portion, credits the artist and does not stand in for buying the song. The ethical line is crossed if the poster earns money from it, uses a pirated copy of the track, or presents the song as their own. Legal and ethical are not the same: it may be a technical infringement and still be ethically harmless.

Set 5 slide 37 · discussionWhich is more likely to be effective in protecting intellectual property in digital media (e.g. CDs, DVDs): tougher copyright laws, or new technologies incorporating more sophisticated anti-copying measures?

Case for tougher copyright laws.

  • Law sets a clear public standard that copying is wrong and gives owners a legal remedy: fines, damages, injunctions and prison.
  • It deters through example: prosecutions of large-scale pirates and websites raise the risk.
  • It also reaches things technology cannot, such as commercial pirate factories and sellers.
  • Law backs up technology. The DMCA made it illegal to circumvent anti-copying technology, so the two are linked (see t14).

Case for anti-copying technology (DRM, encryption, watermarking, see t13).

  • It prevents copying before it happens, instead of punishing afterwards.
  • It works across borders. Laws differ by country and are hard to enforce against millions of individual users.
  • Watermarking allows tracking of copies to their source.

Weaknesses. Laws are slow, hard to enforce, unpopular when they criminalise ordinary users, and can be harshly applied against fair use. Technologies are usually cracked. A protection scheme must be unbreakable everywhere, while a pirate needs to break it once and then share the result. DRM can also block legal fair use and annoy paying customers, who then turn to pirate copies that are easier to use.

Verdict. Neither alone is enough. If forced to choose, technology is more likely to be effective in the short term because it acts directly and automatically, but only if combined with law, since law makes cracking illegal. In the long term the most effective measure may be neither: affordable, convenient legal services reduce the motive to copy. A realistic answer is a combination: technology to prevent, law to punish, and fair pricing to reduce demand for piracy.

Set 5 slide 37 · discussionAs the copying of digital texts, audio, and video grows cheaper, the restrictions needed to enforce copyright grow more expensive and invasive. Does copyright have a future in the digital age? Or are new technologies steadily making it obsolete?

The problem. Digital copies are perfect, free and instant. To stop them, owners want DRM, monitoring of networks, filtering by internet providers and tracing of users. These are expensive and invasive: they threaten privacy, restrict fair use and treat every customer as a suspect.

Case that copyright is becoming obsolete.

  • The cost of copying is near zero, so the old business of selling copies fails.
  • Enforcement against millions of ordinary users is impractical and harms civil liberties.
  • Alternatives exist: open-source software and Creative Commons show that creators can share freely and still be rewarded through service, reputation, donations, advertising or live performance.
  • Strict copyright can block creativity and access to knowledge, a serious problem in poorer countries.

Case that copyright has a future.

  • The purpose of copyright is to reward creators so that they keep creating (the consequentialist argument; also the rights-based argument that creators deserve control of their labour). That purpose does not disappear because copying is easy.
  • Copyright adapts: new business models such as streaming and subscriptions make legal access cheaper and easier than piracy.
  • Open-source and CC licences themselves depend on copyright. Without copyright, the GPL's share-alike condition and a CC author's choices could not be enforced.
  • Large investments such as films and games need legal protection to recover costs.

Verdict. Copyright has a future, but in a changed form. It will not be enforced by ever more invasive measures, because the cost to privacy and fair use is too high. Expect shorter or lighter enforcement, licensing models that give the author choice (open source, Creative Commons), and business models that sell convenience and service. Technology is not making copyright obsolete. It is forcing it to become more flexible.

Marker words: the discussion questions

Say it like this:

To judge fair use, courts consider the purpose and character of use, the nature of the work, the amount of the work copied and the effect on the commercial market. Protection of digital media needs prevention (DRM), tracking (watermarking) and punishing (law), but each has costs.
