Part 6

Safety and risk

2 sections, about 1 h 10 min of reading.

Safety, risk and acceptable risk

~35 min to readMedium priority7 questions

Source: Set 6, pages 4-7 (Unit IV: Safety and Risk). Costs of unsafe design, job risks, the safety-has-a-price curve, knowledge of risk, uncertainties and testing continue in the next section.

Lead-in: engineering as social experimentation and the role of rules

Set 6 opens this part with the closing points of the previous topic. They set the frame for everything on safety.

  • Laws and regulations (repeated from t10) also act as a powerful support and defence for engineers who want to act ethically in situations where ethical conduct may not be welcome (for example, a manager who wants a shortcut).
  • Viewing engineering as social experimentation gives engineers a better perspective on laws and regulations. Every new product is partly an experiment carried out on the public.
  • Precise rules and enforceable sanctions are appropriate for misconduct that breaks well-established, regularly re-examined procedures whose purpose is the safety of the public.
  • In areas of experimentation, rules must not try to cover every possible outcome and must not force the engineer into one rigidly specified course of action. Here regulations should be broad guidelines that still hold the engineer accountable for his or her decisions.

The thought experiment and who is affected

Imagine you are a fresh graduate and you are offered a job as an engineer in a large atomic power plant. Would you take it? Under what conditions would you take it, and under what conditions would you refuse? Why? The point of the exercise is that your answer depends on how much risk you judge acceptable, how well you know that risk, and how much control you have over it. Different people will answer differently. That difference is the whole subject of this section.

People as consumers

GroupMeaningExamples in the slides
Active consumersDirectly involve themselves in using the product, so they have choice and control.Mowing the lawn, washing clothes, toasting bread.
Passive consumersHave less choice and less control.Water, electricity, petrol.
BystandersNot users at all, but exposed to the effects.Exposure to pollution from unknown sources.

What is safe differs by group

  • What is safe to entrepreneurs may not be safe to engineers. Example: pilots say "Indian airports are not safe; low vision in fog", while the airport owners treat them as acceptable beyond the slides (my reading of the example).
  • What is safe to engineers may not be safe to the public. Example: the top-loading washing machine. The engineer sees it as safe by design standards, but an ordinary user can still be hurt, beyond the slides for example by reaching into a spinning drum.

Typically several groups of people are involved in safety matters, and each has its own interests at stake. Each group may differ in what it counts as safe and what it counts as unsafe. So "safe" is never one fixed fact that everyone agrees on.

The concept of safety and why the simple definition fails

The slides give two quotations as the starting definitions.

  1. "A ship in harbor is safe, but that is not what ships are built for." (John A. Shedd). A thing that avoids all risk would be useless. Safety cannot mean doing nothing. Engineering products have to be used, and use brings risk.
  2. "A thing is safe if its risks are judged to be acceptable." (William W. Lawrence).

Why Lawrence's definition will not do in real life

The slides test it with three cases and ask: how does a judge pass judgement on safety in each?

CaseWhat goes wrong
We buy an ill-designed iron box in a sale.Underestimating risk. We judge the risk acceptable, but only because we have not seen how dangerous the design is.
We judge that fluoride in water can kill lots of people.Overestimating risk. We reject something that is, in fact, low risk.
We hire a taxi without thinking about its safety.Not estimating risk. We never made a judgement at all.

In all three, "judged to be acceptable" is a bad test, because the judgement is uninformed or distorted. Also, what is acceptable depends on the value judgement of the individual or group. So the definition needs two repairs: the people judging must know the risks, and they must judge by their most settled values.

The working definition: Martin and Schinzinger

Learn this word for word. "A thing is safe (to a certain degree) with respect to a given person or group at a given time if, were they fully aware of its risks and expressing their most settled values, they would judge those risks to be acceptable (to that certain degree)." (Mike Martin and Roland Schinzinger)

Read it in pieces. To a certain degree: safety comes in degrees, not all or nothing. With respect to a given person or group at a given time: it is relative to who is judging and when. Fully aware of its risks: the judgement must be informed. Most settled values: not a panicked or careless mood, but their considered values. Judge those risks to be acceptable: the final test is acceptable risk.

Not safe

A thing is not safe if it exposes us to unacceptable danger or hazard.

2017 Q5A · 3 marksDefine the concept of safety as applied in the Engineering profession.

Safety is acceptable risk. In the definition of Martin and Schinzinger, a thing is safe (to a certain degree) with respect to a given person or group at a given time if, were they fully aware of its risks and expressing their most settled values, they would judge those risks to be acceptable.

The earlier definition, a thing is safe if its risks are judged to be acceptable (William Lawrence), is not enough on its own, because people may be underestimating, overestimating or not estimating risk.

Conversely, a thing is not safe if it exposes us to unacceptable danger or hazard. Safety is relative to who is judging, so it is partly objective and partly subjective.

CAT 2021-22 Q5a · marks not shownDescribe your understanding of the safety concept as applied to the Engineer's discipline.

Safety does not mean freedom from all risk. True safety never exists except in hypothetical situations; a ship in harbour is safe but that is not what ships are built for (Shedd). In engineering, safety means the risks are acceptable (Lawrence).

A better working definition (Martin and Schinzinger): a thing is safe to a certain degree, for a given person or group at a given time, if, fully aware of its risks and expressing their most settled values, they would judge those risks acceptable.

So safety is a matter of how people find risks acceptable or unacceptable. It is objective to the extent that people judge informed by the facts, and subjective because perspectives differ between engineers, entrepreneurs, consumers and bystanders. Safety is therefore acceptable risk.

Note. The unofficial solution file defines safety as designing and operating projects to minimise risk to human life, property and the environment. That is a reasonable supporting sentence, but the slides' wording above is what to lead with.

CAT 2021-22 Exam Q6A · marks not shownDefine safety and risk in respect to an engineering design and highlight differences between these two terms.

Safety. A thing is safe if, were people fully aware of its risks and expressing their most settled values, they would judge those risks to be acceptable. Safety is therefore acceptable risk. A thing is not safe if it exposes us to unacceptable danger or hazard.

Risk. Risk is the potential that something unwanted and harmful may occur. In a design it can mean bodily harm, economic loss or environmental degradation.

Differences.

  • Risk is a fact about the design: it always exists. Safety is a judgement about whether that risk is acceptable, so it depends on the person judging.
  • Risk can be described, estimated and reduced. Safety in the absolute sense is never attained.
  • Safety is partly subjective because perspectives differ. Risk is the thing being judged.
  • We take a risk when we use a product that is not safe.

Note. The unofficial solution says safety is proactive and risk management reactive. The slides do not say this. Use the slide points above.

Risk, and why risk is reality and safety is fantasy

Definition. Risk is the potential that something unwanted and harmful may occur.

We take a risk when we undertake something or use a product that is not safe. Risk in technology includes the dangers of three kinds of harm:

  1. Bodily harm (injury, illness, death).
  2. Economic loss.
  3. Environmental degradation.

The surprising reversal

Some people assume that safety is a concrete concept and risk is a vague, hypothetical one. The slides say it is the other way round.

  • Risks always exist.
  • True safety never exists, except in hypothetical situations.
  • So: risk is reality, safety is fantasy.

This is why the working definition of safety is built from risk. We cannot remove all risk, so the real question is always how much risk is acceptable.

2017 Q5B · 4 marksExplain the term RISK and its relation to safety in Engineering.

Risk is the potential that something unwanted and harmful may occur. We take a risk when we undertake something or use a product that is not safe. In technology it includes bodily harm, economic loss and environmental degradation.

Relation to safety.

  • Safety is defined through risk: a thing is safe when its risks are judged acceptable by people fully aware of them. So safety is acceptable risk.
  • Risks always exist, while true safety never exists except in hypothetical situations. Risk is reality, safety is fantasy.
  • A thing is not safe when its risk is unacceptable, so engineers must find out what degree of risk is acceptable to those affected.
2015 exam Q2a · 2 marksWhat do you understand by risk? [reconstructed from garbled scan]

Risk is the potential that something unwanted and harmful may occur. It arises whenever we undertake something or use a product that is not safe. In technology the harm may be bodily harm, economic loss or environmental degradation. Risk always exists; the engineer's task is to judge whether it is acceptable to those affected.

CAT 2021-22 Q5b · marks not shownExplain the term risk and how it is related to safety in Engineering.

Risk is the potential that something unwanted and harmful may occur: bodily harm, economic loss or environmental degradation. Engineers can estimate it by considering how likely the harm is and how severe it would be.

Risk and safety are linked because safety is acceptable risk. Risks always exist and true safety never does, so engineers cannot promise zero risk. They must reduce risk until those affected, fully aware of it, would judge it acceptable. A product exposing people to unacceptable danger or hazard is not safe.

Safety as acceptable risk, and what makes a risk acceptable

What degree of risk is acceptable? The slides answer in steps.

  • Safety is a matter of how people would find risks acceptable or unacceptable if they knew the risks and were basing their judgements on their most settled value perspective. To this extent, safety is objective.
  • But perspectives differ between people and groups. To this extent, safety is subjective.
  • So: safety is "acceptable risk".

Definition. "A risk is acceptable when those affected are generally no longer (or not) apprehensive about it."

Apprehension factors

Apprehension means anxiety. Whether people are apprehensive depends largely on these factors:

  1. Whether the risk is assumed voluntarily.
  2. How the probabilities of harm (or benefit) are perceived.
  3. Job-related or other pressures that make people aware of risks or overlook them.
  4. Whether the defects of a risky activity or situation are immediately noticeable or close at hand.
  5. Whether the potential victims are identifiable beforehand.

A way to remember the pattern: people are calmer when the risk is their own choice, the odds look good, nothing pressures them, the harm is not visible, and nobody in particular is picked out as the victim. They are more anxious when the risk is imposed, visible, close, and aimed at known people.

CAT 2021-22 Exam Q6C · marks not shownUnder what circumstances would the risk in a given engineering design be considered acceptable and what factors affect this risk acceptability?

When it is acceptable. A risk is acceptable when those affected are generally no longer apprehensive about it. Equivalently, when people fully aware of the risks and expressing their most settled values would judge it acceptable.

Factors (the apprehension factors).

  • Whether the risk is assumed voluntarily: a risk we choose is accepted more readily than one imposed on us.
  • How the probabilities of harm or benefit are perceived.
  • Job-related or other pressures that make people aware of or overlook risks.
  • Whether defects are immediately noticeable or close at hand.
  • Whether the potential victims are identifiable beforehand.

Because perspectives differ, acceptability is partly subjective. The unofficial solution lists severity of harm, probability, risk tolerance and mitigation as factors. These are sensible extras but the five above are the slides' wording.

Anxiety.

Voluntary risk, control and disaster

A person takes a voluntary risk when he is subjected to risk by his own actions or by actions taken by others, and volunteers to take that risk without any apprehension.

Example. John and Ann Smith enjoy riding motorcycles over rough ground for amusement. They take voluntary risk, as part of being engaged in a potentially dangerous sport.

Control

Voluntary risk is connected to control. The Smiths know the accident figures for the sport are high. Yet, like most people, they show an unrealistic confidence when they believe the dangers are under their control. In terms of engineering as social experimentation, people are more willing to be the subjects of their own experiments than of someone else's, whether social experiment or not.

Chauncey Starr

Starr found that individuals are more ready to assume voluntary risks than involuntary risks, even when the voluntary risks are 1000 times more likely to produce a fatality than the involuntary ones. So a risk that is imposed (a nearby plant, a passive-consumer service) is judged far more harshly than a risk we choose (a sport, driving), regardless of the numbers. This is why engineers cannot decide acceptability from statistics alone.

Disaster

Definition. A disaster = a seriously disruptive event + a state of unpreparedness.

Example: the Titanic collision with an iceberg at night. The collision alone was an emergency. Fewer lifeboats than needed, inadequate training, and iceberg warnings that were not heeded turned the emergency into a disaster. beyond the slides Preparedness is therefore an engineering responsibility: it decides whether a serious event stays an emergency or becomes a disaster.

How information is presented changes how risk is perceived

The way information needed for a decision is presented can greatly influence how risks are perceived. The slides show this with a disaster-management experiment in which the lives of 600 people are at stake. The only options are given to two groups in two different ways, and each person must choose.

Version 1: stated as lives saved

  • Program A: 200 people will be saved.
  • Program B: a 1/3 probability that 600 people will be saved and a 2/3 probability that nobody will be saved.

Response: 72% chose A and 28% chose B.

Version 2: stated as lives lost

  • Program A: 400 people will die.
  • Program B: a 1/3 probability that nobody will die and a 2/3 probability that 600 people will die.

Response: this time only 22% chose A and 78% chose B.

The arithmetic: the two versions are identical

OptionWorkingExpected lives saved
Version 1, A200 saved for certain200
Version 1, B(1/3 x 600) + (2/3 x 0) = 200 + 0200
Version 2, A400 die for certain, so 600 - 400 = 200 saved200
Version 2, BExpected deaths (1/3 x 0) + (2/3 x 600) = 400, so 600 - 400 = 200 saved200

All four options give an expected 200 lives saved and 400 lives lost. Version 2 A is exactly Version 1 A in different words, and Version 2 B is exactly Version 1 B. Yet the share choosing the sure option fell from 72% to 22%. Only the wording changed.

Conclusions (the slides' two)

  1. The option perceived as yielding a firm gain will tend to be preferred over options whose gains are perceived as risky or only probable. (Version 1: "200 saved" for certain wins.)
  2. The option emphasizing firm losses will tend to be avoided in favour of options whose chances of success are perceived as probable. (Version 2: "400 will die" for certain is avoided, so people gamble on B.)

Key point. Equal risks can be judged acceptable or unacceptable depending on whether they are described as gains or as losses. So when engineers or companies communicate risk, how they frame it affects what the public accepts. This links back to acceptable risk: apprehension depends on perception, not only on the facts.

Watch out. In an exam, do not just report 72/28 and 22/78. Say that the expected outcome is the same in both versions (200 saved) and that only the framing differs. That is the point of the example.

Next: the costs of unsafe design, job-related risks, why safety has a price, and the uncertainties in estimating risk.

Costs of unsafe design, uncertainty and testing

~35 min to readMedium priority11 questions

Source: Set 6, pages 7-9 (from "Secondary costs of products"). Earlier pages, up to the information-framing example, are in the safety, risk and acceptable risk section.

Secondary costs of products

A product has a primary cost, the cost of producing it. If it is designed unsafely it also carries secondary costs, which fall on the producer after the product leaves the factory. The slides say the cost of a product is high if it is designed unsafely, and list five items:

  • Returns and warranty expenses: faulty units come back and must be repaired or replaced free.
  • Loss of customer goodwill: buyers stop trusting the brand.
  • Cost of litigation: court cases, legal fees and compensation after injuries.
  • Loss of customers due to injuries in using the product.
  • Cost of rework and lost time in attending to design problems: engineers and the factory must stop to fix the design.

The point is that skimping on safety does not save money. The saving at the design stage is paid back, usually with interest, through these secondary costs.

2017 Q5C · 5 marksList any five costs associated with unsafe engineering designs.
  1. Returns and warranty expenses: unsafe units are sent back and must be repaired or replaced.
  2. Loss of customer goodwill: customers lose trust in the manufacturer.
  3. Cost of litigation: lawsuits, legal fees and compensation for victims.
  4. Loss of customers due to injuries in using the product: sales fall.
  5. Cost of rework and lost time attending to design problems: production stops while the design is corrected.

These are the secondary costs, over and above the primary (production) costs.

CAT 2021-22 Q5c · marks as setDescribe any five costs that come with unsafe engineering equipment and/or design.

Same five slide costs, each with one line of description. Say what the cost is and who pays it.

  1. Returns and warranty expenses: the producer repairs or replaces defective units at its own cost.
  2. Loss of customer goodwill: a reputation for unsafe products drives buyers to competitors.
  3. Cost of litigation: injured users sue, and the producer pays legal fees, damages and fines.
  4. Loss of customers due to injuries: people hurt or frightened by the product do not buy again.
  5. Cost of rework and lost time: engineers redesign and the line is delayed.

The unofficial solution file lists human, financial, reputation, environmental and legal and regulatory costs instead. These are acceptable extra points (human cost: injury and death; environmental cost: pollution), but the slide list above is the lecturer's wording, so lead with it. Add one of the solution-file costs only as a sixth point.

Why manufacturer and buyer must understand the risk

The manufacturer must understand the risk in a product:

  • to help reduce secondary costs;
  • to know the possible risk for purposes of pricing, disclaimers, legal terms and conditions and so on;
  • to know the cost of reducing the risks;
  • to take a decision before finalizing the design. After the design is fixed, change is expensive.

The buyer must understand the risk in a product:

  • to judge whether he or she wants to take the risks;
  • to judge whether "risk versus costs" justifies taking the risk.

Link to voluntary risk: a buyer can only take a risk voluntarily if the risk has been disclosed. A buyer who is not told is exposed to an involuntary risk.

2017 Q5D · 3 + 2 marks · also CAT 2021-22 Q5eExplain why a clear understanding of the risks in a product design is necessary for (i) the product manufacturer (3 marks) and (ii) product buyers (2 marks).

(i) Product manufacturer

  • To reduce secondary costs such as warranty claims, lost goodwill and litigation.
  • To know the possible risk for pricing, disclaimers, legal terms and conditions.
  • To know the cost of reducing the risks and to take a decision before finalizing the design, when changes are still cheap.

(ii) Product buyers

  • To judge whether he or she wants to take the risks, so that the choice is an informed one.
  • To judge whether "risk versus costs" justifies taking the risk: whether the benefit of the product is worth the danger and the price.

beyond the slides If the question is worded as in CAT 2021-22 Q5e (Q5 is 20 marks; part marks not printed), Explain how good risk assessment in product design (manufacture) is important for the following groups of people: (i) Product manufacturer. (ii) Product buyers (customers). (the 2017 version, Q5D, gives 3 marks and 2 marks), add one sentence each. Manufacturer: good risk assessment reduces liability, recalls and lawsuits, and protects product quality and brand reputation. Buyers: it gives assurance that the product is safe enough, supports informed purchasing decisions and builds consumer confidence.

The manufacturer must understand the risk before finalizing the design, and the buyer must understand it to judge whether risk versus costs justifies taking it.

Job-related risks

Many workers take risks in their jobs in their stride, for example exposure to asbestos. The slides make these points:

  • Exposure to risk on a job is in one sense voluntary, since a worker can always refuse the work or may have control over how the job is done.
  • In practice workers generally have no choice. They stick to the only job available to them.
  • They are not generally informed about exposure to toxic substances and other dangers that cannot be readily seen, smelt, heard or otherwise sensed.
  • Occupational health and safety regulations and unions can have a better say in correcting these situations, but things are still far below expected safety standards.
  • Engineers designing work stations must take into account the casual attitude of workers on safety, especially when they are paid on piece rate. A worker paid per item has an incentive to skip safety steps to go faster.

Key point. Job risk is only "voluntary" on paper. A worker without another job, and without information about hidden hazards, is not choosing freely. Compare the voluntary-risk idea in the previous section.

Problems engineers face with the public concept of safety

The slides name two problems:

  1. An optimistic attitude: people believe that things that are familiar, that have not caused harm before and over which they have some control present no risks.
  2. A serious shock when an accident kills or maims people in large numbers or harms people we know, even though, statistically, such accidents might occur infrequently.

The first makes the public under-estimate risk, so they ignore warnings. The second makes the public over-react to rare events. Engineers must design for the real risk, while dealing with a public whose perception is skewed in both directions.

2017 Q5E · 5 marks (also CAT 2021-22 Q5d)List any five questionable or clearly wrong practices by engineers over the course of their work that would negatively affect public safety associated with their projects.

The slides do not list these as a set. The list below comes from the unofficial solution file and general professional-ethics knowledge. Pick five.

  1. Cutting corners on safety standards and regulations to meet deadlines or budgets.
  2. Falsifying data or test results to hide safety hazards or design deficiencies.
  3. Ignoring or downplaying safety concerns raised by workers, communities or regulators.
  4. Prioritizing profit over safety or acting under a conflict of interest, so the quality of the work suffers.
  5. Concealing or minimizing risks to win approvals, permits or funding.
  6. Skipping or poorly carrying out testing, for example not repeating a prototype test or not running quality assurance on production runs (see testing strategies below).
  7. Ignoring the casual attitude of workers to safety when designing work stations (see job-related risks above).

Marker words: job risks and public concept of safety

Say it like this:

Job-related risk is only voluntary in one sense, because workers usually have no choice and are not informed of hidden dangers. Engineers must also deal with the public's optimistic attitude to familiar things and its serious shock at large accidents, even if they are statistically infrequent.

The two problems engineers face about the public concept of safety.
The optimistic attitude that things that are familiar, that have not caused harm before and over which we have some control present no risks; and the serious shock people feel when an accident kills or maims people in large numbers or harms those we know, even though statistically such accidents might occur infrequently.

"Safety in a commodity comes with a price"

The slides pose this as an "Explain" question. The argument has four steps.

  1. Absolute safety is never possible, and safety can be improved in an engineering product only with an increase in cost.
  2. On the other hand, unsafe products incur secondary costs to the producer beyond the primary (production) costs: warranty costs, loss of goodwill, loss of customers, litigation costs, downtime costs in manufacturing and so on.
  3. The cost curves. P is the primary cost. It is high for a highly safe (low risk) product and low for a risky one. S is the secondary cost. It is high for a highly risky (less safe) product and low for a very safe one.
  4. Adding them gives the total cost curve T = P + S. There is a point M at which the total cost is a minimum, and the cost cannot be reduced below it.

If the risk at the minimum total cost point M is not acceptable, the producer must choose a lower, acceptable risk value. The total cost is then higher than at M, and the product is designed accordingly. So safety "comes with a price" in the sense that going beyond the cheapest point costs extra money.

The figure, described in words

The original figure is not reproduced in the notes. This is how to draw it. The horizontal axis is risk, running from low risk (very safe) on the left to high risk on the right. The vertical axis is cost.

  • Curve P (primary cost) starts high at the left, where the product is very safe, and falls steadily as risk increases to the right.
  • Curve S (secondary cost) starts low at the left and rises steeply towards the right, where the product is risky.
  • Curve T = P + S is the sum of the two at each risk level. It is U-shaped: high at both ends, with a lowest point M in the middle, where P is falling and S is rising at equal rates.
  • If the risk at M is acceptable, design at M. If it is not, move left along T to a lower risk, and accept a higher total cost.

The numbers below are illustrative only, invented to show the shape. They are not from the slides.

Risk level (illustrative)P: primary costS: secondary costT = P + S
1 (very low risk)90595
2601575
3403070 (minimum, point M)
4305080
5 (very high risk)2585110

P falls and S rises as risk goes up. T is lowest at level 3. If level 3 is judged an unacceptable risk, the producer must go to level 2 and pay a total of 75 instead of 70. That extra 5 is the price of safety.

Set 6 slide question · marks as set"Safety in a commodity comes with a price." Explain.

Absolute safety is never possible to attain, and safety can be improved in a product only with an increase in cost. The primary (production) cost P is therefore high for a highly safe, low-risk product.

On the other hand, unsafe products incur secondary costs S to the producer: warranty costs, loss of goodwill, loss of customers, litigation and downtime costs. S is high for a highly risky product.

The total cost T = P + S is U-shaped, with a minimum total cost point M below which cost cannot be reduced. If the risk at M is not acceptable, the producer must choose a lower acceptable risk, and the total cost will be higher than M. That extra cost is the price of safety.

Marker words: safety comes with a price

Say it like this:

Absolute safety is never possible, and safety can be improved only with an increase in cost, but unsafe products incur secondary costs. The total cost T = P + S has a minimum at point M, and if the risk there is not acceptable the producer must choose a lower risk at a higher total cost.

Knowledge of risk for better safety

Robert Stephenson, the nineteenth-century engineer, wrote that all accidents, the harms caused and the means used to repair the damage should be recorded for the benefit of the younger members of the profession. A faithful account of accidents and of how the damage was contained is more valuable than a description of successful work.

So it is imperative that knowledge of risks will help to attain better safety. But gaps remain, for two reasons:

  1. some industries do not freely share information;
  2. there are always new applications of old technology that make the available information less useful.

Uncertainties encountered in the design process

The slides list seven sources of uncertainty:

  • A decision on maximising profit or maximising the return on investment. This pushes safety margins down.
  • Uncertainties about applications, such as dynamic loading instead of static loading, vibrations and wind speeds.
  • Uncertainties regarding the materials and skills required in manufacturing.
  • Changing economic realities.
  • Unfamiliar environmental conditions, such as very low temperature.
  • Standard data on items like steel, resistors, insulators and optical glass are based on statistical averages only. A given batch can be weaker than average.
  • By the nature of processes, all components have a tolerance in design, so the capability of assemblies is assessed by probability statistics.

Testing strategies for safety

Commonly used testing methods:

  • Using past experience in checking the design and performance.
  • Prototype testing. The one product tested may not be representative of the population of products.
  • Tests simulated under approximately actual conditions, to find performance flaws on safety.
  • Routine quality assurance tests on production runs.

These procedures are not always carried out properly, so testing procedures cannot be trusted uncritically. Some tests are also destructive, and it is obviously impossible to do destructive testing on every product and still improve safety. In such cases a simulation that traces hypothetical risky outcomes can be applied. The slides name two such techniques:

  • Scenario analysis: start from an event and trace its consequences (event to consequences).
  • Failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA): go through the failure modes of each component and work out their effects.

Watch out. Do not mix the two. Scenario analysis begins with an event and asks "what follows?". FMEA begins with a component and asks "how can it fail, and what then?".

Marker words: knowledge of risk, uncertainty and testing

Say it like this:

Safety is helped by recorded knowledge of accidents (Stephenson), but design remains uncertain because standard data are statistical averages and components have tolerances. Testing by prototype testing, simulated tests and quality assurance cannot be trusted uncritically, so for destructive tests engineers use scenario analysis and failure modes and effects analysis.

Practice: uncertainties, testing and the safety questions

Practice · 8 marksDescribe the uncertainties an engineer meets in the design process and the testing strategies used to deal with them.

Uncertainties.

  • Standard data are statistical averages only, for items such as steel, resistors, insulators and optical glass, so a given batch can be weaker than average.
  • All components have a tolerance in design, so the capability of an assembly is assessed by probability statistics.
  • Uncertain applications, such as dynamic instead of static loading, vibration and wind speed.
  • Uncertain materials and skills in manufacturing, changing economic realities and unfamiliar environmental conditions such as very low temperature.
  • The decision to maximise profit or return on investment pushes safety margins down.

Testing strategies.

  • Use past experience and recorded accidents (Stephenson) to check design and performance.
  • Prototype testing: the one unit tested may not represent the whole population.
  • Tests simulated under approximately actual conditions to find safety flaws.
  • Routine quality assurance tests on production runs.
  • For destructive tests, a simulation that traces hypothetical risky outcomes: scenario analysis (event to consequences) or failure modes and effects analysis (each component).

Testing procedures are not always carried out properly, so they cannot be trusted uncritically.

Exam 2021-22 Q6B · 4 strategiesDescribe four strategies that should be adopted to ensure that a given engineering design (product) meets the necessary safety requirements.
  1. Learn from past experience and recorded accidents. Check the design against known failures, as Stephenson urged, so old mistakes are not repeated.
  2. Prototype testing. Test a prototype for safety, remembering that one unit may not represent the whole population of products.
  3. Simulated tests under approximately actual conditions. Where tests are destructive, use scenario analysis or failure modes and effects analysis to trace hypothetical risky outcomes.
  4. Routine quality assurance tests on production runs, so each batch meets the safety specification.

beyond the slides The solution file gives a different four that are also acceptable as support: risk assessment, compliance with standards and codes, testing and validation and design review. Also understand the risk before finalizing the design, when change is still cheap.

Exam 2021-22 Q6D · 3 reasonsGive three reasons that necessitate carrying out a risk-benefit analysis of an engineering design.
  1. To know the cost of reducing the risk: compare the primary cost P of more safety with the secondary cost S of less, and find the minimum total cost point M (T = P + S).
  2. To judge whether risk versus costs justifies taking the risk, for the manufacturer and for the buyer, so the decision is informed and the risk is acceptable.
  3. To take a decision before finalizing the design, when change is cheap, and so reduce secondary costs and set pricing, disclaimers and terms.

beyond the slides Extra reasons from the solution file: safety assurance, decision making on accepting, modifying or rejecting a design, and regulatory compliance.

QB Sec B Q2b · 14 marksIf engineers are not afforded the luxury of seeking perfection, it follows that they must be willing to risk failure. Do you agree? Discuss this in view of engineering product safety and ethics. [reconstructed from garbled scan]

Position. I agree that engineers must accept that absolute safety is never possible, but this does not allow carelessness. Engineers must keep the risk acceptable, informed and disclosed, and hold public safety paramount.

For the statement.

  1. True safety never exists; risk is reality, safety is fantasy. Safety means acceptable risk, so some risk always remains.
  2. Safety has a price. Total cost T = P + S has a minimum at point M. Pushing risk to zero makes primary cost P unaffordable, so a product nobody can buy helps nobody.
  3. Design is uncertain: standard data are statistical averages, components have tolerance, and new applications and environments appear.
  4. Testing cannot be trusted uncritically: a prototype may not represent the population and destructive tests cannot be run on every unit.
  5. Engineering is social experimentation: every new product is tried out on society, so some failure is possible.

Against, or the limits.

  1. Willingness to risk failure is not willingness to hide it. Risk must be disclosed so that those exposed give informed consent. A voluntary risk is tolerated far more than an imposed one.
  2. Failure also has secondary costs: returns and warranty expenses, lost goodwill, litigation, lost customers and rework. Cutting safety to save money is false economy.
  3. Engineers must learn from recorded failures (Stephenson), test, simulate and use quality assurance to keep risk low.
  4. Ethically the engineer is accountable. The codes put safety, health and welfare of the public first, so risk may not be pushed onto people who do not know of it.

Verdict. Zero risk is unattainable, so engineers must accept some risk of failure. But the risk must be kept at an acceptable level, understood before the design is finalized, disclosed to those affected, and never traded against public safety.

beyond the slides The phrases "social experimentation" and "informed consent" come from general engineering ethics texts.

Risk management process and risk control options beyond the slides

beyond the slides The slides do not cover this, but a past paper asks for it. The standard answer, from general engineering practice, is below.

  • Four elements of the risk management process: risk identification (find the hazards), risk analysis (estimate likelihood and consequence), risk evaluation (decide whether the risk is acceptable) and risk control (act on it and monitor). Some textbooks use "assessment", "treatment" or "monitoring and review" for the last steps.
  • Risk control options: avoid the risk (drop the hazardous design or activity); reduce it (redesign, add safety devices, train, inspect); transfer it (insurance, contracts); accept what is left and monitor it.
2015 Q2b, c · 2 + 6 marks · also QB Sec B Q2a, two papers · beyond the slides(b) Identify the four major elements of the risk management process. (c) Engineers seldom manage to eliminate risk in their projects. Identify and explain three risk control options available to an engineer. [reconstructed from garbled scan]

(b) Risk identification; risk analysis; risk evaluation; risk control.

(c) Any three:

  1. Risk avoidance: remove the hazard completely, for example by choosing a different design.
  2. Risk reduction: lower the likelihood or the consequence, for example by redundancy, guards and testing.
  3. Risk transfer: pass the financial burden to another party, for example by insurance.
  4. Risk acceptance: accept a small residual risk that is judged acceptable and monitor it.

For the definition of risk in 2015 Q2a (2 marks: What do you understand by risk?), see the previous section.

QB Sec B Q2a (6 marks): identify three strategies to manage risk in engineering. Avoid the risk, reduce it, transfer it (insurance) or accept the residual risk: give any three, two marks each. From the slides, add the practical strategies: testing (prototype, simulated, quality assurance), learning from recorded accidents, and simulation by scenario analysis or FMEA.

2015 Q2d(i) · 2 marks · beyond the slidesWhat do you understand by Strict Liability?

Strict liability is liability for harm caused by a defective product regardless of fault or negligence by the producer. The injured person need only show that the product was defective and caused the harm, not that the manufacturer was careless.

Privacy, the law and government surveillance

~40 min to readMedium priority9 questions

Source: Set 7 (Lecture 4: Privacy), slides 1-8 and the legal summary on slide 28. Continues in encryption and identity theft and profiling, workplace monitoring and advanced surveillance.

Privacy protection and the law: the ethical conundrum

The lecture opens with a conundrum. A conundrum is a puzzling question: a problem with no easy answer because two good things pull against each other. Here the two things are the needs of those who use information and the privacy rights of the people the information is about.

The slides set the problem out in four steps.

  1. IT technology allows businesses to gather information. Gathering is cheap, fast and automatic.
  2. The users of this information must be balanced against the privacy rights of the people whose information may be used. That is the conundrum itself: the organisation has a legitimate need, the person has a legitimate right.
  3. Systems collect and store key data from every interaction with customers. Examples on the slide: purchasing habits, contacts, search terms. Every click, purchase and search leaves a record.
  4. Many people object to the data-collection policies of government and business. The objection is that collection strips people of the power to control their own personal information. The slide adds a dry remark: IT does this on a regular basis. In other words, the objection is serious, but the practice is routine.

Key point. The core ethical complaint about data collection is loss of control. The person no longer decides who holds their information or what it is used for. Use the words "power to control their own personal information" in an essay.

Why privacy matters, reasonable limits and the Fourth Amendment

Slide 3 continues in three moves.

  • Privacy is a key concern of Internet users. It is also the top reason why non-users still avoid the Internet, according to US Census data. So weak privacy protection does not only hurt users. It also keeps people away from the technology and its benefits.
  • Reasonable limits must be set. Information and communication technologies must be developed to protect privacy rather than diminish it. This is the lecturer's conclusion on the conundrum: neither side wins outright, but limits are needed, and technology should be designed with privacy in mind.
  • Historical perspective on the right to privacy. The slide names the Fourth Amendment (dated 1789 on the slide) of the US Constitution. It gives a reasonable expectation of privacy and protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. beyond the slides The Bill of Rights was in fact ratified in 1791. Use the slide's wording for the exam, but do not be surprised if a textbook gives a different date.

The two vocabulary items from slide 7 belong here. The Fourth Amendment is the right to be protected from unreasonable search. The First Amendment is freedom of speech, and the like. The First Amendment matters in privacy debates because anonymity and private communication help people speak freely, and surveillance can make them hold back (a "chilling" effect).

Watch out. The Fourth Amendment is a US law. It restrains the government, not private employers (see workplace monitoring in the next section). In a Ugandan exam, present it as the historical source of the idea of privacy, then argue the principle, not the US legal detail.

Slides 2-3 · Practice · 3 marksWhat is the ethical conundrum in business and government collection of personal data?

The ethical conundrum is the need to balance the needs of those who use information against the privacy rights of the people whose information is used. IT lets businesses gather information from every customer interaction (purchasing habits, contacts, search terms), but many people object because it strips them of the power to control their own personal information. Reasonable limits must be set, so that technology protects privacy rather than diminishes it.

Key privacy and anonymity issues

Slide 4 is a list of eight issues. This lecture treats each one in turn, so the list is also a map of the whole privacy topic. Learn it whole.

  1. Government electronic surveillance (this section)
  2. Data encryption (next section)
  3. Identity theft (next section)
  4. Customer profiling (after that)
  5. Need to treat customer data responsibly (after that)
  6. Workplace monitoring (after that)
  7. Spamming (after that)
  8. Advanced surveillance techniques (after that)

The slide title joins privacy with anonymity. Privacy is control over personal information. Anonymity is being able to act, browse or speak without being identified. Encryption and anonymous browsing protect it. Surveillance and profiling erode it.

The eight key privacy and anonymity issues.
Government electronic surveillance; data encryption; identity theft; customer profiling; need to treat customer data responsibly; workplace monitoring; spamming; advanced surveillance techniques.

Governmental electronic surveillance and the USA Patriot Act of 2001

Slide 5 is the main legal slide. Its facts, in order:

  • Full title. The USA PATRIOT Act of 2001 is "Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism". The word PATRIOT is an acronym built from these words. Learn the full title: it can be asked.
  • Passed just after 9/11. It is more than 340 pages long and quite complex, yet it passed into law only five weeks after being introduced. The point to draw out: very little time for debate on a very large law.
  • Sweeping new powers to two groups: domestic law enforcement, including wiretaps without court order, and international intelligence agencies.
  • Critics' argument. The Act removes the checks and balances that previously gave courts the opportunity to ensure that law enforcement agencies did not abuse their powers. A court order was the check. Take it away and nobody independent confirms that a wiretap is justified.
  • Sunset provisions. The Act contains several "sunset" provisions covering increased searches and electronic surveillance. A sunset provision is a clause that makes a power expire on a set date unless it is renewed. These ones were due to terminate on 12/31/05 (31 December 2005).
  • An amendment to FISA. The Act amends the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA, 1978; see the legal summary below).

Provisions subject to sunset (slides 6 and 8) and the terms used (slide 7)

Slides 6 and 8 are two tables, headed "Key Provisions of USA Patriot Act Subject to Sunset" (slide 6) and "...(continued)" (slide 8). They list the sections of the Act that were due to expire. The slide 6 caption says they are primarily those that modified Title III and FISA. Together the two slides give this list.

SectionIssue addressedSummary
201Wiretapping in terrorism casesAdded several crimes for which federal courts may authorize wiretapping of people's communications.
202Wiretapping in computer fraud and abuse felony casesAdded computer fraud and abuse to the list of crimes the FBI may obtain a court order to investigate under Title III.
203 bSharing wiretap informationAllows the FBI to disclose evidence obtained under Title III to other federal officials, including “law enforcement, intelligence, protective, immigration, national defense, [and] national security” officials.
203 dSharing foreign intelligence informationProvides for disclosure of threat information obtained during criminal investigations to “appropriate” federal, state, local, or foreign government officials for the purpose of responding to the threat.
204FISA pen register/trap-and-trace exceptionsExempts foreign intelligence surveillance from statutory prohibitions against the use of pen register or trap-and-trace devices, which capture “addressing” information about the sender and recipient of a communication. It also exempts the U.S. government from general prohibitions against intercepting electronic communications and allows stored voice-mail communication to be obtained by the government through a search warrant rather than more stringent wiretap orders.
206FISA roving wiretapsExpands FISA to permit “roving wiretap” authority, which allows the FBI to intercept any communications to or by an intelligence target without specifying the telephone line, computer, or other facility to be monitored.
207Duration of FISA surveillance of non-U.S. agents of a foreign powerExtends the duration of FISA wiretap orders relating to an agent of a foreign power from 90 days to 120 days, and allows an extension in 1-year intervals instead of 90-day increments.
209Seizure of voice-mail messages pursuant to warrantsEnables the government to obtain voice-mail messages under Title III using just a search warrant rather than a wiretap order, which is more difficult to obtain. Messages stored on an answering machine tape, however, remain outside the scope of this section.
212Emergency disclosure of electronic surveillancePermits providers of communication services (such as telephone companies and Internet service providers) to disclose consumer records to the FBI if they believe immediate danger of serious physical injury is involved. Communication providers cannot be sued for such disclosure.
214FISA pen register/trap-and-trace authorityAllows the government to obtain a pen register/trap-and-trace device “for any investigation to gather foreign intelligence information.” It prohibits the use of FISA pen register/trap-and-trace surveillance against a U.S. citizen when the investigation is conducted “solely on the basis of activities protected by the First Amendment.”
215FISA access to tangible itemsPermits the FBI to compel production of any record or item without showing probable cause. People served with a search warrant issued under FISA rules may not disclose, under penalty of law, the existence of the warrant or the fact that records were provided to the government. It prohibits investigation of a U.S. citizen when it is conducted solely on the basis of activities protected by the First Amendment.
217Interception of computer trespasser communicationsCreates a new exception to Title III that permits the government to intercept the “communications of a computer trespasser” if the owner or operator of a “protected computer” authorizes it. It defines a protected computer as any computer “used in interstate or foreign commerce or communication” (because of the Internet, this effectively includes almost every computer).
220Nationwide service of search warrants for electronic evidenceExpands the geographic scope where the FBI can obtain search warrants or court orders for electronic communications and customer records.
223Civil liability and discipline for privacy violationsProvides that people can sue the government for unauthorized disclosure of information obtained through surveillance.
225Provider immunity for FISA wiretap assistanceProvides immunity from lawsuits for people who disclose information to the government pursuant to a FISA wiretap order, physical search order, or an emergency wiretap or search.

Pattern to remember. More crimes covered, more sharing between agencies, longer orders, and less need for a court order or probable cause. The only privacy-side clauses are 223 (the right to sue) and the First Amendment limits in 214 and 215.

The caption on slide 6 says the sunset provisions are primarily those that modified Title III and FISA. The slide explains what that means: these changes allow the government to conduct wiretaps without a court order.

  • Title III is the part of an older US law that sets the rules for police wiretapping of ordinary crime suspects. beyond the slides It is the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968. It normally requires a judge's permission before a phone is tapped.
  • FISA is the law that governs surveillance for foreign intelligence purposes (wiretapping aliens, per slide 28).
  • The Patriot Act modified both so that more surveillance could happen with less court involvement. These modified parts were the ones with the expiry date.

Slide 7 gives the terms needed to read this material.

TermMeaning on the slide
Pen registerCollects the outgoing phone numbers placed from a specific telephone line.
Trap and trace deviceCaptures the incoming numbers placed to a specific phone line. Example: a caller-ID box is a trap and trace device.
First AmendmentFreedom of speech, etc.
Fourth AmendmentRight to be protected from unreasonable search, etc.
ConundrumA puzzling question.

Together, a pen register and a trap and trace device record who called whom (not what was said). This is called "metadata" today. beyond the slides Even without content, a call log reveals a lot about a person's life.

Provisions for increased searches and electronic surveillance that terminated on 12/31/05; primarily those that modified Title III and FISA (allow government to conduct wiretaps without court order).
Four facts about the Patriot Act's passage and powers.
Passed just after 9/11; over 340 pages but passed five weeks after introduction; sweeping new powers to domestic law enforcement (wiretaps without court order) and international intelligence agencies; amendment to FISA.

Legal summary: the right to privacy and the main surveillance laws (slide 28)

Slide 28 is the lecture summary. Two parts of it belong to this section.

1. The legal concept of the right to privacy has four aspects. The slide lists them in shorthand:

  1. Web-surfing kept private: what you browse should not be tracked and exposed without your say.
  2. Identity theft: protection against others using your personal data in your name.
  3. HIPPA (spelled so on the slide; the US health-records privacy law is normally written HIPAA): privacy of medical information.
  4. False information about someone on the web: protection against untrue information being published about a person.

2. A number of laws enacted over the past 40 years affect a person's privacy. The three named on the slide:

LawYearWhat the slide says
FISA (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act)1978Wiretapping aliens.
ECPA (Electronic Communications Privacy Act)1986Set standards for access to stored email and other electronic communication.
US PATRIOT Act2001Authorises surveillance powers (see above).

The slide's conclusion: these and other laws authorize electronic surveillance by the government. So the law both protects privacy (ECPA sets standards for access to stored communication) and permits intrusion (FISA, Patriot Act). That double role is why the right to privacy is always argued as a balance. The rest of slide 28 (encryption, identity theft) is in the next section, and the profiling, workplace and surveillance summary on slide 29 is in the section after.

Privacy versus security when monitoring or censoring the Internet

This is the most likely essay on this topic. The slides give you the building blocks: the conundrum (balance), government surveillance, the Patriot Act and its critics, anonymity, and (in the later slides) workplace monitoring and surveillance cameras. The answer below uses them and adds a few points from general knowledge.

QB A2 · 8 marksWhat are the main ethical issues in sustaining a delicate balance between Privacy and Security issues when monitoring/censoring use of the internet technologies? Discuss with examples.

Governments and organisations monitor and censor Internet use to keep people secure (fighting terrorism, crime, fraud, harmful content). But monitoring intrudes on the right to privacy. The ethical issue is how to balance the two, so reasonable limits are set.

1. Loss of control over personal information. Monitoring strips people of the power to control their own information. Example: under the Patriot Act, a pen register or trap and trace device can log every number a person calls or is called from, without a court order.

2. Abuse of power and loss of checks and balances. Surveillance without a court order or independent oversight can be misused. Example: the USA Patriot Act 2001 allowed wiretaps without court order, and critics said it removed checks and balances. Powers can be used for intimidation of political dissenters or blackmail.

3. Freedom of speech and expression. Censorship limits free speech (First Amendment idea) and access to information. People who know they are watched stop speaking freely. Example: a state blocking social media during protests or elections.

4. Anonymity and confidentiality. Monitoring defeats anonymity and breaks encryption. Example: Moxie Marlinspike was asked to help a telecom intercept encrypted WhatsApp and Twitter traffic, which would expose every user, not only terrorists.

5. Proportionality and consent. Is the intrusion in proportion to the threat, and do people know they are being watched? Transparency and consent reduce the harm. Example: employers who monitor email must tell staff of the policy.

6. Security of the collected data. Stored data can be leaked or stolen. Example: a leaked government database can expose millions to identity theft.

Conclusion. Security is a legitimate aim, but surveillance and censorship must be limited, lawful, transparent and under independent oversight, so that technology protects privacy rather than diminishes it.

How the marks come. 8 marks means about 4 issues with an example each, plus a short balancing introduction and conclusion. Name the issue first, in the marker words, then the example. Do not write a general essay on privacy without examples: the question says "with examples".

Case: Moxie Marlinspike and the Saudi surveillance request

The case (2013/14 paper, Q3d, 5 marks; the exact question is below). Moxie Marlinspike is a cyber-security expert based in San Francisco. He describes himself as having worked as a software engineer, hacker, sailor, captain and shipwright. The Wall Street Journal identified him as chief technology officer and co-founder of Whisper Systems, which makes privacy and security software.

In May 2013 he wrote on his blog that an employee of a Saudi Arabian telecommunications company had contacted him by email. The employee wanted his help setting up a surveillance programme at the request of the Saudi government. The programme was meant to monitor communications on Twitter, WhatsApp, Viber and Line (apps that allow users to make calls and send texts). The employee sent design documents suggesting tactics such as compelling a certificate authority in the jurisdiction of the UAE or Saudi Arabia to produce SSL certificates they could use for interception, and purchasing SSL vulnerabilities or other exploits.

Marlinspike asked questions to understand the programme better, then declined to help. The contact replied that Saudi Arabia was trying to respond to an ongoing terrorist threat and that this was why he sought help. He added that if Marlinspike was not interested, perhaps he was indirectly helping those who curb freedom with their brutal activities. Marlinspike wrote that this kind of surveillance is "currently happening everywhere". The case text is by Irina Raicu.

The certificate authority link: in public-key systems a Certificate Authority vouches for a site's identity (see encryption). If an authority issues false certificates, an interceptor can pose as the site and read supposedly secure traffic.

2013/14 paper Q3d · 5 marksAssuming that all the details of Marlinspike's account are correct, did Marlinspike act ethically in rejecting the request from the telecom? Why, or why not?

Yes, he acted ethically. The main reasons:

1. Protecting the right to privacy. The programme would intercept the private communications of every user of the apps, not just terrorists. Helping would violate the right to privacy of many innocent people. This is also the engineer's duty to public welfare.

2. Weakening security for everyone. The tactics were forged SSL certificates and bought vulnerabilities. Weaknesses built to spy can be used by criminals and other governments, so he would harm the safety of all users and go against his own work in privacy and security software (professional integrity and competence).

3. No checks and balances. The request comes with no sign of a court order, oversight or limits, so the programme could be abused against political dissenters and journalists, not just terrorists.

4. The terrorism argument does not justify it. Security is a legitimate aim and he should take it seriously. But the means were disproportionate (mass interception) and the emotional appeal ("you are helping those who curb freedom") is not a reason. He also asked questions first, so he judged on facts.

Counter-view. A utilitarian could say that if the programme really stopped terrorist attacks, the lives saved outweigh the loss of privacy. But the harm to all users, the risk of abuse and the lack of oversight weigh more. He also did not act to expose it, though refusing was still defensible.

Case: smart lampposts and surveillance in cities (CAT 1 2021-22, Q3)

The case. Smart lampposts carry Internet-of-Things (IoT) sensors. In Hong Kong (article of August 2018) they collect real-time city data: weather, air quality, temperature, people and vehicle flow. They also provide wifi hotspots, electric vehicle charging, information dashboards, real-time traffic updates and parking-space information. They are adopted to cut energy use and raise public safety. Lights dim when streets are empty and brighten when motion sensors trigger.

  • United States. Los Angeles is equipping streetlights with sensors that can detect gunshots and other noises that may threaten public safety. Schenectady, New York, installed LED lights in 5,000 streetlights, managed through a secure web browser. Its mayor said that if you walk your dog at 10 pm and the lights come on, you get an added level of security. San Jose, California, approved 1,000 smart streetlights in 2018 that detect car crashes, gunshots and earthquakes. An NBC report said they also have facial recognition, cameras and audio recording. A councilman raised privacy concerns, while one resident said that if people know they are being watched, they do not do stupid things.
  • Singapore. The Smart Nation Sensor Platform (2018) plans to fit all 100,000 lampposts with sensors. Privacy concerns were raised about facial recognition combined with high-definition cameras. An official said there were no plans to probe into how people live or to do "moral policing". A local professor said cyber security and data leaks could be the bigger dangers.
  • Hong Kong rollout. The rollout began in July 2019. During mass protests that August, demonstrators worried about government surveillance cut down the new lampposts. The government admitted the hardware could spy on citizens but said the fears were unfounded. Officials promised to disable some features (licence-plate recognition, continuous audiovisual surveillance) and said the posts could not do the invasive facial recognition used in China. After 20 lampposts were destroyed, a local company ended its contract after its staff and executives' families received threats. It hoped to "reassure the public" and noted that the public had grown cautious and mistrustful of technology.

The question has six parts (a to f). The model answer below is built from the lecture's surveillance material (conundrum, anonymity, abuse of power, checks and balances, advanced surveillance technology) and the solution file's structure.

CAT 1 2021-22 Q3aWho are the stakeholders involved in the development, deployment, and use of smart lampposts?
  • Government and municipal authorities: fund, approve, regulate and manage the project.
  • Technology companies: supply, install and maintain sensors and software, and may hold the data.
  • Citizens and residents: the people observed, and also users of wifi, lighting and safety.
  • Privacy advocates and civil society groups: monitor misuse and defend rights.
  • Police and security agencies: want the data for crime and safety.
  • Businesses and visitors in the area, and protesters, who are most exposed to surveillance.
CAT 1 2021-22 Q3bWho should be consulted about such projects' goals and development?

Everyone affected, before the project starts: local communities where lampposts will stand; civic organisations and rights groups; privacy and cyber-security experts; legal and regulatory authorities that enforce data law; and academics who study cities and technology. Consultation matters because mistrust (as in Hong Kong) can destroy a project, whatever the government promises.

CAT 1 2021-22 Q3cIdentify two dilemmas that you recognize from the above case study.

Dilemma 1: public safety versus privacy. Sensors that detect gunshots and cameras that identify faces make streets safer, but they watch everyone. This is the lecture's conundrum: balance the needs of those who use the information against the privacy rights of those it is collected from. The lecture notes advocates say there is no legitimate expectation of privacy in public places, while critics warn of abuse, such as intimidation of political dissenters.

Dilemma 2: public trust versus the government's assurances. Governments say features are disabled or not intended for spying, yet the hardware could do it. Demonstrators cut down lampposts and a company quit. Should government deploy capable technology and ask the public to trust it, or limit the hardware to what it promises to use?

CAT 1 2021-22 Q3dWhat steps might business and government teams need to take to access the information/perspectives needed to manage the ethical landscape of such projects?
  • Stakeholder consultation: public hearings, surveys and meetings with community groups.
  • Privacy impact assessment and ethical risk assessment before deployment.
  • Clear governance: written policies on what is collected, who sees it, how long it is kept, and independent oversight (the checks and balances the Patriot Act critics wanted).
  • Cyber-security and data-protection measures to prevent leaks.
  • Transparency and public education: publish what each sensor can and cannot do, and allow complaints.
  • Privacy by design: turn off unneeded features (such as face recognition and audio), and set reasonable limits.
CAT 1 2021-22 Q3eWhat are some ethical issues that should be addressed as part of the deployment of smart lampposts in cities? Do those issues differ from city to city?
  • Privacy and data protection: consent, anonymisation, secure storage, no misuse.
  • Surveillance and civil liberties: freedom of movement, assembly and expression (protesters in Hong Kong).
  • Equity and justice: whether poor areas get more surveillance but fewer benefits.
  • Accountability and transparency: who decides, who checks, who answers when data is misused.
  • Bias: facial recognition errors (the lecture notes Boston's Logan airport test with 96 failures and 153 successes) can falsely accuse people.

Do they differ by city? Yes. The weight of each issue depends on local law, culture, trust in government and political context. In Hong Kong, protests made surveillance fear the main issue. In Schenectady, residents saw safety and energy saving. In Singapore, the debate was about facial recognition and data leaks.

CAT 1 2021-22 Q3fHow might the deployment of smart lampposts be evaluated through the ethical lenses of rights, justice/fairness, utilitarianism, common good, and virtue ethics?
  • Rights: do the lampposts respect the right to privacy, free expression and due process? Constant audio and face capture does not, unless consent and limits exist.
  • Justice/fairness: are the benefits and burdens shared fairly across districts and groups, or do some communities carry the surveillance?
  • Utilitarianism: weigh total benefits (safety, energy saved, better services) against total harms (loss of privacy, data leaks, mistrust). It may approve sensors for lighting and traffic but reject face recognition with audio.
  • Common good: does it improve the community's well-being, such as safer streets and cleaner cities, while respecting every stakeholder's interests?
  • Virtue ethics: do the decision-makers show honesty, integrity, responsibility and accountability? Promising to disable features and then keeping the hardware fails the virtue of honesty.

Overall: acceptable if limited to what is needed, with consent, oversight and transparency; unacceptable as hidden mass surveillance.

The lecture itself only supplies the privacy conundrum, the surveillance advocates-versus-critics argument and the facial recognition example. Encryption and identity theft

~25 min to readLow priority4 questions

Source: Set 7, slides 9-16. Earlier privacy material is in section t18; profiling, workplace monitoring and spam are in section t20.

Priority. No past paper question has been found on these slides. The practice questions below are original, written in the question bank style. Learn the definitions word for word; they are short.

Cryptography and encryption

Cryptography is the science of encoding messages so that only the sender and the intended receiver can understand them. It is the key tool for ensuring three things about electronic messages and online business transactions: confidentiality (nobody else can read the message), integrity (the message was not changed on the way) and authenticity (the message really comes from who it claims to come from).

Encryption is the process of converting electronic messages into a form understood only by the intended recipients. Plain text goes in, unreadable cipher text comes out, and only the holder of the right key can turn it back.

Key point. Cryptography is the science. Encryption is the process. Do not swap the two in a definition.

Define cryptography.

Define encryption.
The process of converting electronic messages into a form understood only by the intended recipients.

Encryption keys, public-key and private-key systems

An encryption key is a (large random) value applied using an algorithm to encrypt or decrypt text. The length of the key determines the strength of the encryption algorithm: a longer key has more possible values, so it is harder to guess.

Public-key encryption system

This system uses two keys, a public key and a private key, both belonging to the message recipient.

  • The recipient's public key is readily available. The sender uses it to encrypt the message.
  • The recipient's private key is mathematically related to the public key. It is kept secret and used for decryption.

RSA is a public-key encryption algorithm. RSA keys are typically 1024 to 2048 bits long.

The public-key diagram (slide 11, a picture)

The picture shows the flow of a message under public-key encryption:

  1. The sender must obtain the recipient's public key from a Certificate Authority. The Certificate Authority is a trusted third party that vouches that the public key really belongs to that recipient.
  2. The sender uses that public key to encrypt the message. It travels across the network as unreadable cipher text.
  3. The recipient decrypts it with their own private key. Only the recipient can read the message, because only they hold the private key.

beyond the slides The Certificate Authority issues a digital certificate that ties a public key to a named person or organisation. Without it, an attacker could hand the sender a fake public key and read the message.

Private-key encryption system

A private-key (symmetric) system uses a single key to encode and decode messages. Its big problem is distributing the key secretly to the sender and the receiver. If the key is intercepted on the way, the security is gone. This is the issue the slides call paramount, and it is the reason public-key systems were invented.

Public-key systemPrivate-key system
Number of keysTwo: public and privateOne single key
EncryptingRecipient's public key, openly availableThe shared key
DecryptingRecipient's private key, kept secretThe same shared key
Main issueSender must obtain a genuine public key (Certificate Authority)Secretly distributing the key to sender and receiver
ExampleRSANot named in the slides
Practice · 4 marksDistinguish between public-key and private-key encryption.

Number of keys. A public-key system uses two keys, a public key and a private key. A private-key system uses a single key to encode and decode messages.

Use of the keys. In public-key encryption the recipient's public key is readily available and used for encryption, while the private key is kept secret and used for decryption. In private-key encryption the same key does both.

Key distribution. A private-key system has the problem of secretly distributing the key to sender and receiver. In public-key encryption the sender gets the public key from a Certificate Authority, so no secret has to be sent.

Example. RSA is a public-key algorithm with keys of 1024-2048 bits.

Building encryption into systems, and export control

Encryption brings management and administration headaches: keys must be generated, stored, shared and recovered if lost. Despite this, most people agree encryption must eventually be built into three places:

  • networks;
  • file servers;
  • tape backup systems.

The slides give one product example. A Seagate Technology hard drive automatically encrypts all data, and the user must know the password to access the data. If the drive is lost or stolen, the data is useless to the thief.

Governments also control encryption. The U.S. Arms Export Control Act controls the export of encryption technology, hardware and software. Violators face a 10-year jail term and a $1M fine.

beyond the slides Ethical tension for discussion: strong encryption protects privacy and business secrets, but it also lets criminals hide communications from law enforcement. This is why governments restrict exports and sometimes demand access.

Practice · 6 marksDiscuss the ethical issues raised by the use of strong encryption, considering both privacy and law enforcement.

Benefits for privacy and security. Encryption ensures confidentiality, integrity and authenticity of electronic messages and online business transactions. Built into networks, file servers and tape backup systems, it protects personal data. A drive such as the Seagate drive that automatically encrypts all data protects people if it is lost.

Risks for law enforcement. Criminals and terrorists can use the same tools to hide their communications, so police cannot read evidence. This is why the Arms Export Control Act controls the export of encryption technology, with violators facing 10 years in jail and a $1M fine.

Costs. Encryption causes management and administration headaches, such as lost keys and lost data.

Judgement. The ethical question is the balance between an individual's right to privacy and society's interest in security. A reasonable position is to allow strong encryption for everyone, while giving law enforcement access only through a court order.
