Identity theft

Identity theft is the theft of key pieces of personal information to gain access to a person's financial accounts. With this information the thief may apply for new credit or financial accounts, register for college courses and so on, all in someone else's name.

The information stolen includes:

  • name;
  • address;
  • date of birth;
  • Social Security number;
  • passport number;
  • driver's license number;
  • mother's maiden name.

Identity theft is the fastest growing form of fraud in the United States. Victims spend more than 600 hours over several years recovering from it. The slides also criticise the lack of initiative by companies in informing people whose data was stolen.

Example: Stony Brook University. The personal information of 90,000 people in a Stony Brook University database was accidentally posted to Google and left there until it was discovered almost two weeks later. No hacker was needed: carelessness by the organisation exposed the data.

Phishing and spear-phishing

Phishing is an attempt to steal personal identity data by tricking users into entering information on a counterfeit web site. The lure is usually a spoof e-mail.

Spear-phishing is a variation in which employees are sent phony e-mails that look like they came from high-level executives within their own organisation. It differs from ordinary phishing because it is targeted at specific people in one organisation and uses a trusted internal name, so it is more convincing.

The phishing e-mail (slide 16, a picture). The slide shows a sample e-mail used by phishers: a message that looks like it comes from a bank or online service and asks the reader to follow a link and enter account details.

beyond the slides Typical tell-tale signs of a phishing e-mail: a generic greeting such as "Dear customer"; an urgent threat, for example "your account will be closed in 24 hours"; a sender address that does not match the real organisation's domain; a link whose real address differs from the text shown; spelling and grammar errors; a request for a password, PIN or Social Security number, which genuine organisations do not ask for by e-mail; and an unexpected attachment.

Spyware and the law

Spyware is keystroke-logging software downloaded to a user's computer without consent. It captures account usernames, passwords, credit card numbers and other sensitive information. It operates even if the infected computer is not connected to the Internet: it records keystrokes until the user reconnects, and the data collected is then e-mailed to the spy or posted to a web site.

The Identity Theft and Assumption Deterrence Act of 1998 was passed to fight identity fraud. It makes identity theft a Federal felony, punishable by 3 to 25 years in prison.

Practice · 4 marksHow does spear-phishing differ from phishing? Name one other way identity theft is carried out.

Phishing is an attempt to steal personal identity data by tricking users into entering information on a counterfeit web site, using spoof e-mails sent to many people.

Spear-phishing is a variation in which employees are sent phony e-mails that look like they came from high-level executives within their own organisation. It is targeted and uses a trusted name, so it is harder to spot.

Other method. Spyware is keystroke-logging software downloaded without consent that captures usernames, passwords and credit card numbers.

Practice · 5 marksExplain what is meant by identity theft. State the information that is stolen and describe two ways in which the problem can be reduced.

Identity theft is the theft of key pieces of personal information to gain access to a person's financial accounts. The thief may apply for new credit or accounts in someone else's name.

The information includes name, address, date of birth, Social Security number, passport number, driver's license number and mother's maiden name.

Reducing it. (1) Legislation: the Identity Theft and Assumption Deterrence Act of 1998 makes it a Federal felony of 3-25 years in prison. (2) Companies must take initiative to inform people whose data was stolen, and protect databases, as the Stony Brook case of 90,000 people shows. Users can also avoid entering details on suspicious sites.

How this section fits together. Slides 17-20 explain how companies profile consumers. Slides 21-22 say how to treat that data responsibly. Slide 23 covers employers watching employees. Slides 24-25 cover spam. Slides 26-27 cover cameras, facial recognition and GPS. Slides 28-29 are summaries. Every one of these topics has the same shape: a useful capability set against a privacy cost. That is the "ethical conundrum" the lecturer keeps naming, and it is the frame for every essay answer here.

Consumer profiling: how data is collected (slides 17-19)

The opening claim of the slides is that companies can collect information about consumers without their explicit permission. Some collection is open. Companies openly collect personal information about Internet users when they register at web sites, complete surveys, fill out forms or enter contests online. The user knows they typed something in. The hidden collection is the problem.

Cookies and tracking software

  • Cookies are text files a web site places on the user's hard drive so that it can remember information. Examples: site preferences and the contents of an electronic shopping cart.
  • The browser sends the cookie back to the server unchanged each time it accesses that server. This is how the site recognises you on your next visit.
  • Tracking software identifies visitors to your web site, for example from pay-per-click accounts. The site owner learns where the visitor came from.

Offline profiling

Similar methods are used outside the Web. Marketing firms warehouse consumer data: credit card purchases, frequent flier points, mail-order catalogue purchases and phone surveys. The result is databases that contain a huge amount of consumer behavioural data. So profiling is not only a web problem. Online and offline records can be combined.

Affiliated web sites and DoubleClick

An affiliated web site group is a group of web sites served by a single advertising network. DoubleClick was the slides' example. It tracks ad clicks and web purchases across the group, which is useful for marketers and sellers. Because one network sees your visits to many sites, it can build a much fuller picture of you than any single site could. Marketers use cookies to recognise return visitors and store useful information about them, which gives customised service for each consumer. The same mechanism that makes service convenient is the one that builds the profile.

Types of data collected while surfing

Data typeWhat it is
GET dataThe affiliated web sites visited and the information requested.
POST dataForm data: what you typed into forms.
Click-stream dataMonitoring of consumer surfing activity: the trail of clicks.

Four ways to limit or stop cookies

  1. Set the browser to limit or stop cookies.
  2. Manually delete them from the hard drive.
  3. Download and install a cookie-management program.
  4. Use anonymous browsing programs that do not accept cookies. Example: anonymizer.com lets you hide your identity while browsing.
What are cookies?
Text files a web site places on the user's hard drive so that it can remember information (for example site preferences, contents of a shopping cart). The browser sends them back to the server unchanged each time it accesses that server.
What is an affiliated web site group? Give the slides' example.
A group of web sites served by a single advertising network. Example: DoubleClick, which tracks ad clicks and web purchases.
The three types of data collected while surfing the Web.
GET data (affiliated web sites visited and information requested); POST data (form data); click-stream data (monitoring of consumer surfing activity).
Four ways to limit or stop the deposit of cookies.
Set the browser to limit or stop cookies; manually delete them from the hard drive; install a cookie-management program; use anonymous browsing programs that do not accept cookies.

Personalization software and P3P (slide 20)

Marketers use personalization software to optimise the number, frequency and mixture of their ad placements. There are four kinds.

TypeHow it decides what to show you
Rules-basedUses business rules tied to customer-provided preferences or online behaviour to determine the most appropriate page views.
Collaborative filteringGives consumer recommendations based on products purchased by customers with similar buying habits.
Demographic filteringConsiders user zip codes, age and sex when making product suggestions.
Contextual commerceAssociates product promotions or ads with the content the user is currently viewing.

Quick way to tell them apart: rules = "if the customer did X, show Y"; collaborative = "people like you bought"; demographic = "people of your age, sex and area"; contextual = "ads that match the page you are on".

Platform for Privacy Preferences (P3P)

P3P is the technical defence. It shields users from sites that do not provide the desired level of privacy protection. P3P software in a browser downloads the privacy policy for each site visited and notifies the user if the policy does not match their preferences. The user sets preferences once; the browser compares them with each site's policy.

The four types of personalization software.
Rules-based; collaborative filtering; demographic filtering; contextual commerce.
Collaborative filtering.
Consumer recommendations based on products purchased by customers with similar buying habits.
Contextual commerce.
Associates product promotions/ads with content the user is currently viewing.
What does P3P do?
Shields users from sites that do not provide the desired level of privacy protection. P3P software in a browser downloads the privacy policy of each site visited and notifies users if the policy does not match their preferences.

Data mining and privacy

beyond the slides The slides do not define data mining, but profiling is its everyday form: large stores of consumer data (the warehoused credit card, mail-order and click-stream records above) are searched by software for patterns about individuals and groups. The privacy issues follow from that.

QB D3 · 5 marks (also sol_exam2122 Q4c)What ethical issues does the use of data mining raise with respect to privacy?

Invasion of privacy. Data mining collects and analyses personal information (purchases, clicks, forms) without the individual's knowledge. Profiles are built that the person never agreed to. Dilemma: should the organisation use data mining for research or commercial benefit, or protect the individual's right to privacy and autonomy?

Lack of informed consent. Users do not know the extent of collection or how the data will be used, so they cannot make an informed decision. Data given for one purpose (a contest entry) is reused for another (marketing). Dilemma: should the firm use all the data it can gather, or respect users' ability to make informed decisions about how their data is used (transparency)?

Secondary use and sale of data. Data is shared with affiliated sites and third parties and combined with offline records into one profile. Dilemma: should the firm earn from selling or reusing the data, or keep to the original purpose for which it was given?

Discrimination and bias. Patterns drawn from historical data can reinforce bias, for example by excluding certain groups from offers or credit. Dilemma of fairness and justice: should the firm use patterns from historical data to target offers efficiently, or avoid harming marginalised groups?

Security risk. Large warehouses of personal data are targets for hacking and breaches, leading to identity theft (see t19). Dilemma: the value of storing large datasets against the organisation's responsibility to safeguard personal information.

Balance. The benefits (research, personalised service) must be weighed against the individual's right to privacy and autonomy.

Treating consumer data responsibly (slides 21-22)

The slide's opening: strong measures are required to avoid customer relationship problems. Customers who feel watched leave, complain or sue. The recognised standard is the Code of Fair Information Practices and the 1980 OECD privacy guidelines. Under them a company should:

  1. Collect only the personal information necessary to deliver its products or services.
  2. Protect this information.
  3. Inform customers if it intends to use the information for research or marketing.
  4. Provide a means for customers to opt out.

The summary slide (29) shortens this to: to protect consumer data, organisations only collect personal information necessary to deliver the product or service.

Chief privacy officer (CPO)

A CPO is an executive who oversees data privacy policies and initiatives. The role avoids violating government regulations and assures customers that their privacy will be protected.

The manager's checklist (slide 22)

Slide 22, "Manager's Checklist for Treating Consumer Data Responsibly", is a table of eight questions, each answered Yes or No. It is the practical form of slide 21. A responsible manager should be able to answer Yes to all eight:

  1. Do you have a written data privacy policy that is followed?
  2. Can consumers easily view your data privacy policy?
  3. Are consumers given an opportunity to opt in or opt out of your data policy?
  4. Do you collect only the personal information needed to deliver your product or service?
  5. Do you ensure that the information is carefully protected and accessible only by those with a need to know?
  6. Do you provide a process for consumers to review their own data and make corrections?
  7. Do you inform your customers if you intend to use their information for research or marketing and provide a means for them to opt out?
  8. Have you identified a person who has full responsibility for implementing your data policy and dealing with consumer data issues?

Notice what the checklist adds to slide 21: a written, followed, easily viewable privacy policy, a chance to opt in as well as opt out, a way for consumers to review and correct their own data, and access only by those with a need to know.

Manager's checklist for treating consumer data responsibly: the eight questions (slide 22).
Written data privacy policy that is followed; consumers can easily view it; opportunity to opt in or opt out; collect only the information needed; information protected and accessible only to those with a need to know; process for consumers to review their data and make corrections; inform customers of research or marketing use with a means to opt out; a named person with full responsibility for the data policy.
What a company should do under the Code of Fair Information Practices and 1980 OECD guidelines (4 points).
Collect only the personal information necessary to deliver its products/services; protect this information; inform customers if it intends to use it for research or marketing; provide a means for customers to opt out.
Chief privacy officer (CPO).
An executive to oversee data privacy policies and initiatives; avoids violating government regulations and assures customers that their privacy will be protected.

Workplace monitoring (slide 23)

The ethical conundrum: how do you ensure worker productivity without violating the privacy rights of employees? Employers monitor workers by recording email, surfing activity and files, and even by videotaping employees on the job. The employer's aim is to ensure that the corporate IT usage policy is followed.

The legal position (US, as in the slides). The Fourth Amendment cannot be used to limit how a private employer treats its employees. Public-sector employees have far greater privacy rights, because of the "reasonable expectation of privacy" test from Katz v. U.S. (the slide gives it as a Supreme Court ruling, dated 1998 on the slide). A private employee therefore has little constitutional protection against the employer.

Watch out. The slide writes "1998" for Katz v. US. Reproduce the slide's wording in the exam. beyond the slides The historical Katz decision is from 1967, which is where the "reasonable expectation of privacy" idea comes from. If you mention a date, hedge or leave it out.

What privacy advocates want. Federal legislation to keep employers from infringing employees' privacy rights; employees to be informed of electronic monitoring devices; and a restriction on the type of information collected.

beyond the slides In Uganda the relevant protection is Article 27 of the Constitution (right to privacy of person, home and other property and communications) and the Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019, which requires data to be collected for a lawful purpose, with consent or another legal basis, and limits what is kept. Name them only as supporting points.

QB A1(ii) · 5 marksSimon is a social media consultant. The CIO asks him to collect personal data on the staff in the IT department via Facebook and LinkedIn. How ethical or legal is it for the CIO to use employees' personal social media activity in the HR monitoring process?

The ethical analysis with the 7-step template is in t07. This part asks only about ethics and legality, 5 marks.

Legality. Employers have a wide legal right to monitor work email, surfing and files to ensure the corporate IT usage policy is followed. In the slides' US position the Fourth Amendment does not limit a private employer, so monitoring work systems is generally lawful. But the CIO is collecting personal data from the employees' private accounts, outside work systems. This is legal only if it is within the policy and the employees were informed and it relates to the job. Under data protection law (in Uganda, the Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 and Article 27 of the Constitution) personal data must be collected for a lawful, specific purpose and with consent. Collecting private profiles without it is likely unlawful. Public-sector staff have a reasonable expectation of privacy (Katz).

Ethics. It fails the informed consent test if staff do not know. It crosses from productivity into the employees' private life, so it is not proportionate to the aim. It risks discrimination (judging staff on opinions, religion or lifestyle) and destroys trust. Where the information is public and the employer only reviews what staff chose to post openly, with a published policy, it is more defensible.

Conclusion. Acceptable only if limited to job-relevant information, announced in advance, and applied fairly to all staff; otherwise it is unethical and probably illegal.

2014 and 2015 papers Q5(c) · 4 marksIdentify two ways in which a company may violate an employee's right to privacy.

1. Monitoring communications and activity without telling the employee. Recording email, surfing activity and files, or videotaping employees, without informing them or beyond what the IT usage policy allows, is a violation. Staff have a reasonable expectation of privacy over personal messages and private spaces such as toilets.

2. Collecting, using or disclosing personal data without consent. Gathering personal information that has nothing to do with the job (for example from social media), or passing employee records (health, salary, ID numbers) to third parties without consent, violates privacy and the right to informed consent.

Other ways it can happen: tracking location by GPS outside working hours; searching personal belongings or phones without cause.

Herman case (2014/15 Q5d). That question (8 marks) reads: With reference to Herman's case, comment on the view that employers do not have responsibilities (to employees) beyond those of the employment contract. In the case, Herman works more than 10 hours a day and six days a week, 300 km from his family, and his contract states no working hours or days. It is about employer duties and work-life balance, not privacy. It is not covered here; see t09 and t10 for employer duties and contracts. Q5(b) (6 marks: Identify and explain three (3) ethical responsibilities of employers towards employees), sits with the same material.

The ethical conundrum of workplace monitoring.
Ensuring worker productivity without violating the privacy rights of employees.
Why can the Fourth Amendment not protect most employees from monitoring?
It cannot be used to limit how a private employer treats its employees. Public-sector employees have far greater privacy rights: the "reasonable expectation of privacy" (Katz v. U.S.).
What privacy advocates want on workplace monitoring.
Federal legislation to keep employers from infringing employees' privacy rights; inform employees of electronic monitoring devices; restrict the type of information collected.

Spamming (slides 24-25)

Spamming is the transmission of the same e-mail message to a large number of people. It is an extremely inexpensive method of marketing. Compared with a direct-mail campaign:

Spam campaignDirect-mail campaign
Cost$1K$10K
Time to develop3 weeks3 months
Time for feedback48 hours3 weeks

Many legitimate organisations use it, for example for product announcements. But it can also contain unwanted and objectionable material. The slide says these last two points are the ethical conundrum: a cheap, legitimate tool that also floods people with unwanted content.

Statistics on the slide:

  • Spam is 40% of all email.
  • 12.4 billion spam emails are sent daily.
  • Each person receives 6 spam emails a day, about 2,200 a year.
  • Cost to all non-corporate Internet users: $255 million.
  • Cost to all U.S. corporations in 2002: $8.9 billion.
  • 26 states had anti-spam laws.

The CAN-SPAM Act 2004

Full name: Controlling the Assault of Non-Solicited Pornography and Marketing Act. It says it is legal to spam but:

  • spammers cannot disguise their identity;
  • there must be a label in the message specifying that the e-mail is an ad or solicitation;
  • they must include a way for recipients to indicate they do not want future mass mailings (opt out).

Criticism: the Act may have actually increased the flow of spam, because it legalises the sending of unsolicited e-mail.

What is spamming?
Transmission of the same e-mail message to a large number of people.
What the CAN-SPAM Act 2004 requires of spammers (it says spamming is legal but...).
They cannot disguise their identity; there must be a label specifying the e-mail is an ad or solicitation; they must include a way for recipients to opt out of future mass mailings.
The main criticism of CAN-SPAM.
It may have actually increased the flow of spam, as it legalises the sending of unsolicited e-mail.
Spam versus direct mail: cost, development time, feedback time.
$1K vs $10K; 3 weeks vs 3 months; 48 hours vs 3 weeks.

Advanced surveillance technology (slides 26-27)

These tools provide exciting new data-gathering capabilities versus personal-privacy issues. The two sides:

  • Advocates: people have no legitimate expectation of privacy in public places.
  • Critics: it creates potential for abuse, such as intimidation of political dissenters and blackmail of people caught with the "wrong" person or in the "wrong" place.

Camera surveillance

U.S. cities plan to expand surveillance systems. London has one of the world's largest public surveillance systems. A "smart surveillance system" singles out people acting suspiciously, so a computer, not a human, decides who is watched. (The smart-city lamppost case is in t18.)

Facial recognition software

It identifies criminal suspects and other undesirable characters, but it yields mixed results. At Boston's Logan airport it produced 96 failures and 153 successes. That is 249 trials, so roughly 61% worked and about 39% failed. (Do not claim more than the slide: it shows the technology works often but not reliably.) A failure means either a suspect is missed or an innocent person is flagged.

GPS chips

Global Positioning System chips are placed in many devices, such as cars and cellphones, to precisely locate users.

  • Good: accurately respond to 911 callers; real-time, location-aware marketing.
  • Bad: wireless spamming from local restaurants and similar businesses; your whereabouts are always known.
QB D4 · 4 marks (also CAT 2021-22 Q4d)What ethical issues does the use of facial recognition systems raise with respect to privacy?

Lack of informed consent. Faces are captured and analysed in public without the person's knowledge or consent.

Surveillance and tracking. It enables mass surveillance of movements and associations, with potential for abuse: intimidation of political dissenters and blackmail of people in the "wrong" place.

Inaccuracy and bias. Results are mixed: at Boston's Logan airport there were 96 failures against 153 successes. False matches can wrongly label innocent people as suspects, and accuracy is often worse for some demographic groups, causing discrimination.

Lack of transparency and accountability. Governments and firms often give no safeguards on who sees or keeps the images, so there is risk of misuse and breaches.

QB D5 · 8 marks (also CAT 2021-22 Q4e, which asks for two reasons)"Honest, upright, law-abiding citizens have nothing to fear from the distribution of their personal data." Do you agree or not? Give at least three reasons for your position and one reasonable objection to it.

Position: I disagree. Being law-abiding does not remove the risks of distributing personal data.

Reason 1: privacy is a right, not a privilege of wrongdoers. Even law-abiding people have a right to privacy and to control who knows their health, finances, beliefs and location. We close the bathroom door although we do nothing illegal.

Reason 2: risk of misuse. Data can be misused or stolen: identity theft, fraud, blackmail, and targeted advertising or manipulation. Honest people are the victims, not the culprits (t19).

Reason 3: data can be wrong or misread. Profiles contain false or out-of-context information, and mining can discriminate. Honest people have been refused jobs, credit or entry because of errors. Facial recognition at Logan airport failed 96 times.

Reason 4: abuse of power and chilling effect. What is lawful today may be targeted tomorrow. Governments or employers can use data for intimidation of dissenters, which makes honest citizens afraid to speak or associate freely.

Reason 5: no consent. Data given for one purpose is reused for another without informed consent.

Reasonable objection. Distribution of data can help honest people: it supports crime prevention and national security, gets faster 911 response through GPS, fraud detection and better personalised service. If data is protected by the Code of Fair Information Practices (collect only what is necessary, inform, opt out), honest citizens may indeed have little to fear.

Reply. That depends on trustworthy handlers and strong safeguards, which cannot be assumed. The benefits can be had with limited, consented and secured data collection.

Advocates: people have no legitimate expectation of privacy in public places. Critics: creates potential for abuse - intimidation of political dissenters, blackmail of people caught with the "wrong" person or in the "wrong" place.
What is a "smart surveillance system"?
A camera surveillance system that singles out people acting suspiciously.
The Logan airport facial recognition result.
Mixed results at Boston's Logan airport: 96 failures, 153 successes.
The good and the bad of GPS chips (slide wording).
Good: accurately respond to 911 callers; real-time location-aware marketing. Bad: wireless spamming from local restaurants etc.; your whereabouts are always known.

Summary of the privacy topic (slides 28-29)

Slide 28 recaps earlier material: the legal right to privacy has four aspects (web-surfing privacy, identity theft, HIPAA, false information about someone on the web). Laws of the past 40 years affect privacy: FISA 1978 (wiretapping aliens), ECPA 1986 (standards for access to stored email and other electronic communication) and the US PATRIOT Act 2001. These and other laws authorise government electronic surveillance. Data encryption has public key and private key systems, and identity theft is the last item. See t18 and t19.

Slide 29 recaps this section: consumer behaviour data is collected both online and offline (consumer profiling); the Code of Fair Information Practices and 1980 OECD guidelines say organisations should only collect personal information necessary to deliver the product or service; employers record and review employee communications and activities on the job (workplace monitoring); and information technology advances for surveillance include surveillance cameras, facial recognition software and GPS systems.

Four aspects of the legal right to privacy (slide 28; see t18).
Web-surfing privacy; identity theft; HIPAA; false information about someone on the web.

Key point. In an essay on any of these topics, use the same four moves: state the benefit, state the privacy cost, name the standard that balances them (fair information practices, informed consent, notice and opt-out) and conclude with a recommendation.

Profession versus occupation, whistleblowing and conflict of interest

~1 h 00 min to readHigh priority18 questions

Source: not in your slides. Built from the question bank, the 2011-2018 papers, the CAT papers and the three solution files. The only slide material used is the model-rules wording in Set 4, slides 11-25 (whistle blowing and conflict of interest clauses).

Not in your slides. The lecturer never taught profession versus occupation, whistleblowing or conflict of interest as separate slide topics, but they come up in almost every CAT and exam: profession and occupation in 2016, 2017, CAT 2021-22 and the 2021-22 exam; whistleblowing in 2011/12 and 2013/14; conflict of interest in 2011/12, 2013/14 and two CAT 2 papers. Treat this as a full topic. Where a passage is general knowledge and not from a slide or a solution file it carries the label beyond the slides. Where the wording is a Set 4 model rule, the text says so.

How the Must/Should tags work here. The rule is: Must = phrase is in the slides and in a past paper or solution; Should = slides only. Because most of this section is not in the slides, almost every marker below is tagged by what the pool shows. Where a phrase is not in the slides but appears in all the solution files (for example "specialized knowledge", "code of ethics"), it is tagged Must and the row says why. Phrases that appear only in one paper or one solution are tagged Should.

Profession versus occupation

An occupation is any activity a person does to earn a living. It covers every kind of paid work: driving a taxi, selling goods, cleaning, farming, clerical work, and also medicine or engineering. A profession is a special kind of occupation. It is a vocation that needs specialized knowledge, long training and formal qualifications, and it is organised and regulated by a professional body that sets standards of competence and a code of ethics. All professions are occupations. Not all occupations are professions.

The solution files give the same core split in three places. The CAT 2021-22 solution says a profession is "a paid occupation that requires specialized knowledge, training, and often formal qualifications, such as medicine or law" while an occupation is "a broader term that encompasses any activity or job that a person does to earn a living". The 2020-21 exam solution adds that a profession is "often regulated by a professional body or association" and that professions involve "a higher level of expertise, ethical standards, and professional responsibilities". The 2021-22 exam solution compares on four points: level of specialization, formal education, autonomy, and adherence to a code of ethics.

The points of difference

PointProfessionOccupation
KnowledgeSpecialized, theoretical and technical body of knowledgeSkills that can be learned on the job; no deep theory required
Education and trainingLong formal education (a degree), then supervised practiceShort training, apprenticeship or none
Entry and licensingQualification, registration or licensing before you may practise (for engineers, registration with the ERB and UIPE)Anyone may enter; no licence needed
RegulationGoverned by a professional body that sets standards and disciplines membersGoverned by the employer and general law only
Code of ethicsBinding code, breach can lead to sanctions or deregistrationUsually no profession-wide code, only company rules
AutonomyPractitioner uses independent professional judgmentFollows instructions and procedures set by the employer
ResponsibilityDuty to the public and personal accountability for resultsAccountable mainly to the employer
PurposeService to society as well as earning a livingMainly earning a living

Examples

The 2021-22 exam solution uses two pairs. Nursing versus housekeeping: nursing needs specialized education, licensure, a professional code of ethics and autonomy in decisions about patient care. Housekeeping is cleaning work done without the same formal education, specialized training or code. Law versus retail sales: law has extensive formal education, specialized training, licensure, a code of conduct and autonomy in giving legal advice. Retail sales is selling products without those requirements. Other pairs that work: engineer versus bricklayer, doctor versus shop attendant, accountant versus cashier.

Watch out. Do not say that an occupation has no skill or no value. The difference is in the features above, not in how important the job is. A skilled welder has an occupation. A welding engineer registered with the ERB who signs off a design is practising a profession.

ethics-cat-1 Q1a · 3 marksExplain the difference between an occupation and a profession.

An occupation is any activity a person does to earn a living. A profession is a paid occupation that requires specialized knowledge, training and formal qualifications and is regulated by a professional body.

1. Knowledge and training. A profession needs specialized knowledge gained through long formal education, for example a degree in engineering. An occupation such as taxi driving needs only basic skills.

2. Regulation and code of ethics. A profession is regulated by a professional body (for engineers, the UIPE and the ERB) that registers or licenses members and enforces a code of ethics. An occupation has no such body or code.

3. Autonomy and public responsibility. A professional uses independent judgment and has a duty to the public, not only to the employer. A person in an occupation follows the employer's instructions.

CAT 2021-22 Q1 (iii) / 2016 Q1c · part of 12 marksDifferentiate between the following: ... Profession and Occupation.

A profession is an occupation that needs specialized knowledge, training and skills, with formal qualifications, and is regulated by a professional body or association. It carries ethical standards and professional responsibilities, for example medicine, law or engineering.

An occupation is any form of employment or work a person engages in to earn a living, whether professional or non-professional, for example retail sales or housekeeping.

So every profession is an occupation, but an occupation is a profession only when it has the specialized knowledge, regulation and code of ethics.

Exam 2021-22 Q1b · marks not printedWith aid of examples briefly describe how profession differs from a mere occupation.

The difference is mainly in level of specialization, formal education, autonomy and adherence to a code of ethics.

Nursing versus housekeeping. Nursing is a profession: it needs specialized education, licensure, a professional code of ethics and autonomy in decision-making over patient care. Housekeeping is an occupation: cleaning tasks done without that formal education, specialized training or specific code.

Law versus retail sales. Law has extensive formal education, specialized training, licensure, a code of conduct and autonomy in giving legal services. Retail sales is selling products without those requirements.

In engineering the same split holds: a registered engineer versus a general labourer on the same site.

What qualifies engineering as a profession

Engineering qualifies as a profession because it has every feature in the table above. The question asks you to show that the features apply to engineering, so state the feature and attach engineering to it.

  1. Specialized body of knowledge. Engineering rests on mathematics, science and design methods that take years to master.
  2. Long formal education. A university degree is required, followed by supervised experience.
  3. Registration and licensing. In Uganda, graduate engineers register with the Engineers Registration Board (ERB) and join the Uganda Institute of Professional Engineers (UIPE). Graduation alone does not make you registered. The ERB is the statutory regulator that registers engineers; the UIPE is the professional membership body. They have different functions (the question bank statement that they "serve the same function" is false), and registration or membership is by application, not automatic. The question bank has a statement that qualified engineers are "automatically registered on graduation": it is false.
  4. A professional body. UIPE and international bodies (IEEE, ASCE, ASME) set standards and represent members.
  5. A code of ethics. Engineers are bound by canons that put the safety, health and welfare of the public first.
  6. Autonomy and judgment. Engineers make independent technical decisions, such as approving a design, that others rely on.
  7. Public service and public trust. Engineering work affects lives (bridges, power, communications), so society trusts and expects accountability from engineers.
  8. Accountability and discipline. Breach of the code can lead to disciplinary action, loss of registration, and legal liability.
2017 Q5F · 3 marksWhat qualifies Engineering as a profession?

Engineering qualifies as a profession because it has the features that distinguish a profession from an occupation.

1. Specialized knowledge and long formal education. It rests on specialized knowledge in science, mathematics and design, gained through a university degree and supervised experience.

2. Registration and a professional body. Engineers must be registered or licensed (ERB) and belong to a professional body (UIPE) that sets standards of competence and discipline.

3. A code of ethics and public service. Engineers follow a code of ethics that puts the safety, health and welfare of the public first, and they use independent professional judgment.

Characteristics that distinguish a professional body

A professional body is an organisation of qualified practitioners of one profession. The Uganda Institute of Professional Engineers (UIPE) is the engineering example in the papers. Its purpose is to regulate and serve its profession. Other social organisations, such as clubs, churches or charities, may have members and rules, but they do not control entry to a trade or license people to practise. The solution files list five distinguishing features.

  1. Regulation of standards. The body establishes and maintains standards of competence, conduct and ethics for the profession.
  2. Certification, licensing and registration. The body, or a board it works with (the ERB for engineers), oversees who is qualified to practise. People who do not meet the qualifications are excluded.
  3. Continuing professional development (CPD). The body offers training, seminars and courses so members keep learning and stay competent.
  4. Advocacy and representation. The body speaks for its members and for the profession to government, regulators and other stakeholders, and it advises on policy and law.
  5. Ethics and discipline. The body publishes a code of ethics and runs disciplinary procedures, so misconduct can be punished by warning, suspension or removal from the register.

beyond the slides Other features you can add if the question asks for more: it accredits university programmes; it sets entry exams; it is self-governing; it protects the public by guaranteeing a minimum standard; it gives members a professional title and identity.

QB B1 · 4 marksGive four characteristics that distinguish a professional body from other social organizations.

1. Regulation of standards. A professional body establishes and maintains standards of competence, conduct and ethics for its profession.

2. Certification, licensing and registration. It oversees certification, licensing or registration so only qualified people practise. For engineers this is done with the ERB.

3. Continuing professional development. It provides continuing professional development (CPD) so members keep their skills current.

4. Ethics and discipline. It publishes a code of ethics and applies disciplinary procedures against misconduct. (A fifth feature, advocacy and representation of members to government, can replace any of these.)

Exam 2020-21 Q1C · marks not printedWhich distinguishing features do professional bodies like the Uganda Institute of Professional Engineers (UIPE) have over other social organizations?

Professional bodies like UIPE differ from other social organisations in that they:

1. Regulate standards of competence, conduct and ethics in the profession.

2. Certify, license or register practitioners so that only those who meet established qualifications practise.

3. Offer continuing professional development for ongoing learning and growth of members.

4. Advocate for and represent members before regulators, government agencies and other stakeholders.

5. Enforce a code of ethics and discipline to uphold standards and deal with misconduct. Social clubs and charities do none of these things with legal or professional force.

Factors that motivate engineers to practise their profession well

The ethics-cat-1 question says: "discuss the factors that would motivate engineers to practice their profession while carrying out their day-to-day activities". Read it as: what drives engineers to practise ethically and competently every day, not only to turn up for work. Say this reading in your first line. It is a "discuss" question, so give four or five factors, each with a reason and an engineering example.

beyond the slides The factors, grouped:

  • Public safety and welfare. Engineers know people use and live with what they build. The first canon, holding paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public, is a constant reason to practise carefully.
  • The code of ethics and professional standards. The UIPE code and its canons tell the engineer what is expected. Following it gives clear direction in daily decisions.
  • Registration, licensing and discipline. An engineer who breaks the code risks warnings, suspension and loss of registration. This is a strong external motive.
  • Legal liability. Negligence can lead to lawsuits, compensation and criminal charges.
  • Personal integrity, conscience and professional pride. Good engineers want to be able to stand behind their work. This is an internal, virtue-based motive.
  • Reputation and career progress. Honest, competent work builds trust with clients, employers and peers, brings promotion, and wins future contracts.
  • Public trust in the profession. Each engineer's conduct affects how society views all engineers.
  • Employer expectations and a good ethical climate. Management that supports safety reporting and rewards honest work encourages ethical practice.
  • Fair rewards and working conditions. Decent pay and recognition reduce the temptation to take shortcuts or accept bribes.
  • Continuing professional development. Staying current keeps the engineer competent, which is itself an ethical duty.
ethics-cat-1 Q1b · marks not statedDiscuss the factors that would motivate engineers to practice their profession while carrying out their day-to-day activities.

I read this as the factors that motivate engineers to practise ethically and competently in their daily work.

1. Public safety and welfare. The engineer's work affects lives, and the first canon is to hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public. A design engineer checking a load calculation twice is acting on this.

2. The code of ethics. The code of ethics of UIPE sets out what is expected and gives guidance in daily decisions, such as refusing to sign a design outside one's competence.

3. Registration and discipline. Registration with the ERB and disciplinary action for misconduct give a strong reason not to cut corners, because misconduct can cost an engineer the right to practise.

4. Professional integrity and pride. Engineers want to protect their integrity and be proud of work they can stand behind.

5. Reputation and public trust. Honest work earns public trust, repeat clients and career progress. Legal liability for negligence adds a further reason to take care.

Name five factors that motivate engineers to practise ethically (short form).
Public safety and welfare; code of ethics; registration and discipline; professional integrity and pride; reputation and public trust.

Whistleblowing: meaning, internal versus external

Whistleblowing is the act of an employee or member of an organisation disclosing information about wrongdoing in that organisation, such as a danger to public safety, illegal activity, fraud or corruption, to people who can act on it. The whistleblower is usually motivated by concern for the public and not by personal gain. beyond the slides A whistleblower acts when normal reporting has failed, and the act often goes against the employer's wishes. That conflict is why it is an ethical dilemma: loyalty to the employer against duty to the public.

The Set 4 model rules (slide wording). The Set 4 engineering code lists "Whistle blowing" under obligation to society. Rule 3 says: "If an engineer's professional judgment is overruled resulting in danger to the life, health, welfare, or property of the public, the engineer shall notify his/her employer or client and any appropriate authority." Rule 8, the "Final Obligation to Society", says engineers who know of a possible violation of the rules "shall provide pertinent information and assist the state board in reaching final determination of the possible violation". So the code does not ask the engineer to keep quiet: it requires notification first of the employer or client, then of the appropriate authority.

Internal versus external whistleblowing

PointInternal whistleblowingExternal whistleblowing
Who is toldSomeone inside the organisation: supervisor, higher management, ethics officer, audit committee or boardSomeone outside: regulator, police, a government authority, the professional body, the press, or the public
AimLet the organisation correct the problem itselfForce correction when the organisation will not act, or protect the public
Risk to whistleblowerLower, but still possible retaliationHigher: dismissal, legal action, loss of reputation
Risk to organisationContained, problem handled privatelyPublic exposure, fines, reputational damage
When usedFirst step, always tried firstLast resort, after internal channels have failed
ExampleThe BART engineers' memos to their managers (2017 paper Q4, see section t07)Dr Hansen speaking to the press about NASA climate censorship
2013/14 Q4b and 2011/12 Q4b · 4 marksDistinguish between internal and external whistleblowing.

Internal whistleblowing is reporting a wrongdoing to someone within the organisation, for example the supervisor, senior management, an ethics officer or the board, through the normal internal channels. The aim is to let the organisation correct itself, and the risk to the whistleblower is lower.

External whistleblowing is disclosing the wrongdoing to someone outside the organisation, such as a regulator, the police, the professional body or the media. It is used as a last resort when internal channels fail or the public is in danger, and it carries a greater risk of retaliation and loss of employment.

The code of ethics asks the engineer first to notify the employer or client and then any appropriate authority, so internal comes before external.

Conditions for blowing the whistle, critical loyalty and impacts

Conditions that must be met

beyond the slides The standard conditions come from the ethicist Richard De George. They answer the question: when is a person morally justified in blowing the whistle against an employer? Papers ask for three, so learn these three first and the extra two as a bonus.

  1. The harm is serious and considerable. The wrongdoing must threaten serious harm to the public or to others, for example a defect that can kill. Trivial complaints do not justify going against the employer.
  2. The matter has been reported internally first. The person has told the immediate superior and, if that failed, has used all available internal channels up to the highest authority. External whistleblowing comes only after these fail.
  3. The evidence is documented and convincing. The person has good evidence that would persuade a reasonable, impartial observer that the harm is real. Rumour is not enough.
  4. Extra: The person has good reason to believe that going public will actually prevent the harm. If it will achieve nothing, the cost to the whistleblower is hard to justify.
  5. Extra: The motive is good faith concern for the public, not revenge, personal gain or spite.

Watch out. The question bank has the true-or-false statement "To qualify as a whistleblower, one must be an expert in the field in which they suspect illegal acts to be occurring." This is false. What is needed is reasonable belief supported by evidence, not expert status. A clerk who sees fraud can blow the whistle.

2013/14 Q4a and 2011/12 Q4a · 6 marksIdentify and explain three (3) essential conditions for one intending to "blow the whistle" against his or her employer.

1. The harm must be serious. The wrongdoing must threaten serious and considerable harm to the public, such as danger to life, health or safety. A minor policy dispute does not justify whistleblowing.

2. Internal channels must be exhausted. The person must first report the matter to the immediate superior and use all internal channels. External whistleblowing is a last resort when the organisation fails to act. This matches the code, which asks the engineer first to notify the employer or client.

3. There must be documented evidence. The person must have sufficient, documented evidence that would convince a reasonable, impartial observer. Rumour or suspicion is not enough.

Two further conditions, if time allows: there must be a reasonable chance of success in preventing the harm, and the motive must be good faith concern for the public.

Critical loyalty

beyond the slides Critical loyalty is loyalty to an employer that is not blind obedience. The loyal employee is committed to the organisation's real, legitimate interests and long-term good, and therefore speaks up, questions decisions and reports wrongdoing when it would harm the organisation, its customers or the public. It contrasts with uncritical or blind loyalty, where the employee obeys every instruction and keeps quiet about wrongdoing. The key idea is that criticism through the right channels is a form of loyalty: a company that sells unsafe products will eventually suffer lawsuits, fines and loss of trust, so the engineer who reports the fault is protecting the employer. This is how the engineer can reconcile whistleblowing with the duty to act as a "faithful agent or trustee" of the employer (Set 4, model rules).

2013/14 Q4c and 2011/12 Q4c · 3 marksWhat do you understand by "critical loyalty" to an employer?

Critical loyalty is loyalty to an employer that is not blind obedience. The employee stays committed to the organisation's legitimate interests but is willing to question and criticise decisions and to report wrongdoing, through the proper channels, when they would harm the organisation or the public.

It differs from uncritical loyalty, which means doing whatever the employer says. Example: an engineer who reports a safety defect to management is being loyal, because shipping the unsafe product would eventually damage the company.

Impacts on the whistleblower

The 2013/14 paper (Q4d; marks not legible in the scan, 7 by subtraction from the 20-mark total) asks: Discuss the most likely impacts on the whistle blower in an organization after they have revealed information. The impacts are mostly negative for the person, though some are positive.

  • Retaliation and dismissal. Sacking, demotion, transfer to a worse post, denial of promotion, or non-renewal of a contract.
  • Harassment and isolation. Colleagues who fear for their own jobs may shun the person, and management may bully or monitor them.
  • Blacklisting. Difficulty getting a new job in the same industry because employers see the person as a troublemaker. In Jenny's case (section t06) this is the same fear a whistleblower like Jenny faces.
  • Financial and legal strain. Loss of income, legal costs, and possible lawsuits for breach of confidentiality or defamation.
  • Psychological and family stress. Anxiety, depression, and strain on family relationships.
  • Positive effects. Possible protection under whistleblower laws, support from the professional body, vindication when the wrong is proved, public respect, and reform of the organisation.
2013/14 Q4d · marks as printed, garbledDiscuss the most likely impacts on the whistle blower in an organization after they have revealed information.

1. Retaliation. The most likely impact is retaliation by the employer: dismissal, demotion, denial of promotion or transfer to a less important post.

2. Isolation and harassment. Colleagues and managers may isolate, harass or bully the whistleblower, who is seen as disloyal.

3. Blacklisting and loss of income. The person may be blacklisted in the industry, find it hard to get another job, and face financial hardship and legal costs.

4. Stress. There is psychological and family stress.

5. Possible positive outcomes. If the wrong is proved, the person may be protected by law and vindicated, gain public respect, and the organisation may reform.

Case: Dr James Hansen and NASA

On 29 January 2006 the New York Times reported that Dr James E. Hansen, a NASA climate scientist and Director of the Goddard Institute for Space Studies, said NASA headquarters officials had told public affairs staff to review his coming lectures, papers and website postings and his requests for interviews from journalists. He said the administration of President Bush was trying to stop him from speaking out since he gave a lecture calling for prompt reductions in emissions of greenhouse gases linked to global warming. Hansen said: "They feel their job is to censor information going out to the public." NASA's deputy assistant administrator for public affairs, Dean Acosta, replied that there was no effort to silence Hansen, that this was the usual way of operating at NASA, and that NASA promotes openness. The paper noted that Hansen had issued public warnings about the long-term threat of heat-trapping emissions since 1988, and that he had run-ins with appointees in various administrations. The paper asks you to identify Hansen's dilemma and say whether he acted unethically in insisting on speaking out.

2011/12 Q4(d) · [reconstructed from garbled scan] (i) 3 marks; (ii) marks not shown(i) Identify Dr Hansen's ethical dilemma. (ii) Did Hansen do something unethical by insisting on speaking out? Support your answer.

(i) The dilemma. Hansen must choose between loyalty and obedience to his employer (NASA, a government agency that wants to control public statements) and his duty to the public and to scientific truth. If he obeys, information about a threat to the public welfare (global warming) is kept from the public. If he speaks, he risks discipline or dismissal and breaches the employer's media policy.

(ii) Was he unethical? No. Duty to the public welfare comes first: the code holds the public's safety, health and welfare paramount and requires truthful public statements. On a deontological view he followed the duty of honesty and the duty to inform. On a utilitarian view the benefit to millions from informed climate policy outweighs the cost to NASA's image and to Hansen himself. He also acted as a scientist whose findings were his own professional judgment, he had a history of consistent warnings, and the harm is serious. The weak point is whether he exhausted internal channels first. If he had already raised the matter internally, the external route can be defended as a last resort.

For the full BART whistleblower question (2017 Q4D, 6 marks: Use two different ethical theories to explain/justify the actions of a whistle-blower), see section t07. For Marlinspike and surveillance work, see section t18.

Conflict of interest: meaning, actual versus potential

A conflict of interest is a situation in which a person's private interest, such as financial gain, a family tie, friendship or another loyalty, conflicts with, or could appear to conflict with, the professional duty to act in the best interest of the employer, client or public, so that the person's professional judgment may be compromised. The key idea is that the engineer must act as a faithful agent or trustee, and a competing interest threatens objectivity. Note that a conflict of interest is a situation, not an act. The wrong comes when it is hidden or when the engineer acts on the private interest.

Actual versus potential

TypeMeaningExample
Actual conflict of interestThe conflict exists now: the person has the competing interest and is in a position to decide or influence a matter, so judgment is in fact affected or is being tested.An engineer on a tender panel evaluates a bid from a company owned by her brother.
Potential conflict of interestThe competing interest exists, but no decision has yet been affected; the situation could become an actual conflict in future.An engineer holds shares in a supplier that the company might use next year, and no purchase is pending.

beyond the slides Some textbooks add an apparent (or perceived) conflict: an outsider could reasonably think the judgment is compromised even if it is not. Set 4 clause 2 covers all three: disclose "potential conflicts of interest or any other circumstances that could influence or appear to influence" professional judgment.

The Set 4 model rules (slide wording)

The Set 4 slides give these conflict-of-interest clauses, grouped by who the obligation is owed to. Learn them as quotations.

  • Employers and clients, rule 1. "Engineers shall not solicit or accept direct or indirect considerations, financial or otherwise, from contractors, their agents, or other parties while performing work for employers or clients."
  • Employers and clients, rule 2. "Engineers shall disclose to their employers or clients potential conflicts of interest or any other circumstances that could influence or appear to influence their professional judgment or their service quality."
  • Full disclosure. "An engineer shall not accept financial or other compensation from more than one party for services rendered on one project unless the details are fully disclosed and agreed by all parties."
  • Government conflicts of interest. "To avoid conflicts of interest, engineers shall not solicit or accept a professional contract from a governmental body on which a principal or officer of their firm serves as a member. An engineer who is a principal or employee of a private firm and who serves as a member of a governmental body shall not participate in decisions relating to the professional services solicited or provided by the firm to the governmental body."
  • Obligations to other engineers, conflicts of interest. "Engineers shall not directly or indirectly give, solicit, or receive any gift or commission, or other valuable consideration, in order to obtain work, and shall not make contribution to any political body with intent of influencing the award of contract by governmental body."
  • Obligation to society, the duty of full disclosure. Engineers shall not express a professional opinion on matters for which they are motivated or paid unless they identify the parties on whose behalf they speak and reveal those parties' interest.
  • Canon: act for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees, and avoid conflicts of interest. See section t09 for the full list of obligations and section t11 for the canons.

How to handle a conflict of interest

beyond the slides Four steps: (1) identify the conflict early; (2) disclose it in writing to the employer, client or committee; (3) withdraw or recuse yourself from the decision, or divest the competing interest; (4) let someone independent decide and keep a record. Disclosure alone is not always enough: if the interest is large, you must step aside.

2013/14 Q5a · 2 marks; 2011/12 Q5a · 2 marksWhat do you understand by "conflict of interest"?

A conflict of interest is a situation in which a person's private or personal interest (financial, family or another loyalty) conflicts with their professional duty to act in the best interest of the employer, client or public, so that their professional judgment may be, or may appear to be, compromised.

Example: an engineer chosen to evaluate bids who owns shares in one of the bidding firms.

2013/14 Q5b, 2011/12 Q5b, CAT 2 2013/14 Q1a, CAT 2 2014/15 Q1a · 2 to 4 marksDistinguish between actual and potential conflicts of interest.

An actual conflict of interest exists now: the person has a private interest that competes with their duty and is in a position to influence the decision, so their judgment is affected or at risk. Example: an engineer awards a contract to his own firm.

A potential conflict of interest is one that could arise in the future: the competing interest exists but has not yet affected any decision. Example: an engineer holds shares in a supplier the employer may use later.

A potential conflict must still be disclosed, because it can become actual, and the code says engineers shall disclose potential conflicts.

CAT 2 2014/15 Q1b and CAT 2 2013/14 Q1b · 2 to 4 marksDescribe two unique situations in which an employee may experience an actual conflict of interest.

1. Awarding or evaluating a contract involving own interests. An engineer in charge of choosing a supplier or contractor has a financial interest or family tie in one of the bidders, for example shares in the firm or a relative who owns it. The duty to select the best bid conflicts with private gain.

2. Working for a competitor or having a second job. An employee who does outside consulting or part-time work for a competitor or a client of the employer, or uses employer time and information for it, faces a conflict between loyalty to the employer and personal income.

Other situations that can replace either: accepting gifts or commissions from a contractor; being paid by two parties on the same project without disclosure.

2013/14 Q5c and 2011/12 Q5c · 6 marksIdentify three (3) unique situations that can present conflict of interest for an engineer.

1. Gifts, bribes and commissions. An engineer who accepts gifts, commissions or favours from contractors or suppliers may be influenced in choosing them. The code says engineers shall not solicit or accept such considerations while working for an employer or client.

2. Financial or family interest in a bidder or supplier. An engineer who owns shares in, or is related to the owner of, a firm competing for the employer's contract cannot judge it objectively.

3. Dual roles and double payment. An engineer who is paid by more than one party for the same project without disclosure, or a part-time government engineer who also runs a private consulting firm bidding for government work, serves two masters. The code allows double payment only if fully disclosed and agreed by all parties, and forbids a government-body member from taking part in decisions about their own firm's services.

(Other valid situations: using employer's confidential information for a private business; moonlighting for a competitor.)

Say it like this:

A conflict of interest is a situation where a private interest conflicts with professional duty and may compromise professional judgment; it is actual when it exists now and potential when it could arise, and it must be disclosed to the employer or client.

Set 4 rule 2 on conflict of interest (employers and clients).
Engineers shall disclose to their employers or clients potential conflicts of interest or any other circumstances that could influence or appear to influence their professional judgment or their service quality.
Set 4 rule on full disclosure (double compensation).
An engineer shall not accept financial or other compensation from more than one party for services rendered on one project unless the details are fully disclosed and agreed by all parties.
Three situations that present conflict of interest.
Accepting gifts or commissions from contractors; financial or family interest in a bidder or supplier; dual roles or double payment on one project.

Conflict of interest cases: Engineer A and B, and Maggie and Red Sky

Case 1: Engineer A, Engineer B and Smithtown

Engineer A is the part-time town engineer for Smithtown and also runs a consulting engineering practice. With A's advice and agreement, the town hires Engineer B to design a local road project. After B starts the preliminary design, A, acting as town engineer, reviews B's work and becomes convinced that B's performance does not meet the standards in B's contract with the town. B is terminated under the terms of his contract. A then offers, and Smithtown agrees, that A's own firm will do the road design. The questions: was it ethical for A to tell the town that B's performance fell short? Was it ethical for A to offer and agree to do the design work?

2013/14 Q5(d) · 8 marksEngineer A is the part-time town engineer for Smithtown and also has a consulting engineering practice. [Case as above.] 1. Was it ethical for Engineer A to contact Smithtown and advise the town that Engineer B's performance did not meet the standards outlined in the contract? 2. Was it ethical for Engineer A to offer and agree to perform the road design work for Smithtown?

Question 1: Yes, it was ethical. As town engineer, A is the town's faithful agent. His job is to review the consultant's work and protect the town from substandard design. Reporting B's failure to meet the contract was therefore his professional duty to the client and to the public who will use the road. He must report it objectively and truthfully, with evidence from the contract standards, and not simply to damage B, since the code forbids maliciously injuring other engineers' reputations. Nothing in this step on its own involves a conflict.

Question 2: No, it was not ethical as done. A has an actual conflict of interest. He holds two roles: the town's engineer, who advises on selecting and reviewing consultants, and a private consultant who stands to gain the contract. He criticised B and then took B's work. This creates the appearance that he judged B harshly in order to win the job, and so it can influence or appear to influence his professional judgment. It also damages public trust in the town's engineer.

What A should have done. He should have disclosed his interest in writing to the town, withdrawn from any decision about who replaces B, and let the town choose through an open, independent process, or recommended another firm. If the town, fully informed, still wanted his firm, the decision should have been made by someone other than A, so the selection does not depend on his own advice. This follows the rule that an engineer serving a governmental body shall not take part in decisions about services provided by his own firm.

Conclusion. Reporting B's failure was ethical; offering and agreeing to do the design himself was a conflict of interest and unethical unless disclosed and decided by an independent party.

Case 2: Maggie and Red Sky

The scan of this question is badly garbled. Reconstructed: Maggie works for Harold Telecom and has been placed in charge of finding a firm to design and produce promotional posters and billboard ads for the launch of a new product line in two months. Red Sky, an advertising and marketing company, is one of the firms expected to bid. Maggie heads the team that will select the most suitable firm. The sentence that states Maggie's link to Red Sky is lost in the scan, but the question is clearly a conflict-of-interest case, so the answer assumes she has a personal tie to Red Sky (a relative, friend or financial interest). Part (i) asks her ethical dilemma (4 marks), part (ii) what she should do (4 marks).

2011/12 Q5(d) · 4 + 4 marks · [reconstructed from garbled scan]Maggie is in charge of the search for a firm to design and produce promotional posters and billboard ads when Harold Telecom launches a new line of products in two months. Red Sky is one of the companies expected to bid. As head of the team selecting the most suitable firm: (i) Identify Maggie's ethical dilemma. (ii) What do you suggest Maggie should do?

(i) The dilemma. Maggie has a duty to her employer, Harold Telecom, to pick the best firm on merit, as its faithful agent. But her personal link to Red Sky gives her a private interest in the result. This is a conflict of interest: she may favour Red Sky, or be seen to favour it, or she may be unfair to Red Sky to prove her fairness. Her objectivity and the fairness of the bidding are at stake, and so are the interests of competing bidders and the company. It is a potential conflict now because the selection has not happened, and it becomes actual once she takes part in judging the bids.

(ii) What she should do.

  1. Disclose the relationship to her employer (her manager or the company's ethics or procurement office) in writing and early, before the bids are opened.
  2. Recuse herself from evaluating and voting on Red Sky's bid, or step down from heading the selection team if the link is strong.
  3. Let another member or a neutral party run the evaluation, using transparent, written criteria (price, quality, track record, delivery time).
  4. Keep a record of the process so that the decision can be audited. Red Sky should compete on equal terms and neither gain nor lose because of her.
  5. Make sure she does not accept gifts or favours from Red Sky or any other bidder.

With the time limit of two months, there is still time to follow this process, so urgency is no excuse.

The Phillip case (an employee reading a client's e-mails, CAT 2 2013/14 Q1c: Describe Phillip's ethical dilemma (3 marks) and What should Phillip as young professional do in these circumstances? (3 marks)) and Jenny's case (CAT 2 2014/15 Q2, 12 marks: Describe Jenny's ethical dilemma and explain what should she do as a young professional in her circumstances?) are dilemma-resolution cases about reporting wrongdoing; they belong to section t06. They use the same idea as this section: weigh duty to the employer against duty to the public, and report through proper channels first.
